en: The Glorious Garland of Verses on the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā]

I take refuge in that Lord of the Great Goddess, who performs the play of creating the universe and other such acts, who is sinless, the abode of all auspicious qualities, the one to be worshipped, the bestower of liberation, and the ultimate goal.
May the lotus feet of Rāmānuja shine forever in my mind, by whose fragrance the peerless Vaiṣṇava lineage shines resplendent in the world. || 2 ||

Because it protects the noble path at the end of the three Vedas, this [work] bestows the highest good and nothing else on earth; by relying upon it, the wise cross the ocean of existence with ease. (3)
May that most excellent teacher, Śrī Rāghava, through meditation upon whose feet I have attained existence with my impurities destroyed, grant me intelligence regarding this commentary.
May the great lord of ascetics, the younger brother of Śrī Raṅgarāmānuja, who is solely devoted to the inquiry into the meaning of Vedānta, shine eternally within my heart. (5)

Having heard from my teacher the principal meanings of the topics (*adhikaraṇa*) of the illustrious *Bhāṣya*, I shall now write them down according to my understanding, with the permission of my preceptor. (6)
I do not undertake such a task for the sake of proclaiming my own scholarship and so forth;
rather, it is out of a desire for the immediate fruit known as the contemplation of the meaning of the Bhāṣya. (7)
This speech of this fool may indeed bring joy to the great;
but does not the word of a female parrot bring delight even to the wise? (8)
Vyāsa, the knower of reality, caused his own disciple, the sage Jaimini, to determine the meaning of the Vedas through a collection of sixteen chapters of aphorisms.
In the *Dvayayugādhyāyaśārīraśāstra*, Viṣṇu himself, as Vyāsa,
has correctly expounded that Brahman which is to be known through Vedānta.
The Lord Rāmānuja Muni himself, an incarnation of Vyāsa,
composed a great and wonderful commentary on the sūtras contained in that very chapter.
By the first pair [of verses], the causality of Īśvara is established; by the latter pair, the means and the fruit are stated in succession. (12)
In the first chapter, the *Samanvaya-adhyāya*, through the determination of the purport of the scriptural texts, it was established that Brahman is the cause of the entire universe. (13)
In that regard, it was established in the first chapter [the *Ayogavyavaccheda-pāda*] through an investigation of various scriptural passages that Brahman alone is indeed the cause. (14)
First, here in this section consisting of four sūtras, the argument that the treatise should not be commenced is thoroughly refuted by means of reasonings consistent with valid cognition.
Thus ends the introduction.
The First Section: The Enquiry into Brahman (Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa)
Oṃ. Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into Brahman.
This is stated immediately after the knowledge of ritual action, which yields results that are limited and impermanent;
for that very reason, Brahman, whose fruit is infinite, is said to be the object of inquiry. || 16 ||

In this section on the qualification for inquiry (*jijñāsādhikāra*), the objection that the scripture should not be commenced because linguistic proficiency is impossible is refuted by sound arguments. (17)
Because derivation is impossible without depending on the linguistic usage of elders, and because such usage is the cause for knowing the meaning of an action [in that context]. (18)
It is certain that the authority of a word lies solely in its capacity to convey something to be accomplished (kārya);
since Brahman is of an already established nature (siddharūpa), the Śruti cannot be a means of knowledge regarding it. || 19 ||
Therefore, the view that "an investigation into this should not be undertaken here" is not correct;
for [the Lord] points out the various objects situated before him by means of a finger-gesture. (20)
By employing various words that denote those respective objects, Janaka and others diligently instruct children, saying, "Understand this," and so forth. (21)
Therefore, they themselves gradually come to possess knowledge of the power of words and their meanings, since the acquisition of proficiency is possible through such means as these. (22)
The authority of all scriptures, up to and including the Vedas, is well-established once Brahman is proven;
therefore, it has been demonstrated that the inquiry into Brahman (Brahmamīmāṃsā) must indeed be undertaken. || 23 ||
Thus, the objection and the established conclusion (siddhānta) are indicated in the first aphorism,
because the status of Brahman as the subject of inquiry is demonstrated here.
Thus concludes the section on the inquiry [into Brahman].
The Section on "Origin and so forth" (Janmādyadhikaraṇa).
[The Brahman is that] from which there is the origin and so forth of this [world].
"What is the definition of this Brahman which is said to be the object of inquiry?"—it is for the fulfillment of such an expectation that the definition of Brahman is stated. (25)
In the Taittirīyaka, the following passages are recited: "That from which the birth, sustenance, and dissolution of this world proceed... (26).
The definition of Brahman, such as being the cause of birth and so forth, is stated;
however, Brahman cannot be apprehended through its definition or through verbal testimony alone. (27)
Whether as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), it would likewise be impossible for birth and the other [characteristics] to serve as the definition of this Brahman. (28)
For, on the view that they are qualifiers, because they serve to differentiate, Brahman—differentiated by those three—would likewise become manifold. (29)
In the second case as well, the known form of the object to be characterized is required;
since that is absent in the case of Brahman, this position too is not tenable. (30)
Thus, Brahman cannot be apprehended through its defining characteristics;
therefore, the argument that it is not a fit object of inquiry is untenable. (31)
It is not correct to attribute multiplicity to this Brahman by means of non-contradictory qualifiers, such as differences in time or its being the cause of birth and so forth. (32)
And that entity which has been established elsewhere as the Lord of Śrī and so forth is here made known as the referent of the word "Brahman" by means of those defining characteristics. (33)
Therefore, the triad of being the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world] constitutes the definition of this Brahman both individually and collectively. (34)
Thus concludes the section concerning "origination and so forth" (Janmādyadhikaraṇa).
The Section on Scripture Being the Source [of Brahman] (Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa)
Because [Brahman] has the sacred scripture as its source.
Although Brahman can be understood through its defining characteristics,
nevertheless, that Brahman is to be known by means of the instrument of inference.
Therefore, that which is known through scripture must be unknowable by any other means of knowledge;
consequently, the authority of statements such as "because" [of this] is not applicable here. (36)
Do not say so; for Brahman, who is desired to be proven as omniscient, omnipotent, and distinct from the individual soul (jīva), cannot be established by means of inference.

Therefore, because Brahman is not cognizable through other means of knowledge and is the exclusive object of scripture, there is no impairment whatsoever to the authority of the scriptures regarding it. (38)
Thus concludes the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] entitled "Having Scripture as its Source" (Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa).
The Section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa)
But that [Brahman is the cause], because of the harmony [of all scriptural texts].
Even if it were unattained by other means of knowledge, there would be no connection [of those means] with activity and so forth;
furthermore, because Brahman is of an established nature, it cannot be of the nature of a purpose [to be achieved]. || 39 ||
Since it is impossible for the scripture to possess authority regarding that [self], the claim that he cannot be enlightened by it is utterly inconsistent. (40)
The status of the scripture as a means of valid knowledge arises from its connection with that [Brahman] as the human goal;
for Brahman indeed exists, and the Vedāntas lead a person toward the Supreme. (41)
For they indeed make known the nature of transcendent bliss,
just as one possesses the knowledge of the life of a virtuous son, father, and so forth.
Even such knowledge of Brahman would become a human goal (puruṣārtha) in its own right,
for it consists of this most exalted human purpose which bestows supreme bliss.

Because it is connected with the scripture through its nature as bliss and by way of being that which makes [it] known, that Brahman is established as having the scripture as its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 44 ||
Thus concludes the section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa).
The Section on "Because of Beholding" (Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa)
Because of seeing; [the cause] is not that which is not based on scripture.
Thus has the justification for the commencement of the treatise been established by means of these four aphorisms;
now, the doctrine that Pradhāna and other principles are the cause [of the world] will be refuted in due order.
In the *Ṣaḍvidyā*, the causality of insentient *prakṛti* is heard [in scripture].
How can there be the possibility of the cause of the world being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)? (46)
Thus, to quell such an objection, the section concerning the "Iksati" (He sees) was introduced;
for this world, which consists of the three qualities (guṇas), has such a nature as its reality.
In that case, the material cause would have to be of the same genus as its effect;
for instance, in passages such as "That fire thought," the act of seeing is heard to be figurative. (48)
Even in the sentence "It thought" (tadaikṣata), the act of seeing must be figurative;
for here, because of the statement of the proposition and the illustrative example, it is inferential.
The view that the Pradhāna alone is what is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being) and so forth is an incorrect opinion;
for the Pradhāna is not the meaning of the word "Sat," because scripture does not attribute the quality of being a seer to that which exists [as the Pradhāna]. (50)

Because it is impossible for Brahman, whose nature consists of both the conscious and the unconscious, to possess a commonality with all things, and because the reason provided here does not establish the possibility of primary "seeing" (īkṣā) [on his part]. || 51 ||

And because there is no cognition through inference regarding the scope of the Chāndogya scripture, the Supreme Person is what is denoted by the word "Being" (sat) in the sentences of the Satvidyā. (52)
If it is argued that [the term "Self"] is used in a secondary sense, we say no, because of the word "Self."
"It beheld" (tadaikṣata) must be secondary because it occurs in association with "secondary beholding";
[we reply: not so, because in this case, which is denoted by the word *sat*, the agent of beholding is designated by the word *ātman*.

In this context, the primary "seeing" pertains to the Self; even the seeing of fire and the other elements is [included] because they are essentially of the nature of Being (Sat), according to the Śruti: "That has that as its essence. (54)
Because liberation is taught for one who is devoted to that.

For the individual soul (jīva) who is devoted to the worship of the Real, the supreme fruit known as liberation (mokṣa) is heard [in scripture]; therefore, Brahman must be denoted by "the Real" (sat), and not by "the Unborn" (aja).
And because there is no mention of [the Self] as something to be abandoned.
If that which is intended here as the primary cause is Pradhāna,
then its status as something to be abandoned would have to be stated, because it is opposed to liberation.
And therefore, the Pradhāna is not intended [as the subject] because it is not stated as something to be abandoned;
for that would contradict the initial proposition.
By this, the proposition that "the unheard becomes heard" is contradicted here. || 57 ||
For here, by means of the knowledge of the six forms of consciousness, the knowledge of the expansion of the conscious and the unconscious is indeed promised;
if this is so, then the primary cause must be explained with respect to the hosts of individual souls.
Since the Pradhāna is not the cause [of cognition], those [objects] are not known by means of that [Pradhāna’s] intellect;
therefore, that proposition would be inconsistent, and for this reason, it is not unborn.
Because of the merging [of the soul] during deep sleep.

Even though the cause for the dissolution of the consciousness of one in deep sleep exists [in the form of pradhāna], the scriptural statement regarding its dissolution would be contradicted, because pradhāna cannot be the cause with respect to consciousness. (60)
Because of the commonality of destiny.
And because this [text] has the same meaning as the statements of other Upaniṣads, the Pradhāna cannot be the cause; the Supreme Brahman alone is the cause.
And because it is so stated in scripture.
In this very Sāman, it is heard: "From the Self [comes] the vital breath," and so forth;
therefore, because of its preeminence, the omniscient Brahman alone is the cause of all else.
Thus concludes the section on "Iksati" (the one who sees).
The Section Concerning that Which Consists of Bliss (Ānandamayādhikaraṇa)
The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of the repetition.

"Since primary seeing is impossible for that which is insentient, it cannot be the cause"—this being stated, the objection that "then let the individual soul (jīva) be [the cause]" is here refuted. (63)

In the Ānandavallī, there is recited the passage beginning with "Thus, different from the one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya), there is another inner Self consisting of bliss (ānandamaya). (64)
And that living being (jīva) consists of bliss, because scripture declares it to be the "embodied one" (śārīra);
moreover, this state of being embodied is unique to the jīva, and therefore belongs to him alone. (65)
"In this regard, creation preceded by deliberation is well-established because of [the Creator's] sentience;
do not think so, for here the Supreme, consisting of bliss, is distinct from the individual soul. (66)

Due to the absence of any excellence [in the individual soul], such a state of union with bliss as is attained through yoga by one who has practiced bliss cannot possibly belong to this living being (jīva). || 67 ||
The status of being the body belongs primarily to Brahman alone, which consists of both consciousness and the unconscious;
therefore, it is proclaimed here that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is the Supreme Self.
"If it be argued that [the Self] is not [denoted by the word 'Self'] because the word refers to a modification, we say no, because of its predominance."

If it is argued that because the suffix *mayaṭ* here signifies a modification (*vikāra*), the Supreme Being, being unmodified, cannot be expressed by this term—this is not so; for this *mayaṭ* indicates abundance (*prācurya*). (69)

The suffix *mayaṭ* used previously is of the same nature; therefore, this Supreme Person is one who possesses an abundance of bliss, as stated in the passage beginning "from whom speech [turns back]. (70)
And because its cause is designated.
And because of the scriptural statement that "He alone causes bliss to the individual soul," it is therefore said that this one, whose nature is bliss, must be different from the individual soul.
And it is proclaimed as being based precisely on the wording of the mantra.
For it is Brahman alone that is celebrated here as expressed by the mantra beginning with "Truth" (satyam);
therefore, by the word "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), the Supreme who consists of bliss is meant.
It is not the other, because that is untenable.

The individual soul (jīva) that is distinct from Brahman cannot be mentioned in the words of the Mantras, because the property of being exclusively wise like Brahman would otherwise be untenable. (73)
And because there is a designation of difference.
Therefore, by the phrase "From that, verily," the distinction of this one consisting of bliss from the one consisting of consciousness is stated; hence, it is superior to the individual soul (jīva).
And because [the object] is directly perceived, there is no dependence on inference.
The creation of the world occurs through His volition; He has no dependence on anything else.
The individual soul (jīva), however, depends upon Him even for the slightest thing; therefore, He is the Supreme Person.
And in this [world], he teaches his union with that.

The yoga of bliss is said to belong to the individual soul (jīva) within that which consists of bliss; for this is known from such scriptural passages as "For it is only by tasting... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1). Therefore, [the Self] is held to be distinct from the individual soul.
Thus concludes the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa).
The Section on Internal [Dissolution] (Antaradhikaraṇa)
[The person] within [the sun and the eye is Brahman], because of the teaching of its attributes.
The causality of the soul in general was previously refuted; now, having raised that doubt regarding its specific form, it is rejected in this present argument. (77)

The person heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad in the passage beginning "He who is within," by virtue of having the eye and the sun as his abodes, is the individual soul (jīva) and is distinct [from the Supreme Self]. (78)
"Because it is heard that they possess bodies, the individual souls (jīvas) alone are indeed joined with them.
"Not so; for those abiding in the eye and the sun are the Supreme Self alone, and not others. (79)
Due to the teaching [of the Self] and the collection of qualities such as being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva), corporeality cannot indeed be the proof for being subject to karma. (80)
It is known by all the scriptures that his divine and auspicious form is non-material, corresponding to his own nature, and is assumed solely by his own will. (81)
And [the Self] is other [than the body], because there is a designation of difference.
Because of the teaching of difference through such statements as "He who is in the self," the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the Inner Self, distinct from the individual soul whose mouth is the sun. (82)
Thus ends the section on the intermediate state.
The Section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa)
It is space, because of its characteristic marks.
The cause, as an established entity, is determined to be distinct from both the conscious and the unconscious;
that it is "unattached" (asaṅgata) is the doctrine here refuted.

In passages such as "All [beings] are in the Sāman," that which is heard as the cause must be the ether (ākāśa), specifically the physical space (viyat), because of its usage in common worldly parlance.
Since there would otherwise be no determination as to from what the elements arise, the statement "from space" (ākāśāt) serves to provide that specific detail. (85)
It should not be thought that the Supreme Person is what is denoted here by the word "space";
for there are many scriptural indications that are exclusively characteristic of [the Supreme Person] as distinct from the elemental ether. (86)
For indeed, a sentence heard here has the form of a restatement of what is already established;
therefore, it depends upon the attainment [of its object] through another means of valid cognition.
Brahman, called Nārāyaṇa, awakens all measure;
because it expands through manifestation, it possesses that denotability by the word [ākāśa]. 88.
Thus concludes the section concerning the ether (ākāśa).
The Section Concerning the Vital Breath (Prāṇa)
For this very reason, [the word "breath" (prāṇa) refers to Brahman].
In the preceding section, the status of space as the cause of all things was refuted; here, the causality of wind asserted by others is likewise rejected. (89)
In this context, the scriptural passage beginning with "All these [beings] enter into breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.11.5) is heard;
and here, just like the word "ether" (ākāśa), the word "breath" (prāṇa) also denotes Brahman.

Because it is illustrated as if well-known through a mark that is unique [to the subject], there is here a greater degree of doubt regarding the existence of the collection of elements and so forth. (91)
"One might argue that because it is dependent on the vital breath (prāṇa), air should be considered the material cause [of sound];
however, that objection does not apply to stone and the like, nor to the nature of consciousness."
Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa).
The Section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa)
[The Brahman is] light, because of the mention of its feet.
Having thus refuted the causality of space and air in due order, the causality of fire is now rejected in this system of logic. (93)
Beyond this, in the sentence "the light beyond heaven," that which is heard to be exceedingly luminous must be the Cause, together with the gastric light.

"Because of the instruction regarding oneness, let that which is well-known as light be what is spoken of here."—Do not say so; that which is denoted by the word "light" here is Brahman alone, and nothing else. (95)
Because the preceding statement describes the state of moving through all beings, and because that [attribute] belongs to Brahman alone, as is well known from the Puruṣasūkta and other sources. (96)

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [meant here] because of the mention of a meter, we say no; for there is a scriptural teaching on the fixing of the mind [on the Self], and such is seen [in other passages].

If it is argued that the Gāyatrī metre mentioned in the preceding statement is what is being sung here by means of the Ṛk verse that explains its meaning, and therefore that [verse] is not Brahman—no, that is not so. (97)
For the sake of the result, the perception of equality with the *gāyatrī* is enjoined; for this four-footed Brahman, there is such a balance with it. 98.
In the Saṃvarga-vidyā and other instances, the connection with meters is observed despite the similarity [of the subject matter];
and it is likewise because the designation of "feet" (pādas) consisting of the elements and so forth is logically consistent.
This statement, "She is four-footed," serves to make known that she has the elements and so forth as her feet. (99)
This [attainment] is possible only in this Brahman denoted by the word *gāyatrī*.
If it be argued that it is not so because of the difference in instruction, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case.
The repetition "divo divi" [is used] because of the distinction between different meanings and case endings. || 100 ||
It is not the case that Brahman, as previously heard, is not recognized here;
for it is not so, since the nature of the object is one and the same despite the two modes of instruction. (101)
Since recognition is uncontradicted, it is stated here that [the self] is indeed other [than the body];
furthermore, it is certain that the instruction regarding the identity with the gastric fire is solely for the sake of a specific result. (102)
Furthermore, the nature of the fire-god as being identical with the Supreme Self has been declared in the Gītā;
therefore, it is firmly established here that he is indeed the Supreme Self. 103.
Thus concludes the section concerning light.
The Section Concerning Indra and Prāṇa.
Likewise, the vital breath [is Brahman], because of the accompanying presence.
The causality of the sun and other luminaries, designated by the term "light," has already been refuted; now, the status of Indra as their lord is being rejected. (104)
In the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, within the discourse beginning with "Pratardana," that which is denoted by the terms Indra and Prāṇa is taught as the object of meditation for the sake of liberation. (105)

The word "Indra" refers to the individual soul (jīva) alone, because it is well-known to denote that; likewise, the word "prāṇa" also refers to it. Thus, in this context, he [the teacher] intends the meditation upon one's own self.
He taught the most beneficial means for attaining immortality;
for the worship of the Cause alone is the cause for the attainment of immortality. (107)
From the scriptural statement "of him, for so long," it is known that the cause is this very Indra, whose status as a living being (jīva) is well-established; such is the certainty. (108)

It is not so; the one denoted by the words "Indra" and "Prāṇa" is not merely the individual soul (jīva), but rather, on account of those two terms, it is another entity—Brahman—which is the subject introduced. || 109 ||
Because of the scriptural declarations of its being established in its own nature, bliss, immortality, and so forth;

if it be argued that [the Self taught here] is not the one taught by the Vākya-kartṛ (the speaker of the Chāndogya), we say no, for in this [text], there is an abundance of internal (adhyātma) connections.
This [teaching] concerns the very self whose nature as the living principle (jīva) has been recognized, regarding its state as the object of worship.
Therefore, it is said that the individual soul (jīva) alone, which was introduced as the object of meditation, is what is being described here.
Not so; for the attributes mentioned in this scripture are consistent only with the Supreme Self.

The state of being the object of meditation for the sake of liberation, the state of being the substratum of all, and the state of being the impeller of actions—these and other such qualities indeed belong to the Supreme. (112)
But the instruction is given from the perspective of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva.

Having understood from the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa and other passages that the Self is the inner controller (śarīrin), and from such phrases as "by this living soul" that words denote the individual soul (jīva); || 113 ||
From the statement, "Worship Me as the final goal," he taught that his own body is the Supreme Brahman to be worshipped. (114)
Vāmadeva and other preeminent knowers of the supreme self likewise speak in many ways, such as "I am Manu, I am all," and so forth. (115)

If it be argued that [the Self spoken of here] is not the Supreme Self because of the indicative marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), we say no; for there is a threefoldness of meditation, and because those [marks] are applicable here due to their being resorted to [for the purpose of meditation].

Because the characteristics pertaining to the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) are observed here, there is no definitive conclusion regarding the meaning on account of the abundance of internal (adhyātma) connections mentioned previously. || 116 ||
Do not think so, for here the meditation is intended to be threefold:
[meditation] on [Brahman] in its own essential nature, as the Self of the individual soul (jīvātman), and likewise as having that [soul] as its body.
Thus, the worship of the Supreme Self is threefold by virtue of its being composed of the vital breaths;
and for the sake of instructing that [worship], it is spoken of through various specific terms in a threefold manner. (118)
Moreover, this threefold meditation is heard of elsewhere in the Śruti as well;
therefore, this context is intended to teach such meditations. (119)
Therefore, here the Supreme Self—other than the individual soul (jīva), denoted by the words Indra and Prāṇa, and possessing the body of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed—is taught. || 120 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Indra and Prāṇa.
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter.
The Second Quarter of the First Chapter.
The Section on Universal Renown (Sarvatraprasiddhyadhikaraṇa).
Because the teaching is established everywhere, the section concerning passages containing less clear marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth has been examined.
Now, in this [third] section, a collection of passages with indistinct marks is being investigated. (121)
Since it has been stated that the status of being the cause and the status of being the object of worship belong to the one whose body is prāṇa,
the possibility that both of these might belong to the individual soul (jīva) is raised and then refuted.
In passages such as "All this, indeed," [the Self] is heard to be the essence of all;
for it is the individual soul (jīva) alone in whom the identity with everything is possible.
The state of being Brahmā and all other [entities] arises for that very [Self] through limiting adjuncts (upādhi);
for that Supreme [Self], which is untouched by defects, such a state is not logically possible.
Furthermore, the word "Brahman" is sometimes employed even for the individual soul (jīva) in certain scriptural passages;
this is because birth and so forth have their cause in the karma belonging to that [soul], and because [the world] originates from it (tajjala).
It is not a sound view that even the statement regarding the cause would be logical;
for the Supreme Person, Brahman, is declared to be the Self within all things. (126)

Since that very [nature] which is well-known in another context is restated here, having restated its being produced from that and so forth, its being caused by that and its being identical to that is stated. (127)

For the individual self (jīvātman), which assumes forms such as gods or mortals through the performance of karma, there can be no [birth and so forth] in the Vedāntic statements, since birth and other states are heard of [in scripture] only in relation to that [which is not the self]. 128.
He alone should be the one denoted here by the word "Brahman," for He is the Supreme Person;
since the conscious and unconscious entities constitute the body of Brahman, [the term applies] to the Embodied One.

Consequently, the defects residing in the body would not belong to him, and thus he would be entirely free from defect; however, the universal identity of the individual soul (jīva) that has been taught would then become untenable. (130)
Because identity is impossible between those [individual souls] which are distinct from their respective bodies, they cannot be mutually identical;
therefore, in this context, it is the Supreme Self alone that is intended by the word "Brahman. (131)
And because the intended qualities are applicable [to Brahman].

Furthermore, all these qualities, such as being mind-made and so forth, when intended [as attributes], are possible only in the Supreme Being, who is endowed with the power of true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatā). || 132 ||
But because of the impossibility [of its being so], it is not the embodied soul.
Because these qualities are impossible in this embodied being, this is not the embodied self; rather, it is the Supreme Brahman that is celebrated here.
And because of the designation of [the Self] as both the object and the agent of action.
"He who thinks, 'I shall attain [it],' is the object of meditation and is described as that which is to be attained;
the individual soul (jīva) is described as the attainer. Therefore, the Supreme Person is other than the individual soul. (134)
Because of the distinction of the word.

In the statement "This is my Self," the embodied soul is expressed by the genitive case; however, the one to be meditated upon is the Supreme Person, who is distinct from that, as indicated by the nominative case. (135)
And because of Smṛti.
Furthermore, the Smṛti text beginning with "I am all" declares that the individual soul is the worshiper and the Supreme Self is the object of worship; therefore, the soul is distinct from Him. (136)

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the Supreme Self] because of its having a small abode and because of the designation of such [attributes], we say no; for it is to be perceived as such, and it is like space.

If it is argued that this [Brahman] is not the Supreme because of designations such as "not small" and "having few abodes," we say no; for this is an instruction based on the fact that it is to be meditated upon in such a manner. (137)
The smallness of its own nature is not indicated, because of the designation of its greatness.
If it be argued that [the individual soul] would attain the same enjoyment [as the Lord], we say no, because of the difference in nature.
If that Supreme Self resides within the body of a lay follower (upāsaka), [then... || 138 ||
If it is argued that the attainment of the experience of pleasure and pain occurs in the same way for this [self], we say no; for residing within the body is not the sole cause. (139)

Subjection to karma alone is the cause for experiencing [the fruits of action], and not so for one who is intent on that [liberation], who is the adversary of all that is to be abandoned, and an ocean of all auspicious qualities. (140)
Thus concludes the section on the universal establishment [of Brahman].
The Section on the Eating of Remnants (Attra-adhikaraṇa)
The Self [is meant], because of the mention of both the moving and the non-moving.
If there were no other [self] who is the enjoyer, then the one heard of as the enjoyer would have to be the individual soul (jīva) everywhere; it is this claim that is refuted here. (141)

In the mantra beginning with "yasya brahma" found in the Kaṭhavallī, that which is heard as the "eater" (attā) is the individual soul (jīva), because it is possible for that alone to be the enjoyer of the fruits of karma. (142)

It is not so; for here, by the scriptural statement of being the consumer of the universe, it is the Supreme Self alone [that is meant], since the eating of the whole is described as being accompanied by death as the condiment. (143)
And such a consumption is intended here as the dissolution of all things;
this state of being an enjoyer conditioned by karma does not belong to the Supreme Self. (144)
Therefore, this state of being the sustainer and the enjoyer of the worlds is impossible for the individual soul (jīva); consequently, the Supreme Person is the Eater.
And because of the context.
"This Self is great and all-pervading," and "this Self is not [the body],"—this section belongs to the Supreme; therefore, this is the Supreme Person. (146)
For the two selves have entered the cave, because of the perception thereof.

In the verse "The two drinking the *ṛta*," the one who is heard as the enjoyer of the fruit is the individual soul (*jīva*) together with the vital breath (*prāṇa*); therefore, it is incorrect to say that the "eater" here is that [Brahman]. (147)
It is said that both the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Soul (para) have entered the cave; indeed, their entry into that very place is perceived here. 148.

The abiding of the Supreme in the cave is described by the Śruti as "difficult to see," whereas the abiding of the individual soul (jīva) therein is established by the statement, "by means of the vital breath" (prāṇena). || 149 ||
The statement "the two drinking the Truth" (ṛtaṃ pibantau) is consistent through the analogy of the umbrella-bearers;
for the other [Self] may be connected with the act of drinking either as the actual agent or as the instigator. (150)
And because of the qualification.

From the beginning to the end of this treatise, both the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) are distinguished by their respective attributes; therefore, the Supreme Person is the Eater (attā). || 151 ||
Thus ends this section.
The Section on the Intermediate State.
On account of the intermediate arising.
The difficulty of knowing the Supreme was previously stated by the words "Who indeed... and so forth;
[now] this is being refuted: that the Supreme is not what has been described as the object of perception. (152)
From the statement, "He who is this in the eye," it is heard that the support in the eye is either the individual soul (jīva), or a reflection, or the presiding deity of the eye. (153)
By virtue of being spoken of as something already established, it must be one of these very [elements];
however, because visibility is not established in the case of the Supreme Self, it is not mentioned here.

Do not say so; for by logical reasoning, the Supreme Lord resides within that very [heart], as He possesses the wealth of eternal natural qualities such as being the "gatherer of all blessings" (saṃyadvāma) and the rest. 155.
And because of the designation of place and so forth.

Since it is heard in such passages as "He who [is] the eyes" that this very Supreme Self is the controller of the abiding [of the senses] in the eye, therefore the one residing in the eye is the Supreme.
Therefore, a statement as if [the object] were well-known is appropriate only with respect to the Supreme Self;
here, the expression "is seen" is based on the reason that it is visible to yogins. (157)
And because it is designated as being distinguished by bliss.

By means of the passage beginning with "Kaṃ brahma" and so forth, [the text] previously established that the very same Supreme Being under discussion is characterized by the excellence of bliss, for the purpose of determining His locus of worship and other such attributes. (158)
Because of the designation "He who is this," the person within the eye here is the Supreme;
and for that very reason, He is Brahman.
How is that which was proclaimed by the passage beginning with "What is Brahman? described as Brahman? || 159 ||
If it is argued that there should be a distinction between the vision of Brahman as *kaṃ* (bliss) and as *kha* (space), that is not so;
for that which is indeed *kaṃ* is precisely that [which is *kha*], since in that context the entity of space is [identical]. 160.
Therefore, the teaching on the excellence of bliss is here designated by the word "kha";
for the supreme Brahman, which is space (ākāśa), consists of unlimited bliss.
It has been stated at the end that they spoke of both the vital breath (prāṇa) and this space (ākāśa) to him;
therefore, the Brahman under discussion prior to that consists of the nature of unlimited bliss.
Because it is heard here as well that [the Self] has the eye as its support, the Supreme is located in the eye;
and because there is a description of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads.
That destination which is to be reached by those who have realized the true nature of Brahman.
Elsewhere, the path beginning with light (arcirādi) is heard as leading to the attainment of Brahman;
here, however, it is recited as the destination to be reached by the Person in the Eye who has been heard of [in the preceding text]. (164)
"The one who dwells within the eye, free from all suffering, is determined to be the Supreme Self;
it cannot be anyone else, because of the lack of stability and impossibility."
Because the soul, the reflection, and even the sun are not fixed in one place. || 165 ||
Because qualities that possess the nature of being free from limiting adjuncts cannot possibly exist in the eyes by necessity, the person within the eye is indeed the Supreme Self. 166.
Thus concludes the section on the intermediate state.
The Section on the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa)
The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) [is Brahman] because His attributes are designated in relation to the deities, the worlds, and so forth.
Having first established the existence of another's eye, the object [of perception] was proven; now, the doctrine that the existence [of the object] belongs to the soul alone is refuted here. (167)

In the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa, that which is heard as the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) through the statement "He who is within the earth," must be the individual soul (jīva), because of its possession of seeing and other such faculties. (168)

Furthermore, this doctrine is not accepted because it negates another seer, whereas the scripture contains statements marked by such terms as "with reference to the deities" (adhidaiva) and "with reference to the worlds" (adhiloka). (169)
The Inner Controller is indeed the Supreme Self, because His attributes are designated [in scripture];
likewise, He possesses the world as His body and is the Inner Controller of all. (170)
In this very context, such qualities as these are taught as being dependent upon Nārāyaṇa;
for the direct perception of form and so forth is not possible otherwise.
The statement "there is nothing else here" negates [the existence of] a seer other than that which is equal [to the Self];
nor is it the one taught in the Smṛti, because its attributes are not predicated [of it], and because it is the embodied one.
Likewise, neither the Pradhāna nor the Jīva is the inner controller (antaryāmī) of those two.
Because they repeatedly express doctrines that are impossible, these [Buddhists] are as unfit for respect as an insentient thing; such is the case with those who possess consciousness.
For both [schools] indeed study this [text] with a distinction.
Since the Kāṇvas and Mādhyandinas study the Inner Controller as distinct from the individual soul (jīva), ending with the words, "He who is in knowledge, he who is in the self. (174)
Therefore, this Supreme Person, the Inner Controller, is distinct from the individual soul;
He is the Self beyond all, free from evil—He is established as Nārāyaṇa. (175)
Thus ends the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmi-Adhikaraṇa).
The Section Concerning the One Possessing Qualities such as Invisibility.
The one possessing qualities such as invisibility [is Brahman], because of the statement of its attributes.

The doubt that "where the state of being the supreme self, characterized by being the seer and so forth, was previously stated not to exist, there it must be the Pradhāna alone" is hereby dispelled. (176)
That which is heard in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad in passages such as "that which is invisible," and "the source of beings," and also "higher than the high Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.5–6); || 177 ||
In this context, "dense" (ghana) refers respectively to the cowherd and the dense [cloud];
because of the negation [of consciousness] and because of being insentient, abiding in non-consciousness, and being an object of perception, it is insentient. 178.

The primary cause (pradhāna) would be of the same class [as the individual soul], as would the imperishable source of beings (bhūtayoni); furthermore, the claim that "beyond the imperishable there is the mass of individual souls (jīvaghana), which is higher" is incorrect. (179)

In this context, the one who possesses qualities such as invisibility and is higher than the Imperishable (akṣara) is the Supreme Self alone, because of the scriptural revelation of His attributes, such as omniscience.

That word ending in the fifth case (the locative) denotes the subtle element of the elements; it is the Imperishable (akṣara), possessing qualities such as invisibility and so forth, which is omnipresent.

Because it is "other" than that which is other than it, and because being "other" would otherwise be impossible, this [Self] is indeed distinguished by such attributes as omniscience and being the source of the world. (182)
And because of the distinction and the designation of attributes, it is neither of the other two.

And here, by means of the great introductory context, as well as through the propositions concerning omniscience and so forth, [the text] distinguishes the Imperishable (akṣara) from both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
By the two terms "parataḥ" (beyond) and "para" (supreme), his distinction [from others] is taught;
therefore, it is said here that the Lord Nārāyaṇa is beyond those two.
And because of the presentation of form.
The form described by the verse beginning with "Agnirmūrdhā" belongs to the Supreme Self alone, who possesses the three worlds as his form; therefore, he is the Supreme Person.
Thus concludes the section concerning the one characterized by qualities such as invisibility.
The Section Concerning Vaiśvānara.
Vaiśvānara [is the Self], because of the distinction of a common term.
The status of being the Supreme Self has been established by virtue of possessing the form of the three worlds;
here, the doubt that this [status] might belong to anyone else is dispelled. (186)
In this context, it is by no means possible to determine that this Vaiśvānara, whose nature is universal, is the Supreme Self. (187)

Because these [words] are used for the digestive fire, for the element, for the divine, and for the Supreme Self—in all four cases—on account of the perception of their respective indicative marks (liṅga) here. || 188 ||
It is not so; the Supreme Person is indeed denoted by the term Vaiśvānara, because this common word [is applied] to Him through His qualities that are unique to the Supreme. (189)
Because it is being qualified here by many attributes such as "being the self of all" and so forth,
that which is being remembered would constitute an inference.
The form of the Vaiśvānara Self, characterized by having heaven as its head and so forth, has thus been described. (190)
And here, that very same [Self] which is well-known from the Śruti and Smṛti is recognized as "this is that" within this Vaiśvānara Self. (191)
This is a mark [indicating] that the Self is other [than the body]; therefore, Vaiśvānara is the Supreme.

If it be argued that He is not [the Supreme] because of the mention of "sound" and so forth, and because He is established within [the body], we say no; for there is instruction regarding Him as such [as the Supreme] through a figurative vision, because [the literal sense] is impossible, and they also study Him as the Puruṣa.
"Agni Vaiśvānara" [is established] through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). || 192 ||

From the conceptualization of the three sacrificial fires, from its location, from the oblation of breath, and likewise from its abiding within the body, its nature as the digestive fire (jāṭhara) is understood. || 193 ||
If it is argued that, for this reason, he cannot be the Supreme Self, we say no;
for such is not the case here, because Vaiśvānara has the digestive fire within the belly as his body.

Because there is an injunction for meditation upon that [Self] as qualified [by the three worlds], whereas for the mere gastric fire, such a thing is impossible since it cannot have the three worlds as its limbs. (195)
In this way, certain Vājasaneyins record the Vaiśvānara as the Self and as the Puruṣa, based on the scriptural statement: "He is this fire. (196)
Indeed, this Lord Nārāyaṇa alone is to be worshipped as the Vaiśvānara Self, for He is designated by the term "the Person free from limiting adjuncts" (nirgatopādhipuruṣa). || 197 ||
For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor a living being.
Since this person is the Vaiśvānara Self, free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi),
and has the three worlds as his limbs, he is therefore neither an element nor a deity.
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even with direct perception.
The word "Agni" here also directly denotes the Supreme Self by virtue of the quality of being the foremost leader, just as the term "Vaiśvānara" does.
Therefore, the designation of Vaiśvānara by the word "Agni" is not contradicted;
the sage Jaimini maintains that this is so in the determination of his supreme nature. (200)
"Because of manifestation," says Āśmarathya.

Regarding this, Āśmarathya says that the teaching concerning the limited nature of the celestial chariot of the Supreme Self is intended for the purpose of manifesting [the status of] a lay devotee (upāsaka). (201)
Bādari [holds that the soul's departure] is for the sake of recollection.
The venerable sage Bādari has stated that the conceptualization of the body here, from the head down to the feet, is likewise for the purpose of meditation.
"Jaimini [holds that the reward comes] from the attainment [of the world], for so the scripture shows."

The arrangement of the householder's fires, such as the Gārhapatya and others, corresponds to the limbs of the lay practitioner (upāsaka) performing daily the rite known as the oblation to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti). || 203 ||
Jaimini declared that it is for the sake of perfecting the Agnihotra; and he shows that perfection in the passage beginning with "He who [knows] this thus. (204)
And they declare him to be in this.

Within this body of the lay devotee (upāsaka), one should [meditate upon] this Vaiśvānara, the supreme Self, whose body consists of heaven, earth, and so forth, by means of the oblation of the vital breaths into the fire.
The introductory passages, such as "They proclaim his words for the sake of worship," establish that Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Person;
thus, it is proven that he is Nārāyaṇa.
Thus concludes the section concerning Vaiśvānara.
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter.
Now begins the third quarter of the first chapter.
The Section Concerning Heaven, Earth, and the Other [Elements] (Dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa)
The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word.
In the preceding section, passages containing indistinct or very indistinct marks (liṅga) and statements (vākya) were examined;
in this [fourth] chapter, passages containing distinct marks of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth are investigated.
The supreme self-nature of that which has heaven, earth, and so forth as its locus has been established;
that very point is now raised as an objection in this section and firmly re-established.
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad it is heard: "In whom heaven and earth rest.
Here, it is the individual soul (jīva) that serves as the locus of the instruments and undergoes manifold births. (209)
"Nor is it the yoga of the channels (nāḍīyoga) and so forth, because of the scriptural teaching on the accumulation of the qualities of the individual soul (jīva);
for this is not so, as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Brahman, on account of its own specific designation. (210)
The word "own" (sva) here refers to such passages as "this is the bridge to immortality";
it is declared that this [knowledge] alone is the cause for attaining immortality. (211)

And here, the word "Self" (ātman) refers to the Supreme Being without any limiting adjuncts; omniscience and other such qualities mentioned here are perfectly consistent with that very [Supreme Being]. (212)

And its being the substratum of the channels is stated by the continuous scriptural passages beginning with "unborn" (ajāyamāna), as well as by the Smṛti which says "He is also unborn" (aja). || 213 ||
It is established that he manifests in many ways by his own will;
it is logical that he, who is the substratum of all, has the mind and other faculties as his locus. (214)
And because there is the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated.

Then, from such scriptural statements as "the wise man [transcends] merit and sin," and because the Supreme Person is designated as that which is to be attained by those liberated from bondage, [He is the goal]. (215)
There is no inference [of such a creator], because of the word "that" (tat) and because [the world] possesses breath.

Just as it is said that the Pradhāna is not the primary subject here because of the absence of a word denoting it, so too this individual soul (prāṇabhṛt) is not what is to be established by the sentence. || 216 ||
Because of the designation of difference.
By the statement beginning with "In the same tree" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1),
the Lord is designated as an ocean of majesty, distinct from the individual soul.
Because of the context.

"Then, by means of the multitude of scriptural words stating 'the supreme [state] of the other alone,' this which is heard in the context is indeed the Supreme Brahman, because it is the subject under discussion. (218)
And on account of abiding and eating.

In the mantra beginning with "dvā suparṇā," the state of being the enjoyer of the fruit is stated for one [of the two birds], while for the other, only its mere residence within the body is demonstrated. (219)
In that state, being unattached and shining brightly, it becomes the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth;
it is not the enjoyer of those things. Therefore, the Supreme Person is the one who has heaven, earth, and the rest as His abode.
Thus concludes the section concerning "Heaven, Earth, and so forth."
The Section on the Abundant (Bhūmā)
The Infinite [is Brahman], because it is taught as being superior to the state of perfect serenity.

The identity with the Supreme Self was established previously through the continuity of the context; now, on the basis of that very reason, the claim that "the Infinite here is the individual soul" is being set aside. (221)
The statement "where one sees nothing else" is recited in the Sāman; therein, the Bhūman is the inner self (pratyagātman) denoted by the word "Prāṇa. (222)

Because the instruction on the Self as consisting of name and so forth has been concluded, and because there is no further question or answer following that, the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa) [is also finished]. || 223 ||
If it is argued that the "plurality" (bhūman) here refers to the inner self (pratyagātman) because of its uninterrupted continuity, that is not so;
for the plurality is the Supreme (para), as it is taught to be superior to the state of perfect serenity (saṃprasāda).
It is determined by another scriptural passage that "the serene one" is the inner self;
for it speaks of the superiority of his own object of meditation for this knower of Prāṇa. (225)

With the word "but" (*tu*), [the text] introduces another proponent of the "exceeding speech" (*ativādin*) himself; having thus proposed this, it proceeds to discuss the one who meditates on the True (*satya-upāsaka*), who is the proponent of the "exceeding of vital breaths" (*prāṇātivādin*). || 226 ||
Because of the statement of superiority, because of the interruption, and because of the context of the vital breath (prāṇa),
that which is denoted by the word "Satya" is declared to be a different entity from the vital breath.
This Lord Nārāyaṇa is the Infinite (bhūman), whose nature is absolute bliss;
and because of the occurrence of [the qualities of] dharma.
And its inherent immortality is its abiding in its own majesty alone. || 228 ||
And since such attributes as being the self of all, which are heard in the context of the *bhūman*,
are logically possible only in the Supreme, the *bhūman* is the Supreme Person.
Thus concludes the section on the Infinite (Bhūmā).
The Section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa)
The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the end of space.
It was previously established that Brahman abides in its own majesty; this [verse] refutes the notion that such [abiding] exists in anything other than that Supreme.
In the question of Gārgī, the passage beginning with "He said, 'This indeed... is recited.
Here, the Imperishable (akṣara) would be the Pradhāna, as it possesses attributes such as being neither coarse nor subtle. (231)
Because the word "akṣara" is used for the Pradhāna [in the phrase] "from the akṣara," [it refers] to the cause even of the ether (ākāśa), which serves as the substratum for all effects. || 232 ||
If that which is spoken in response to a question were "unexplained" (avyākṛta), then it would be a mere syllable;
but this is not so, for here the term "syllable" (akṣara) denotes the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa).
Because it also sustains the Pradhāna, which is as boundless as space—
beginning with the words "that which is above"— it exists throughout the three periods of time.
It is not the air that is declared to be the substratum of all that is born of transformation;
rather, it must be the ether (ambara), which is the unmanifest (avyākṛta) that lies beyond it. || 235 ||
That which is described as their support is not the Pradhāna;
and that [support] is so because of the command.
In that case, the individual soul (jīva) is the imperishable (akṣara), distinct from the entire aggregate of insentient matter.

This doctrine—that [the ether] is established as the substratum—is refuted by the passage beginning with "Of this very syllable" (etasya vā akṣarasya), which establishes that [ether] as belonging to this syllable. 237.
It is taught that steadfastness arises precisely from [his] command;
for such a command could not possibly belong even to one who is bound or one who is liberated. (238)
And because of the exclusion of other states.

The supplementary passage beginning with "the unseen seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11) [establishes] the supreme Self; furthermore, the subsequent portion excludes any difference between this [Self] and the Imperishable (akṣara). (239)
Or rather, it excludes the existence of any other [being] distinguished by such qualities;
therefore, the Supreme Person is the sustainer of all, dependent upon His own teaching. (240)
Thus concludes the section on the syllable *Om*.
The Section Concerning the Object of the Act of Seeing.
"He is that [Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing."
It was previously stated that another [object] cannot be seen by others;
therefore, it is now refuted that what is called "the visible" could not be another. (241)

Furthermore, regarding the question, that which is recited beginning with "by means of the three measures" (trimātra) and so forth, the four-faced one (Caturmukha) is indicated here by the phrase "the Supreme Person" (paraṃ puruṣam). || 242 ||
For those two who worship the Praṇava mantra consisting of one and two mātrās respectively,
the fruits consist, in order, of attaining the world of mortals and attaining the world of the intermediate space (antarikṣa).

Having been described as that which is attained by one who meditates on the three *mātrās*, the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) is situated beyond the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), due to its association with that [state]. (244)
For that very world of Viriñca is indeed being seen by Him who resides therein;
yet it is not so, for the Supreme Person alone is the object of His vision here. (245)

In the final verse of the section beginning with "Beyond the sun" (parāditya), there is instruction regarding the object of the act of seeing as being free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika) and characterized by tranquility, immortality, and so forth. || 246 ||

Thus, when the identity with the Supreme Self is established, that state of the world of Brahmā is what is described here as "that which the seers [call] 'the poets'," which is frequented by the sun-like sages.
It is understood that this refers to that very abode of Vaikuṇṭha;
nor is there any world of the Creator (Brahmā) separated from it by the intermediate space.
Because many worlds, such as heaven and others, arise in the midst [of this], the Lord Nārāyaṇa is heard of here as the object of the act of seeing. (249)
Thus concludes the section concerning the object of the act of seeing.
The Section on the Subtle Space (Daharādhikaraṇa)
The small [ether] is [Brahman], because of the subsequent [scriptural passages].
Previously, the supreme self-nature of that which lies within the city was established; here, the supreme self-nature of that which is designated by the term "ether" is now being proven. (250)
And in the Chāndogya, the passage beginning with "Now, that which is within this" is recited; here, the small ether heard in the text is determined to be the elemental ether. (251)

If it is argued that this is because the word "space" (ākāśa) is preeminently well-known in that very sense, and because it is perceived as the substratum for that which is to be sought, we say: no. (252)
The inner space (daharākāśa) is the Supreme Self (parātmā), because of the attributes stated here in the subsequent passage:
its being the essential nature of the self (svābhāvikātmatva) and its freedom from sin (apahatapāpmatva). || 253 ||
Furthermore, "having true resolve" and "having true desires"—these are the exclusive attributes of the Supreme Self, as they are recited in the subsequent passage. (254)
Furthermore, there is another thing to be sought here: the group of eight qualities residing within that [space].
Having introduced both the small space and the collection of qualities, [the text proceeds] with respect to both of them. (255)
Thus, by such statements as "That is to be sought" and "As far as this space extends, so far," its status as an object of meditation is enjoined. (256)
Furthermore, a clear distinction is perceived between the small space and [ordinary] space;
therefore, the small space must be the Supreme Self and cannot be [ordinary] ether. (257)
On account of the movement and the word; for thus is the mark seen.
And in this small space, there is the daily departure of conscious beings who are unaware [of it], as well as the destination of that small space.
The mention of the "abode of Brahman" and [the mention of] "immortality"—both of these indicate the nature of the Supreme Self of this small space (dahara);
that both are seen elsewhere as well. (259)
According to the Śruti, "Having attained [the state of] Being, one goes to this world of Brahman";
what else could there be here than these two things being heard? (260)
Indeed, there is sufficient evidence for the child (dahara) being the Supreme Self,
because both its supporting and its greatness are perceived within it.
And because it is exclusively Brahman, as proclaimed by all the Vedāntas. || 261 ||
Because the Infinite One, known as the Sustainer of the World, is proclaimed even within this small space, that glorious Daharākāśa is declared to be the Supreme Nārāyaṇa. (262)
And because of common renown.
For, because this term "ether" (ākāśa) is well-known in such passages as "Who indeed shall breathe? and "Who [shall breathe]?
as referring to the Supreme Self, the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is the Supreme Person.
If it be argued that "he" refers to the other [the individual soul] because of the reference to it, we say no, because of impossibility.

If it is argued that this "serenity" (saṃprasāda) mentioned as departing from here is the individual soul (jīva), and not something else, and that it must therefore be the "small ether" (daharākāśa) referred to here—that is not so. (264)
Because the aforementioned qualities residing in the small [space] are impossible in this [state], [it is argued:
"If it is said that [the qualities exist] because of the subsequent [text], then [the soul] has indeed manifested its true nature."
In the subsequent statement regarding Prajāpati, the individual soul (jīva) is likewise of such a nature. || 265 ||
Therefore, the claim that "this small space is [Brahman] because its evil has been destroyed," etc., is incorrect;
for previously its qualities were concealed, but they are revealed through the meditation on Brahman. (266)
But there, the individual soul (jīva) is proclaimed as one whose true nature has become manifest;
since the small [ether] possesses its natural qualities, the notion of a "living being" does not apply here.
And the reference has another purpose.

In this context, the mention of the "living soul" (jīva) is made for the purpose of indicating the Supreme, which is the foremost attainment known as the manifestation of the true nature of the living soul. (268)
If it be argued that this is because [the scripture] has little to hear, that has already been answered.

If it is argued that here the possession of limited honor and learning is appropriate for the individual soul (jīva) alone and not for the greater [Self], the answer to this has already been stated previously. || 169 ||
And because of the imitation of that [world].
For one who is liberated from imitation of others, there is the possession of the eightfold qualities;
therefore, the object of imitation, the small [inner space], is superior to the living self that imitates it. (270)
It is also recorded in the Smṛti.
Through the worship of that [Supreme], it is said that this individual soul attains identity with Him;
thus, according to the Smṛti, "This is knowledge," that which is other than the individual soul is the Supreme.
Thus concludes the section on the "Small" (daharādhikaraṇa).
The Section on the Measured (Pramitādhikaraṇa)
He is known from scripture alone.
The infinite magnitude of the Supreme Self has been illustrated;
now, its having the size of a thumb is likewise declared here. (272)
The verses beginning with "thumb-sized" (aṅguṣṭhamātra) are heard in the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad;
therein, the conclusion is that this being of thumb-measure is indeed the individual soul (jīva). (273)
From such scriptural statements as "The lord of the vital breaths is the size of a thumb," there is the understanding that the individual self (jīvātman) possesses the measurement of a thumb. (274)

Do not think so; for by the exclusive use of the word "Lord" (īśāna) in the phrase "the Supreme Person, measured by the size of a thumb, is the ruler of what has been and what is to be," [it is established]. || 275 ||
But with respect to the heart, [the qualification applies] because human beings are the primary subjects.
Because the heart of a lay devotee is the size of a thumb, and because the Supreme Self resides therein, it is described as being the size of a thumb in relation to that [heart]. (276)

However, since the scripture has human beings as its intended audience, the statement that the Supreme is the size of a thumb is made from their perspective; other arguments for this will also be stated.
The section concerning the deity in the center.
"Even above that [the world of Brahmā], Bādarāyaṇa [maintains it is possible], because of the possibility."

The scripture concerning the meditation on Brahman previously taught was intended for mortals; it is now considered whether or not deities and others possess the qualification for this practice. (278)
Deities and others who are bodiless have no qualification for worship; they lack the capacity for this worship which is to be accomplished by embodied beings. (279)
"Let it not be so; for such worship of another could even occur among the immortals.
Thus does the venerable Vyāsa Bādarāyaṇa consider.
Because the desire and the capacity exist for them,
that longing is directed toward the Supreme Self, who is an ocean of auspicious qualities, through the perception of Him as the object of enjoyment.
Furthermore, their own capacity is also possible;
by virtue of possessing a body, sense organs, and so forth, all the gods likewise possess that [capacity]. (282)
In the Vedānta, [the existence of these] is heard of both in the context of creation and in the context of meditation; therefore, because they exist in those two, there is eligibility for meditation.
If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe the attainment of multiple [bodies].
Even though the gods possess bodies, there would indeed be a contradiction regarding ritual action, since a single-bodied deity could not be simultaneously summoned at many sacrifices. (284)

If it is argued that [the Lord] cannot be present everywhere because of the impossibility of such presence, we say no; for this assumption of multiple bodies is seen in the case of Saubhari and others, by virtue of their own power.
If it be argued that [the world] is [produced from] sound, we say no; because [the world] originates from this [Brahman], as is known through both perception and inference.
There would be a contradiction regarding Vedic speech due to its connection with impermanent objects,
because the bodies of the gods such as Indra are impermanent on account of their birth.
If it is argued that these words existing in the Veda are either devoid of meaning before their destruction or after it, or else that they are impermanent— that is not so.
Furthermore, because the referents such as Indra originate from words such as "Indra" and so forth,
the Vedic words "Indra" and the like do not apply to mere individuals.

Just as in the case of words such as "cow" and the like, because they denote the form (ākṛti), when a single individual instance has perished, [the word] remains through that respective Vedic term. (289)
It is understood that Prajāpati, having perceived the respective objects from the mind's state, creates another Indra of similar form. (290)
Therefore, there is no contradiction regarding the domain of words based on Śruti and Smṛti;
and for this very reason, [the Veda] possesses eternality.
For from the Vedic word, the Creator brings about the recollection of the object that has arisen.
Furthermore, having reflected upon the forms, powers, and other attributes of the sages who composed the mantras and so forth,
[the Lord] at those various times [creates beings] endowed with those very forms and powers.
Having created them, he impels those very [beings] toward the composition of their respective mantras;
therefore, both the eternity of the Vedas and the status of these [beings] as composers of mantras are established. (293)
"And because name and form are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of repetition, on account of both scripture and tradition."

Even in the case of the total destruction and the recurrence of the creation of the world, non-contradiction should be understood through the aforementioned reasoning, because names and forms remain the same. (294)

Furthermore, that Blessed One, having directly created the cosmic egg and the four-faced Brahmā, [reinstated] all the Vedas exactly as they were before, which had been held within his own heart. (295)
Having instructed the four-faced one (Brahmā) as before regarding the task of creation,
and having appointed him to that duty, he himself remains as the sovereign controller.

By remembering that very same prior sequence through firm mental impressions (saṃskāra), the Veda is uttered by means of that [sequence] alone; this constitutes its non-human origin (apauruṣeyatā). // 297 //
Since such a meaning as eternity is established by the Śruti and Smṛti, gods and others indeed possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. (298)
Thus concludes the section concerning the deities.
Now begins the section concerning the Madhu-vidyā.
Jaimini [holds that] there is no entitlement [to the knowledge of Brahman] for those in the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations, because [the requirements] are impossible [for them].
It has been stated that gods possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman;
any doubt regarding the impossibility of that is now refuted with respect to their specific case. (299)

For the Vasus, Ādityas, and other gods who have already attained the status of Vasus and so forth, there can be no desire for, or impossibility of, attaining that [status] again through the Madhu-vidyā and other means which lead to its attainment. (300)
The teacher Jaimini considers that there is an absence of qualification here; for those [deities] who are to be meditated upon in those various sciences have no qualification in this [context]. (301)
And because of the existence [of the word] in the sense of "light."

In this context, the term *brahmopasti* (service to Brahman) has been mentioned; for among the inhabitants of heaven, it is established as common to both gods and mortals by the phrase "him the gods [protect]. (302)

However, the specific scriptural hearing of these [passages] precludes the performance of meditations on Brahman other than those [taught therein]; therefore, they have no qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and similar meditations. (303)
But Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] the existence [of the intermediate state], for it indeed exists.

And regarding the Vasus and others [in the context of] the honey-rite and so forth, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that these gods, the Vasus and the rest, possess the qualification for participation. (304)
Even after experiencing the state of suffering among the Vasus and others during another kalpa, those desiring to attain Brahman at the end [of that period] [should practice] this Madhu-vidyā. (305)

Having taken recourse to the knowledge of Brahman, they are always worthy of meditating upon Brahman as it exists within themselves; therefore, they possess the qualification for this [knowledge]. || 306 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning honey.
Now begins the section concerning those who are not Śūdras (the *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*).
For it is indicated by the hearing of that disregard for Śuka and by his subsequent rushing toward him.
The eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman was stated [previously] with reference to the gods because of their inherent fitness;
now, the objection that the Śūdra should also have eligibility because he likewise possesses that fitness is being refuted. (307)
The Śūdra also possesses the qualification for these knowledges of Brahman;
even in the absence of Vedic study, he may attain it through means such as listening to the Purāṇas.

Because of the possibility of knowledge regarding the nature of Brahman and the method of meditating upon it, because of the possibility of the desire for liberation, and because of the possibility of both capacity and the seeking [of that goal], [the eligibility for initiation exists]. || 309 ||
Therefore, the claim that Raikva addressed Jānaśruti as "Śūdra" and instructed him in the knowledge of Brahman is inconsistent.
From his hearing the words of the swan’s censure of Jānaśruti, and from his very immediate rushing toward the teacher Raikva at that moment, his purity (śuk) is indicated.
The term "Śūdrā" used by the Guru refers specifically to her [the teacher], and not to her caste;
for it is only the realization born from the Vedāntic statements that is being described. (312)

Because it is heard that he [the teacher] possesses the requisite skillful means, and because such means are impossible for one born of the Śūdra caste; and even if he possessed the desire [to learn], he would lack the necessary capacity. (313)
Permission to listen to the Purāṇas has been granted for the sake of pacifying sin;
therefore, a Śūdra has no entitlement whatsoever to the higher forms of worship.
And because of the attainment of the status of a Kṣatriya.
From the statement that he was "one who gives much" to Jānaśruti, who was desirous of hearing,
and from the perception of his being a Kṣatriya, that address [of Prajāpati] was not based on caste.
And because of the indicative mark [found] later in the case of Caitraratha.
In this Saṃvarga-vidyā, at the point of the subsequent narrative,
the connection belongs specifically to a Kṣatriya among the castes other than Brāhmaṇas.
It is understood that Abhipratārin was the one known as Caitraratha; therefore, Janaśruti here is considered a Kṣatriya other than Raikva. (317)
And from the association with Kāpeya, as well as from being seen elsewhere, it is known that Abhipratārin possessed both the status of Caitraratha and the status of a king. (318)
Because of the grasping at mental formations and because of the expression of their non-existence.
Because refinement is required for the statements that impart knowledge,
and because that refinement is absent in the case of a Śūdra, no eligibility exists for him here.
And because activity proceeds when there is the determination of the non-existence of that [object].

Furthermore, since Jābāla’s engagement in instruction occurred only while his lack of Śūdra-status was firmly established through his service, he did not possess the requisite qualification [for Vedic study]. (320)
Because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda].
For a Śūdra, the hearing, study, and other such acts regarding the Veda are prohibited in every respect; therefore, he has no entitlement to meditative worship (upāsana).
And because of Smṛti.

Furthermore, based on Smṛti passages such as "one should not teach him the Dharma," there is a clear prohibition against [him] hearing [the teachings] and so forth; therefore, he lacks the requisite fitness.
Thus concludes the section concerning those who are not Śūdras.
Now follows the supplementary section on the means of valid cognition (*pramitādhikaraṇa-śeṣa*).
Because of trembling.
Having concluded the incidental discussion, the reasoning is now presented to explain how that which is the size of a thumb is indeed the Supreme Self, as was the subject at hand. (323)

From this fear that has been described here in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad with the words "whatever there is," [the soul] always arises from that which is denoted by the term "prāṇa" (vital breath) and measured by the size of a thumb.
Because all the gods tremble violently from his raising the vajra and other weapons,
the Supreme Person is of such a nature that he is measured by the size of a thumb.
Because of the perception of light.
In this place, as well as in the context of the statement beginning with "There the sun [does not shine]," there exists that which is the cause of all lights and is uniquely supreme.
Because he is perceived through the light and because he is eternally free from any increase or decrease,
the glorious Nārāyaṇa is said to be measured by the size of a thumb.
Thus ends the section concerning that which is measured by the thumb.
The Section Concerning the Designation as Being a Different Entity and So Forth.
Space [is distinct from the Self], because it is designated as being a different entity and so forth.

Regarding the word "ether" heard in its general sense in proximity to the "small [space]," the doubt that its referent might be the individual soul (jīva) is raised, and it is established that it is the supreme self (paramātman). || 328 ||
It is recited: "The ether, indeed, [is] the name-and-form.
Here, the ether is the liberated jīva, because it is that very one which is under discussion. (329)
Furthermore, the claim that the word "shaking off" (dhūtvā) occurs in the subsequent sentence is not tenable;
for here, the Supreme Person is the one who carries away name and form, which is the ether (ākāśa). (330)

Because it is taught that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is distinct from the object of contact (sparśa), its agency regarding name-and-form consists in being of the nature of both the bound and the liberated. (331)
One who is bound speaks of this [Self] as being something other [than the Supreme Self] due to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) associated with that state;
however, even one who is liberated is not its bearer, as he remains far removed from the activity of the world.
By such statements as "with this living self," the fact that the Supreme Self is the sustainer of those two—name and form—is established. (333)
In the phrase "having shaken off" (dhūtvā), the Supreme Being is the subject under discussion by virtue of being the one intended to be attained;
therefore, the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the one denoted here by the word "ether" (ākāśa). || 334 ||
On account of the difference between deep sleep and departure.
By virtue of the teaching of identity and by the negation "not this, not that," the doctrine that Brahman is an entity distinct from the individual soul (jīva) is refuted. (335)
