In the two scriptural passages beginning with "by the Prājña" regarding the times of deep sleep and departure,
the embracing and the ascending of the individual soul (jīva) are stated from the perspective of the inner self (pratyagātman).
Furthermore, because another is mentioned as distinct [from oneself], there exists a supreme Person other than that;
for an embrace and so forth with one's own self would indeed be impossible for one who is asleep. (337)
From words such as "lord" (pati) and others.
In this context, regarding the statement "the Lord of all," [it refers] to the Supreme Self;
for from the words "Lord" and so forth heard in the scriptures, [He is understood] as distinct from the individual self (pratyagātman). || 338 ||

It has been established that this statement of identity, as well as the speech denying difference, are characterized by a distinct nature, being prompted by the fact that everything is an effect of Brahman. (339)
Thus concludes the section concerning the designation [of Brahman] as being something else, and so forth.
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter.
Now begins the fourth quarter.
The Section Concerning Those Who Rely on Inference (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa)

If it be argued that for some [the Self] is also inferential, we say no; for [the scripture] shows that it is grasped as presented in the form of the body's metaphorical representation, and it further demonstrates this.

In the preceding section, a passage containing clear indicative marks (liṅga) such as the individual soul (jīva) was examined; here, a passage containing extremely clear indicative marks of the individual soul is being investigated. || 340 ||

And here, by means of an investigation into scriptural passages containing extremely clear indicative marks (liṅga) such as the individual soul (jīva), the over-extension (ativyāpti) of the definition [of Brahman] to that which is distinct from Brahman is avoided. (341)
Previously, the doctrine that there is no entity other than the living soul was refuted; here, that same doctrine is being countered by means of another approach. (342)
In the mantra from the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, "Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest," that which is also the cause, namely Pradhāna, is denoted by the word "Unmanifest. (343)

Because of the recognition of that very system, because there is nothing beyond the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, and because of the exclusion of anything else—stating "there is nothing whatsoever superior to the Puruṣa"—[it is established]. (344)

If it is argued thus, [we reply]: since the body has been characterized as being "like a chariot," therefore the word *vyakta* (manifest) refers to that which is perceptible; hence, what is not so designated by words is not the cause. (345)
Based on the previously cited mantra beginning with "Know the self as the rider of the chariot," the self, the body, and so forth, serve in succession as the means for meditation.

Furthermore, because they are subject to being controlled by charioteers and so forth, these [objects] are described as "superior to the senses" in such mantras as, "Superior to the senses... (Katha Upanishad 1.3.10). || 347 ||
In this context, the faculties and so forth are expressed by their own respective terms;
however, the body is described as being like a chariot, but not by its own specific term.
By process of elimination, that which was previously mentioned by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) is what is understood here; therefore, there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Therefore, the Puruṣa beyond this [twenty-fifth principle] is not declared to be the twenty-fifth;
rather, the Supreme Person is that which is to be attained once one has reached the ultimate limit of what is to be brought under control.
The remainder of the passage clearly demonstrates this point:
"The wise man should restrain speech and mind; he should restrain those two in knowledge. (351)
But it is subtle because of its fitness for that.
Since that which exists in the state of the body is unmanifest yet capable of producing effects,
it is for this reason that the body alone is understood here by the term "unmanifest" (avyakta).
Because it is dependent on that, it is purposeful.
Because it is the body of the Supreme Self and is dependent upon Him, it is purposeful;
for here, by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta), the subtle element of the elements (bhūtasūkṣma) is understood.
And because [the Lord] is not mentioned as an object of knowledge.
If it were the system of Tantra, then its terminology such as "the manifest and the unmanifest" would have been mentioned;
yet even its status as an object of knowledge has not been stated, and therefore that [Tantric system] is not accepted here.
If it be argued that [the Self] speaks, we say no; for it is the intelligent [Self] that speaks, according to the context.
By the statement "without sound," it is taught that the Unmanifest is the object of knowledge;
it is not so for the Prājña, because he is not mentioned there and because he alone is the subject under discussion. (355)
And for these three alone there is both this presentation and the question.

In this section, beginning from the words "yeyam" and continuing until the end, there is an extensive [discussion] regarding the object of meditation, the act of meditation, and the meditator, insofar as they are to be known. (356)
Thus, the introduction as well as the question regarding only three [entities] is observed;
therefore, there is no inclusion here of the "Unmanifest" (avyakta) according to the Tantric system.
And like the Great One.

Just as the "Great Self" (mahān ātmā) mentioned in the phrase "the Great Self of the intellect" is not understood [as the Supreme Self] because of the word "Self," so too it is not the technical [Sāṃkhya] principle when referred to by the term "Unmanifest" (avyakta). || 358 ||
The Section on the Chamasas (Cups)
It is like the cup, because there is no distinction.

The independence of the Pradhāna, which is called the Unmanifest, has been refuted; however, fearing that its existence might be established by the *ajā* mantra, that objection is now being set aside. (359)

In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, the passage beginning with "ajāmekām" (the one unborn) is recited; therein, the "ajā" (unborn) must be understood as established by the Tantras, because of the scriptural statement regarding her being uncreated.
Moreover, because it is heard in scripture that [the Unborn] creates living beings independently, it is not the case that the non-Brahman Unborn is stated to be the cause. (361)
There is no restriction [regarding the creator] simply because of the scriptural mention of the impossibility of birth;
for instance, in passages such as "upward-turned" (RV 10.86.7) and regarding the means called the *camasa* [cup]. (362)
Even when the remainder of the sentence is heard, the understanding that the head is a cup arises;
likewise, in this case, the mention of the goat (ajā) established by the *tantra* [context] is not a restrictive factor for the grasping [of the head].
Only the state of being the cause of creation has been stated here; independence is not asserted.
For it is thus that some [scriptural passages] record [the origin of the world] as beginning with light.
This "unborn" (ajā) is indeed based on Brahman as the cause; likewise, the Taittirīyakas [hold this view]. (364)

In the context of the collection of mantras beginning with "He who is subtler than the subtle" and ending with "the Supreme Self," it is taught that [Brahman] is the self of all through the origination of everything from Him. (365)
"The one unborn" is thus declared; she is indeed the Supreme Self.
And because it is taught as a figurative designation, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and other such examples.
Because of this statement, "The Illusionist [creates]," and because of the instruction regarding creation here [in this context]. (366)
There is no mutual contradiction between the two properties of being unborn and being an effect of Brahman; however, at the time of dissolution, it [the world] abandons name and form.
Therefore, the non-sentient substance remains as the body of Brahman;
thus, at the time of creation, those unborn [powers], having Brahman as their cause, become subject to transformation.

Just as the sun possesses the state of being honey during its manifestation, so too does it possess the state of being an effect; however, at the time of its dissolution, its subtle state of existence is the state of being a non-effect.
Thus concludes the section concerning the cups (camasādhikaraṇa).
The Section Concerning the Comprehension of the Number [of Elements] (Saṅkhyopasaṅgrahādhikaraṇa).
It is not [the case that the five elements are meant], even because of the inclusion of a number, due to their being manifold and because of the excess.
The claim that the unborn (ajā) lacks the nature of Brahman has already been set aside due to the absence of a reason;
here, the argument that "the mark [of Brahman] exists in that [which is eternal]" is being refuted.
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti there is the mantra beginning with "yasmin pañca"; this mantra is held to be the indicator of the principles of the Sāṃkhya system. (371)

Because they consist of the realization of the reality of the tantra numbered as twenty-five, and because they pertain to the domain of liberation, it is certain that these are Tantric [teachings]. (372)
It is not so; for from the statement beginning with "in whom the five groups of five," and because the number twenty-five is included therein, that very term [is used]. (373)
There can be no recognition of these as being part of the Tantra, because they are distinct from them;
for they always have Brahman as their locus, as expressed by the word "in which" (yasmin).
For their nature as Brahman is indeed known through the principle of surplus;
since that which is denoted by the word "Space" is in excess of the twenty-five [tattvas]. (375)
By the word "even" (api), it is made known that there is no inclusion of a numerical total here;
rather, it is stated that there are five [beings] designated as "pañcajanāḥ. (376)
The vital breaths and so forth [are the subject], because of the remainder of the passage.
The five "people" (pañcajanaḥ) are the five beginning with breath (prāṇa), which have Brahman as their support;
this is understood from the supplementary passage, "the breath of breath," and so forth. || 377 ||
According to some, there is light when food is absent.
Even if the reading "pañcajanā ime" does not exist in the Kāṇva recension,
one should understand that the five persons refer to the sense organs, because of the word "light" (jyotis) mentioned previously.
Having stated that Brahman is the illuminator of the illuminators, it was said immediately thereafter that there are "five times five"; for indeed, the sense organs must be of such a nature.
Therefore, since it is taught that the senses abide as the Supreme Self in the passage beginning with "in whom the five, the five," this cannot possibly be described as Tantric.
Thus concludes the section concerning the inclusion of the number.
The Section on Being the Cause.
And because, in the case of ether and so forth, it is taught as the cause exactly as it was described [in the source].
It has been stated that the causality of that which holds Brahman, the Self, or Pradhāna as primary is non-Vedic; in this regard, the assertion of the unanimity of the Vedas is now set forth. (381)
In some cases, it is likewise left undeclared whether "it exists" or "it does not exist";
thus, the causal entity is expressed through statements that bring about the understanding of causality. (382)
If Brahman were the cause, however, there would be a contradiction regarding its existence, non-existence, and so forth;
consequently, all scriptural statements would not be in agreement. But this is not the case when [the cause] is declared according to the Tantras.
Existence, non-existence, and the indeterminate state abide according to the distinction of time;
likewise, due to beginninglessness and due to transformation at the time of creation. (384)
The argument that "because it is unmanifest due to the separation from name-and-form at the time of dissolution,
that cause must therefore be Pradhāna" is inconsistent.
Because he is always proclaimed as the cause in effects such as space and so forth, being distinguished precisely by qualities such as omniscience and the like. (386)

The conclusion reached by all scriptural statements is that Brahman alone is the cause; this refers to the "All-knowing One" (Vipaścit) under discussion in the Śruti passage beginning with "Truth, Knowledge... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
In all subsequent statements, a connection is observed;
for it is exactly thus everywhere, therefore Brahman alone is the cause. (388)
Because of attraction.

In the passage "In the beginning, Being alone was this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), regarding the Brahman who is said to have desired to create the world, and also regarding that which was stated subsequently in the passage "Non-being indeed was this" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7). || 389 ||

And in the sentence "This is that," because of the drawing together [of the two referents], the word "non-existent" (asat) and the word "unmanifest" (avyākṛta) denote Brahman whose body is the unmanifest. (390)
Likewise, the two words "Brahman" and "Self" do not denote the Pradhāna;
therefore, there is no possibility of the Pradhāna being the cause. (391)
Thus concludes the section on being the cause.
The Section on the Denotation of the World.
Because it denotes the world.

It was stated previously that the causality of the world is attributed to consciousness alone; and of that which is conscious, it is the living being who performs action (the *karmī-jīva*), and not anything else. (392)
Therefore, this very Pradhāna, presided over by Him, is accepted as the cause;
thus, this Sāṃkhya doctrine is refuted here in this context. (393)

In the Kauṣītakī Śruti, that which is recited as "O Bālāka," refers to the Person (puruṣa) who is distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti), and who is declared here as the object to be known. || 394 ||
Because the scripture states "of whom this [is the fruit]," it declares a connection with karma;
however, Brahman has no such connection with karma consisting of merit and demerit. (395)
Because the word "karma" is used here in its conventional sense, it refers to that very thing;
therefore, the claim that this primary matter (pradhāna) presided over by the individual soul (jīva) acting as karma is the cause is incorrect. || 396 ||

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he whose work is this," since the word "work" (karman) refers to the world as the effect of Brahman, there is no inclusion of the "Person" (puruṣa) as asserted by the Sāṃkhya school. || 397 ||

Having refuted the reality of those who perform rituals, such as Āditya and others, as declared by Bālāki to be Brahman, [the Upaniṣad] spoke solely for the purpose of making known the Supreme. || 398 ||

In this sentence, the word "karma" (action) does not refer to merit, demerit, and so forth; for [if it did], the function of making known what was previously unknown would not be established, since it is said that "the effect is being produced. (399)
Furthermore, this entire world has been previously introduced as having the Sun for its mouth and being denotable by the word "this" (idam);
therefore, this whole universe is the effect of that Supreme Self. (400)
It is Nārāyaṇa alone who is to be understood here;
if it be argued that this is not so because of the characteristics of the individual soul and the chief vital breath, that has already been explained.
In this very sentence, "evam eva," [the existence] of the experiencer, the jīva, is established by means of its indicative mark (liṅga). || 401 ||

If it is argued that this [Self] is not the Supreme Self because of its connection with the primary vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) in passages such as "Now, in this prāṇa," the refutation of this has already been shown.

When it is determined that [the passage] refers to Brahman by means of introductory statements and other criteria, everything must be interpreted in conformity with that; this is what is meant by the term "indicative mark" (liṅga). || 403 ||

Regarding the mention of the signs of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) in the Prātardana section, it has been stated that this is for the purpose of the meditation on Brahman as having those as its body. (404)

And here, because of the grammatical coordination in the phrase "in this breath," the mention of the breath is appropriate for the purpose of meditating on the inner ruler (antaryāmin) who resides within the breath. (405)
Jaimini, however, [holds that the passage] has another purpose, on account of both the question and the explanation; and some [teachers] also [hold this] thus.
Jaimini maintains that the demonstration of the existence of a soul distinct from the body is intended to make known the existence of Brahman, which is other than that [body]. (406)

From the question, "Where was this then? and from the subsequent answer, "In this prāṇa, my dear," which serves as a meaningful response to the statement beginning with "Being, my dear... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1). || 407 ||
Moreover, certain followers of particular Vedic branches recite in this dialogue a sentence ending with "he lies therein," which has the Supreme Self as its object. (408)
Thus concludes the section concerning the designation of the world.
The Section on the Syntactical Connection of Sentences (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa)
Because of the connection with the sentence.

In the preceding [section], because the word *karman* was taken to mean the "world," the claim that the sentence refers to the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) was refuted; but here, in the context of the qualified [agent] (*adhikṛta*), it is established. (409)

It is directly established that [the self] is indeed the enjoyer of the fruit produced by karma; and it is argued that it is appropriate for the sentence to have that as its primary purport—this is what is being set forth here. (410)
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti, it is stated: "Verily, not for the sake of the husband [does one worship]," and the Puruṣa thus proclaimed as the object to be seen is considered the Tāntrika. (411)

Because of the continuity of affection for one's husband, wife, children, wealth, cattle, and so forth, the perception of a living being exists at the beginning, as well as in the middle and at the end. (412)

For it is precisely the knowledge of the true nature of the soul as distinct from the attributes of the insentient that is declared in the Tantra to be the cause of immortality; therefore, such [knowledge] is what is intended here. (413)
The essential nature [of the Self] is declared as that which is to be seen for the sake of immortality;

Because the entire passage is consistent here with the Supreme Self, that very Supreme Person alone is indicated as the object to be seen. (415)

Since husbands and other such relations are dear to the living being only for the sake of attaining their own desired ends, one should therefore meditate on that form which is free from them, having abandoned those objects of affection. (416)
This statement would be inconsistent, for that which is to be sought after is indeed what is dear;
otherwise, husbands and the like would not be dear to their wives and others for the sake of their own desires. (417)

Having stated, "But for the sake of one's own self," and then saying, "The Self, verily, my dear," that which is indicated as the object to be seen is indeed the Supreme Self, distinct from the individual soul (jīva). || 418 ||
And because He, by His own will, causes husbands and others to feel love toward their own wives and so forth, that Supreme Person, whose resolve is ever-true, is the most beloved. (419)
Āśmarathya [holds that] there is a sign for the establishment of the proposition.
This is considered the mark for establishing the claim of omniscience:
that the Supreme Self is addressed by words denoting the individual soul. (420)
If the individual soul were indeed the supreme self and not its effect, then the knowledge of the individual soul would not be possible through the knowledge of the supreme self. (421)
"Both its origination and its dissolution are known to proceed from the Supreme Self;

Auḍulomi [holds that this occurs] because of the very state of one who is about to depart [from the body].
Because the view that the individual soul (jīva) is an effect of Brahman entails many logical defects, and because its eternity is established by the scriptural text, "It is not born. (423)
"What was stated previously is incorrect; for it is only one who is about to depart [from the body] that is designated by the word 'jīva' because of his nature as Brahman—so says Auḍulomi. (424)
"Because of the abiding [of the individual soul in Brahman], so says Kāśakṛtsna."
Because it is tainted by many defects, this too is inconsistent:

This [Brahman] is designated by the word "jīva" because of its abiding [within it], as is seen in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa and elsewhere in the Śruti. (426)
"The nature of Brahman as having the conscious and the unconscious as its body is proclaimed repeatedly;

Thus ends the section on the syntactical connection of the sentences.
The Section on Primordial Matter (Prakṛti)
And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples.

The other [the Supreme Being] would be merely the efficient cause (nimitta) of the world, not its material cause (upādāna),

This is incorrect, because difference is established by such passages as "The Illusionist [creates] from this," and because it would contradict the scriptural texts concerning the changelessness of Brahman.

By means of the knowledge of Brahman, through the proposition that "by knowing one, all is known," and likewise by the understanding of the statement, "thereby what was unheard becomes heard. (432)
Just as, by means of the illustration of clay and its effects stated in the sentence "O Somya," it is understood that Brahman alone is the material cause, so too is that Brahman [the cause]. 433.
Worldly cognition would then have only its efficient cause as its object, and not the intellect [of the creator];

Of the Supreme Self, which is distinct from everything, all-powerful, and accessible through the scriptures alone, [and] of that which exists in the form of both cause and effect— (435)

Even in the two states, the embodied one remains always a single entity; for his status as both the efficient cause and the material cause is indeed uncontradicted by the conscious and the unconscious.
For modifications are indeed attached only to the insentient substance within the body;

Even though He is the material cause of this universe, His freedom from all defects is understood from such passages as "the Illusionist" (māyī) and so forth. (438)
And because of the teaching on covetousness.
This is because of the teaching that the desire for multiplicity belongs to Brahman itself as the creator—through such passages as "He desired, 'May I be many'" and "He thought, 'May I be many. (439)
It is understood that Brahman alone is both the material cause and the efficient cause of the universe,
because both are directly declared [in scripture].
The Supreme is directly revealed by such [Vedic] passages as "What indeed is the forest? and "Who is He? (RV 10.82.5–6).
Because it creates itself, Brahman alone is both that which is grasped (upādāna) and the causal sign (nimitta); thus, these two are one.
Then, [the phrase] "himself as the self" refers to the Supreme Self under discussion. || 441 ||
In the act of creation, both the state of being the object and the state of being the agent are perceived; that [Brahman] is the other.
It is the substratum of name and form as the effect, yet it is not the substratum of that [name and form] as the agent.
Because of transformation.
In this regard, for the transformation being taught here, there is no possibility of fault whatsoever; rather, it brings about supreme sovereignty in an extreme degree.
In the Śruti, that which is non-distinct from name, form, and so forth, consisting of subtle consciousness and the individual soul as its body,
is described as being divided into name, form, consciousness, and the individual soul as its body.
For the teaching of transformation is indeed based on the statement "this [world] was that";
therefore, defects such as the failure to achieve the goals of human life, which reside in the body and in the conscious and unconscious principles, [do not apply to the Self]. (445)
In both states, Brahman is the very self, free from evil;
it constitutes the body of Brahman for all things, whether in their gross or subtle conditions.
That Brahman is the self of those two is frequently taught in the Vedānta;
therefore, O sinless one, the Supreme Self alone is the cause of both here.
For it is indeed sung as the womb.
The Ṛgvedic verse [RV 10.90.5] refers to the Puruṣa as the source of all beings, the agent, and the Lord;
for He is indeed sung of as the source of the entire universe. (448)
It is understood precisely here that the word *yoni* denotes the material cause (*upādāna*);
thus, by means of the statement regarding the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*), the two-fold nature of the cause [as both efficient and material] is established beyond this. (449)
Thus concludes the section concerning primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The Section on All Explanations.
By this, all [remaining cases] have been explained; they have been explained.
Indeed, it has been stated that Nārāyaṇa is the cause and the object of worship;
however, this is incorrect, for Rudra is mentioned in some Vedic branches as [the cause]. (450)
This section is undertaken to demonstrate that the doubt concerning [the self] being the cause has been refuted by the collection of logical arguments stated previously. (451)

By the words "When there was darkness," and so forth, the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad declares that the one Rudra remains established during the dissolution of the universe; therefore [he is the cause]. (452)
It would follow that this alone is the cause; however, this is untenable, for by the collection of arguments already stated, all proponents of causality [are refuted]. 453.
The Vedāntas have been established as being devoted to the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, through such means as the conceptualization of the manifold manifestations of Nārāyaṇa himself. (454)
When it is firmly established that [the Supreme Being] is the cause by virtue of unique attributes,
words such as "Śiva" and others must be understood as referring to that very being, even if this requires setting aside their conventional meanings.

The doubt as to why there might not be a reversal here cannot arise, because this term *nārāyaṇa* is established either through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or through etymological derivation (*yoga*). (456)

Because it is impossible for it to have any other referent, because the substitution of *ṇ* is impossible [therein], because the rule for *ṇ* applies only when [the word] is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), and also because the status of being "Śrī" is impossible [therein]. (457)
Therefore, the causality and other attributes belong eternally to Nārāyaṇa alone;
for this reason, one should always meditate upon Nārāyaṇa without agitation. 458.
Thus it has been stated in the Veda and by the authors of the Sūtras in the fifth [chapter].
Here, the repetition serves as an indicator of the completion of the chapter. || 459 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the refutation of all other interpretations.
The first chapter is completed.
The Glorious Garland of Verses on the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā]

I take refuge in that Lord of the Great Goddess, who performs the divine play of creating the universe and other such acts, who is sinless, the abode of all auspicious qualities, the one to be worshipped, the bestower of liberation, and the ultimate goal to be attained.
May the lotus feet of Rāmānuja shine forever in my mind,
by whose fragrance the peerless Vaiṣṇava lineage shines resplendent in the world.

Because it protects the noble goal at the end of the three Vedas, this [work] bestows the highest good and nothing else on earth; by relying upon it, the wise cross the ocean of existence with ease. (3)
May that most excellent teacher, Śrī Rāghava, by meditating upon whose feet I have attained existence with my impurities destroyed, grant me intelligence regarding this commentary.
May the great lord of ascetics, the younger brother of Śrī Raṅgarāmānuja, who is solely devoted to the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedānta, shine eternally within my heart. (5)
Having heard from my teacher the principal meanings of the sections (adhikaraṇas) of the illustrious Bhāṣya, I now write them down according to my understanding, under the gaze of my preceptor.
I do not undertake such a task for the sake of proclaiming my own scholarship and so forth;
rather, it is out of a desire for the immediate fruit known as the contemplation of the meaning of the Bhāṣya. (7)
This speech of this fool may indeed bring joy to the great;
does not the song of the female parrot bring delight even to the wise? (8)
Vyāsa, the knower of reality, caused his own disciple, the sage Jaimini, to determine the meaning of the Vedas by means of a collection of sixteen chapters of aphorisms.
In the Dvayugādhyāya-śārīraka-śāstra, that very Vyāsa, who is Viṣṇu,
has correctly expounded Brahman, who is to be known through Vedānta.
The Lord Rāmānuja Muni himself, an incarnation of Vyāsa,
composed a wonderful and great commentary on the sūtras contained in that very chapter.
By the first pair [of verses], the causality of Īśvara is established;
by the subsequent pair, the means and the fruit are stated in sequence.
In the first chapter, the *Samanvaya-adhyāya*, through the determination of the purport of the scriptural texts, it has been established that Brahman is the cause of the entire universe. (13)
In that regard, it was established in the first chapter [the *Ayogavyavaccheda-pāda*] through an investigation of various scriptural passages that Brahman alone is indeed the cause. (14)
Here, at the outset, by means of four sūtras and through arguments consistent with valid cognition, the claim that the treatise need not be commenced is thoroughly refuted. (15)
Thus ends the introduction.
The First Section: The Inquiry into the Desire to Know (Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa)

Oṃ. Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into Brahman. Immediately after the knowledge of ritual action—which yields results that are limited and impermanent—it is said that Brahman, which possesses infinite fruit, is to be inquired into. || 16 ||

In this section on the qualification for the desire to know (jijñāsā-adhikāra), the objection that the scripture should not be commenced because linguistic proficiency is impossible is refuted with sound arguments. (17)

Because derivation is impossible, and because linguistic usage does not depend on the usage of elders [in that case], such usage serves as the cause for knowing the meaning of the word "kārya" (that which is to be done). 18.
The certainty is that the authority of a word lies solely in its [conveying] something to be accomplished;
since Brahman is of an already established nature, the Śruti cannot be a means of knowledge regarding it. (19)
Therefore, the view that "an investigation of this [reality] should not be undertaken here" is not correct;
for [the Buddha], having pointed out various objects situated before him with the gesture of his finger— (20)
By employing various words that denote those respective objects, Janaka and others diligently instruct children, saying, "Understand this," and so forth. (21)
Therefore, they themselves gradually come to know the power of the meaning of words, since the acquisition of proficiency is possible through such means as these. (22)
The authority of all scriptures up to the Vedas is firmly established once Brahman is proven;
therefore, it has been demonstrated that the inquiry into Brahman (Brahmamīmāṃsā) must indeed be undertaken. || 23 ||
Thus, the objection and the established conclusion are indicated in the very first aphorism, because the status of Brahman as the subject of inquiry is demonstrated here. (24)
Thus concludes the section on the desire to know (Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa).
The Section on "Origin and so forth" (Janmādyadhikaraṇa).
[The Brahman is that] from which there is the origin and so forth of this [world].
"What is the definition of this Brahman which is said to be the object of inquiry?"—it is for the fulfillment of such an expectation that the definition of Brahman is stated. (25)
The passages beginning with "yataḥ" are recited in the Taittirīyaka: "That from which the birth, sustenance, and dissolution of this world proceed... (26).
The definition of Brahman, such as being the cause of birth and so forth, is stated;
however, Brahman cannot be apprehended through its definition or through verbal testimony alone. (27)
Whether as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), it is likewise impossible for birth and the other [characteristics] to constitute the definition of this Brahman. (28)
For, on the view that they are qualifiers, because they serve to differentiate, Brahman—differentiated by those three—would likewise become manifold. (29)
In the second case as well, the known form of the object to be characterized is required;
since that is absent in the case of Brahman, this position too is not tenable. (30)
Thus, Brahman cannot be apprehended through its defining characteristics;
therefore, the argument that it is not an object of inquiry is untenable. (31)
It is not possible for this Brahman to be rendered manifold by means of non-contradictory qualifiers—such as differences in time or its being the cause of birth and so forth. (32)
And that entity which is established elsewhere as the Lord of Śrī and so forth is made known here by those defining characteristics as the meaning of the word "Brahman. (33)

Therefore, the triad of being the cause of origination, subsistence, and dissolution shall constitute the individual definition of this Brahman; and it may also constitute its definition collectively.
Thus concludes the section on "origination and so forth" (Janmādyadhikaraṇa).
The Section Concerning Scripture Being the Source [of Brahman] (Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa)
Because [Brahman] has the sacred scriptures as its source.
Although Brahman can be defined by its characteristics and can be realized through them,
nevertheless, that Brahman is not to be known by means of the instrument of inference.
Therefore, that which is known through scripture must be unknowable by any other means of knowledge;
consequently, the authority of statements such as "because" (yataḥ) and so forth is not applicable here.
Let it not be so; for by means of inference, Brahman—intended to be proven as omniscient, omnipotent, and distinct from the individual soul—cannot be established.

Therefore, because it is not cognizable through other means of knowledge and because it is the exclusive object of scripture, there is no impairment whatsoever to the authority of the scriptures regarding Brahman. (38)
Thus ends the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] concerning the fact that [Brahman] has the sacred scriptures as its source.
The Section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa)
But that [Brahman is the cause], because of the harmony [of all scriptural texts].

Even if it were unattained by other means of knowledge, [the Veda] would not lead to activity and so forth because of its lack of connection [to such ends]; furthermore, since Brahman is of an already established nature, it would be devoid of purposeful utility. || 39 ||
"Since it is impossible for the scripture to have authority regarding that [Self], it is utterly inconsistent to argue that it cannot be made known by it. (40)
The status of the scripture as a means of valid knowledge arises from its connection with that [Brahman] as the human goal;
for Brahman, the Vedāntas indeed become the supreme person. (41)
For they indeed bring about the realization of the nature of infinite bliss, just as the knowledge of the life of a virtuous son or father brings joy.
Even such knowledge of Brahman would constitute a human goal (puruṣārtha),
for it itself is this most exalted human purpose, which bestows supreme bliss.

Because it is connected with the scripture through its nature as bliss and by virtue of being that which makes [the scripture] understood, that Brahman is established as having the scripture as its means of valid cognition (pramāṇaka). || 44 ||
Thus concludes the section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa).
The Section on "Because of Beholding" (Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa)
Because of seeing, [the cause] is not that which is not based on scripture.

Thus, the justification for undertaking the treatise has been established by means of these four aphorisms; now, the doctrine that primordial matter (pradhāna) and other such principles are the cause [of the world] will be refuted in due order.
In the *Ṣaḍvidyā*, the causality of the insentient *prakṛti* is heard;

Thus, for the purpose of quieting that objection, there follows the section on "Iksati" (the act of seeing),
[stating] that the substance of this world, which consists of the three qualities (guṇas), is of such a nature.
In that case, the material cause would have to be of the same genus as its effect;
for in such passages as "That fire thought," the act of seeing is heard to be used in a figurative sense. (48)
In the sentence "It thought" (tadaikṣata) as well, the act of seeing must be figurative;
for here, because of the statement of the proposition and the illustrative example, [the self] is known through inference.
The view that the Pradhāna alone is what is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being) and so forth is an incorrect opinion;

Because it is impossible for Brahman, whose nature consists of both consciousness and unconsciousness, to possess a commonality with all things, and because the reason [stated by the opponent]—that primary seeing is impossible here—is not established. || 51 ||

And because [the Supreme Self] is not apprehended through inference, the Supreme Person is denoted by the word "Being" (sat) in the sentences of the Sadvidyā section, which are the object of the Chāndogya Śruti. || 52 ||
If it is argued that [the term "Self"] is used in a secondary sense, we say no, because of the word "Self."

Because liberation is taught for one who is devoted to that.

For the individual soul (jīva) who is steadfast in the worship of the Real, the supreme fruit known as liberation is heard [in scripture]; therefore, that which is denoted by "Real" (sat) is Brahman, and not the Unborn (aja).
And because there is no statement regarding its being something to be abandoned.

Because of [the Lord's] merging [into Himself].

Because of the commonality of their destinies.

The Section Concerning the One Consisting of Bliss (Ānandamayādhikaraṇa)
The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition.

"Since primary seeing is impossible for that which is insentient, it cannot be the cause"—this having been stated, the objection that "then let the individual soul (jīva) be [the cause]" is here refuted. (63)

Due to the absence of any excellence [in the individual soul], and because of its connection with practiced bliss, such a state of possessing that [supreme] bliss would not be possible for this living being. (67)

"If it be argued that [the Self] is not [denoted by the word 'Self'] because the word refers to a modification, we say no; for [the word] is used in the sense of abundance."

And because its cause is designated.

And it is proclaimed as being exactly according to the words of the mantra.
For it is Brahman alone that is celebrated here as expressed in the mantra beginning with "Truth" (satyam);
therefore, by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), the Supreme who consists of bliss is meant.
It is not the other, because that is untenable.

The individual soul (jīva) that is distinct from Brahman cannot be one arisen from the syllables of the mantra, because the property of being a knower whose sole object is Brahman would be untenable [for such a soul]. (73)
And because there is a designation of difference.
Therefore, by the phrase "Or rather," the distinction of this one consisting of bliss from the one consisting of consciousness—namely, that it is beyond the individual soul—is stated. (74)
And because it is a matter of desire, there is no dependence on inference.
The creation of the world occurs through His mere volition; He has no dependence on anything else.
The individual soul (jīva), however, depends upon Him even for the slightest thing; therefore, He is the Supreme Person (para-pumān). || 75 ||
And in this [world], he teaches his union with that [Brahman].

The yoga of bliss is said to belong to the individual soul (jīva) within that which consists of bliss; for this is known from such scriptural passages as "For it is only by tasting... Therefore, [the Self] is held to be distinct from the individual soul.
Thus concludes the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa).
The Section on Disappearance (Antaradhikaraṇa)
[The Self within] is [the Supreme Lord], because of the teaching of His attributes.
The causality of the soul in general was previously refuted; now, having raised that doubt regarding its specific form, it is rejected in this present argument. (77)

The person heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad in the passage "He who is within this [eye]" and "He who is in the sun," by virtue of having the eye and the sun as His abodes, is the individual soul (jīva) and is distinct [from the Supreme Self]. (78)
"It is the individual souls (jīvas) alone who possess that [movement], because they are heard to have bodies;
do not say so, for it is the Supreme Self (paramātman) residing in the eye and the sun, and no other. (79)
Indeed, on account of the teaching regarding the collection of qualities such as being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva),
corporeality cannot be established as a proof for being subject to karma.
That his divine and auspicious form is non-material, conforming to His own nature, and assumed solely by His own will, is known by all the sacred scriptures. (81)
And [the Self] is other [than the body], because there is a designation of difference.
Because of the teaching of difference through such statements as "He who is in the self," the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the Inner Self, distinct from the individual soul whose mouth is the sun. 82.
Thus ends the section on the intermediate state (*antarādhikaraṇa*).
The Section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa)
It is space, because of its characteristic marks.
The cause, the reality determined to be distinct from both the conscious and the unconscious, is said to be unattached; this doctrine is here refuted. (83)

In passages such as "All these are contained within the Sāman," that which is heard to be the cause must be the ether (ākāśa), specifically the physical space (viyat), because of its usage in common worldly parlance.
Since there would otherwise be no determination as to from what the elements are born, the statement "from space," and so forth, serves to provide that specific meaning. (85)

It is not so; the Supreme Person is what is denoted here by the word "space" (ākāśa), because many exclusive characteristics of that [Person] are heard repeatedly in scripture, distinct from the elemental ether.
For in this case, a sentence is heard that has the nature of a restatement of what is already established;
therefore, it depends upon the attainment [of its object] by another means of valid cognition. (87)
Brahman, called Nārāyaṇa, awakens all measure;
because it shines forth through its own manifestation, it is denoted by that word. 88.
Thus concludes the section concerning space (ākāśādhikaraṇa).
The Section Concerning Prāṇa.
For this very reason, it is the vital breath (prāṇa).
In the preceding section, the status of space as the cause of all was refuted; here, the causality of wind asserted by others is rejected. (89)
In this context, the scriptural passage beginning with "All these [beings] enter into breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.11.5) is heard;
and here, just like the word "ether," the word "breath" (prāṇa) is also indicative of Brahman.
Because the unique mark (liṅga) has been cited as if it were well-known, there is here a greater degree of doubt regarding the existence of the collection of elements and so forth. (91)

If it is argued that because air is dependent upon the vital breath (prāṇa), the element air must be the cause [of consciousness], the rebuttal is that this is not the case for stone and the like, nor for the nature of consciousness itself. (92)
Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa).
The Section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa)
[The Brahman is] light, because of the mention of its feet.
Having thus refuted the causality of space and air in due order, the causality of fire is now rejected within this system of logic. (93)
Therefore, in the sentence "the light beyond heaven," that which is heard as exceedingly luminous must be the cause [of the world], together with the light within the body.
"Because of the instruction regarding oneness, let that which is well-known as light be what is spoken of here.
Do not say so; that which is denoted by the word "light" here is Brahman alone, and nothing else. (95)
Because the previous statement describes the act of moving through all beings, and because that [attribute] belongs to Brahman alone, as is well known from the Puruṣasūkta and other sources. (96)

If it be argued that [the Self is not the object of meditation] because of the mention of the meters, we say no; for there is a scriptural teaching regarding the fixing of the mind [upon the Self], and such is indeed seen [in other passages].

If it is argued that the Gāyatrī metre mentioned in the preceding statement is what is being sung here by means of the Ṛk verse that explains its meaning, and therefore that [verse] is not Brahman—this is not so. (97)
For the sake of the result, the perception of equality with the *gāyatrī* is enjoined;
for this four-footed Brahman, there is such a balance with it. (98)
In the Saṃvarga-vidyā and other instances, the connection with meters is observed despite the equality [of the subject matter];
and it is thus because the designation of the quarters as "the elements" and so forth is appropriate.
This statement, "She is four-footed," serves to make known that [Prakṛti] has the elements (bhūtas) and so forth as her feet. || 99 ||
This [instruction] is appropriate only with respect to this Brahman denoted by the word *gāyatrī*.
If it is argued that it is not so because of the difference in instruction, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case.
Because of the difference in case endings, which have distinct meanings, as in the expression "divo divi" (from heaven, in heaven). || 100 ||
It is not the case that the Brahman previously heard [in the first passage] is not recognized here;
for it is not so, since the nature of the object is one and the same despite the two different instructions. (101)
Because recognition is uncontradicted, it is the Supreme Self alone that is spoken of here;
it is certain that the instruction regarding the oneness with the gastric fire is solely for the sake of a specific result. 102.
Furthermore, the nature of the fire as being identical with the Supreme Self is proclaimed in the Gītā;
therefore, it is well-established here that he is indeed the Supreme Self. 103.
Thus ends the section concerning light.
The Section on Indra and Prāṇa.
Likewise, the vital breath [is Brahman], because of the accompanying [text].
The causality of the sun and other luminaries, denoted by the term "jyotis," has been refuted; now, the status of Devendra, who was established as their lord, is being rejected.
In the sentence "Pratardana" found in the Kauṣītaki Śruti, that which is denoted by the words Indra and Prāṇa is taught as the object of meditation for the sake of liberation. (105)

The word "Indra" refers to the individual soul (jīva) because it is well-known to denote that very thing; likewise, the word "Prāṇa" also refers to it, for here he [the soul] is the object of self-worship.
He taught that which is most beneficial, the means for attaining immortality;
for the meditation upon the Cause alone is the cause for the attainment of immortality. (107)
From the Vedic statement "of him, for so long," it is known that this very Indra, who possesses the well-known status of a living being (jīva), is the cause; such is the certainty. (108)

It is not so; the one denoted by the words "Indra" and "Prāṇa" is not merely the individual soul (jīva), but rather a different entity—Brahman—which is the subject introduced by those two terms. (109)
Because of the scriptural declarations of its being established in its own nature as bliss and immortality;

if it be argued that this is not so because of the instruction regarding the Self by the Teacher himself, [we reply] no, for in this [chapter] there is an abundance of internal (adhyātma) connections.
This [teaching] concerns the very self, whose status as the living soul has been made known, as the object of worship.
Therefore, it is said that the individual soul (jīva) alone, which was introduced as the object of meditation, is what is being described here.
Not so; for the attributes mentioned in this scriptural passage are consistent only with the Supreme Self.
Indeed, the attributes of the Supreme are as follows: being the object of meditation for the sake of liberation, being the substratum of all, and being the impeller of actions, and so forth. (112)
But the instruction is according to the perspective of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva.

Having understood from the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa and other passages that the Self is the inner controller (śarīrin), and from such expressions as "by this living soul" (anena jīvena) that words denote the individual soul (jīva); 113.
From the statement, "Worship me as the end and the ultimate," he has taught that one's own body is the Supreme Brahman to be worshipped.
Vāmadeva and other preeminent knowers of the supreme self also speak in this way in many ways, such as: "I am Manu, I am all," and so forth. (115)

If it be argued that [the Self spoken of here] is not the Supreme Self because of the characteristic marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (prāṇa), we say no; for there is a threefoldness of meditation, and because [the other two] are resorted to elsewhere, they are connected with this [context] as well.

Because of the observation here of marks pertaining to the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), there is no definitive conclusion regarding the meaning [of the passage] due to the abundance of previously mentioned internal (adhyātma) connections. || 116 ||

Do not say so; for here, with the intention of presenting worship as threefold, [it is taught] by way of [the Lord's] own essential nature, and likewise by way of His having the individual soul as His body. (117)
Thus, the worship of the Supreme Self is threefold by virtue of its being composed of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the limbs (*aṅga*);
and for the sake of instructing that [worship] in its three forms, it is expressed by various corresponding terms. (118)
And this threefold meditation is heard of elsewhere in the Śruti as well;
therefore, this context is intended to teach such meditations. (119)
Therefore, here the Supreme Self—distinct from the individual soul (jīva), denoted by the words "Indra" and "Prāṇa," and possessing the body of both enjoyer and enjoyed—is taught. || 120 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Indra and Prāṇa.
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter.
The Second Quarter of the First Chapter.
The Section on Universal Renown (Sarvatraprasiddhyadhikaraṇa)

Having examined the passages containing the less clear marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and other such entities under the aphorism "Because of the teaching established everywhere" (*sarvatra prasiddhopadeśāt*),
the collection of passages containing indistinct marks is now being investigated in this section. (121)

The status of being the cause and the status of being the object of worship have been predicated of the one who possesses the vital breath (prāṇa) as his body; fearing that these two might belong to the individual soul (jīva), this [objection] is now refuted. 122.
In passages such as "All this, indeed," the individual soul (jīva) is heard of as being the self of all; for it is only of this [soul] that identity with everything is possible.

The state of being Brahmā and all other beings arises from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of that very [Supreme Being]; for that Supreme Being, who is untouched by defects, such a state is not logically possible [in itself]. || 124 ||

Furthermore, in certain passages, the word "Brahman" is applied even to the individual soul (jīva), because its birth and so forth have their cause in the karma belonging to that [soul], according to the principle "it is born from that, it dissolves into that, and it originates from that. (125)
The statement that even the mention of a cause would be logical is not an accepted view;
for the Supreme Person, Brahman, is declared to be the Self within all things. (126)

Since that very [nature] which is well-known in another context is restated here, having restated its being produced from that and so forth, its being caused by that and being identical with that is stated. (127)

For the individual self (jīvātman), which assumes forms such as gods or mortals produced by karma, there can be no [birth and so forth] in the Vedānta texts, since birth and other states are heard of [only in relation to the body]. || 128 ||
He alone should be the one denoted here by the word "Brahman," for He is the Supreme Person;
since Brahman has the sentient and insentient entities as His body, [the term applies] to the Embodied One.

Consequently, the defects residing in the body would not belong to him; thus, he would be entirely free from defect. Furthermore, the statement that the individual soul (jīva) possesses identity with everything is not tenable.
Since it is impossible for those things distinct from their respective bodies to be identical with one another, the Supreme Self alone is intended here as the meaning of the word "Brahman. (131)
And because the intended qualities are applicable.

Furthermore, all these qualities such as being mind-made (manomaya) and so forth, when intended [as attributes], are appropriate only for the Supreme Being, who is endowed with the power of true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatā). || 132 ||
But because of the impossibility [of its occurrence], it is not the embodied soul.
Because these qualities are impossible in this embodied being, this is not the embodied soul; rather, it is the Supreme Brahman that is celebrated here.
And because of the designation of [Brahman] as both the object and the agent of action.
"He who thinks 'I shall fully realize [it]' is the object of meditation, described as that which is to be attained;
the individual soul (jīva) is described as the attainer. Therefore, the Supreme Person is other than the individual soul. (134)
Because of the distinction in sound.

In the statement "This is my Self," the embodied soul is denoted by the genitive case; however, the one to be meditated upon is the Supreme Person, who is distinct from that, as indicated by the nominative case. (135)
And because of Smṛti.

Furthermore, the traditional teaching beginning with "I am all" speaks of the individual soul as the worshiper and the Supreme Self as the object of worship; therefore, the Supreme Self is distinct from the individual soul. (136)

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of knowledge] because of its having a small abode and because of the designation of such [smallness], we say no; for it is precisely because it is to be perceived as such, and it is like space.

If it is argued that "this [Brahman] is not the Supreme because of designations such as being small or residing in a small place," we say no; for this is an instruction based on the fact that it is to be meditated upon in such a manner. (137)
There is no indication of a diminution in its essential nature, because of the designation of its pre-eminence.
If it be argued that [if the individual soul were omnipresent] there would be the consequence of experiencing [the fruits of others' actions], we say no, because of the difference in status.
If that supreme Self resides within the body of a lay follower (upāsaka), [then... || 138 ||
If it is argued that "in the same way, there is the attainment of the experience of pleasure and pain for this [self] as well," we say no; for residing within the body is not the sole cause. (139)

Subjection to karma alone is the cause for experiencing [the fruits of action], not [the case] with Him who is intent on that [liberation], who is the adversary of all that is to be abandoned, and who is an ocean of all auspicious qualities. (140)
Thus concludes the section on "Establishment Everywhere."
The Section on the Eating of Remnants (attradhikaraṇa).
The Self [is meant], because of the mention of both the moving and the non-moving.
If there were no other [transcendent] enjoyer, then the one heard of as the enjoyer would be the individual soul (jīva) alone everywhere; this doctrine is here refuted. (141)

In the mantra beginning with "yasya brahma" found in the Kaṭhavallī, that which is heard as the "eater" (attā) is the individual soul (jīva), because it is possible for this very soul to be the enjoyer of the fruits of karma. (142)

It is not so; for here, by the scriptural statement of being the consumer of the universe, it is the Supreme Self alone that is meant, since the eating of the whole is spoken of in this context through the mention of death as the condiment. (143)
And such a consumption is intended here as the dissolution of all things;
this agency of being an enjoyer conditioned by karma does not belong to the Supreme Self. (144)
Therefore, this state of being the sustainer and the enjoyer of the worlds is impossible for the individual soul (jīva); consequently, the Supreme Person is the Eater.
And because of the context.
"This Self is great and all-pervading," and "this is not the Self"—since this section concerns the Supreme, therefore this is the Supreme Person. (146)
For by seeing that, the two selves have entered the cave.

In the verse "The two who drink the Truth" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*), that which is heard as the enjoyer of the fruit is the individual soul (*jīva*) together with the vital breath (*prāṇa*); therefore, it is incorrect to say that the "eater" here is that [Supreme Self]. (147)
It is said that both the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) have entered the cave; indeed, their entry into that very place is perceived here. 148.

The abiding of the Supreme in the cave is described by the Śruti as "difficult to see," whereas the abiding of the individual soul (jīva) therein is established by the statement, "by means of the vital breath" (prāṇena). || 149 ||
The statement "the two drinking the Truth" (ṛtaṃ pibantau) is consistent through the analogy of those holding an umbrella;
for the other [the Self] may be connected with the act of drinking either as the actual agent or as the instigator. (150)
And because of the qualification.

From the beginning to the end of this treatise, both the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) are distinguished by their respective attributes; therefore, the Supreme Person is the Eater (attā). || 151 ||
Thus ends this section.
The Section on the Intermediate State.
On account of the intermediate state.
The difficulty of knowing the Supreme was stated previously with the words "Who indeed... and so forth;
therefore, the objection that the Supreme is not described as being visible is now set aside. (152)
Based on the statement, "He who is in the eye," it is heard that the support of the eye is either the individual soul (jīva), or a reflection, or else the presiding deity of the eye. (153)

By virtue of being spoken of as something already established, one of these [three] must be the case; however, it is not stated that the Supreme Self is among them, because its visibility is not established. (154)

Do not say so; for by logical reasoning, the Supreme Lord resides within that very [heart], as evidenced by the abundance of His innate and natural qualities, such as being the "gatherer of all blessings" (saṃyadvāma) and so forth. || 155 ||
And because of the designation of place and so forth.

Since it is heard in such passages as "He who [is] the eyes" that this very Supreme Self alone is the controller of the abiding [of the senses] in the eye, therefore the one residing in the eye is the Supreme.
Therefore, speech that treats [the object] as if it were well-known is appropriate only with respect to the Supreme Self;
here, the statement "it is seen" is based on the reason of being visible to yogis.
And also because it is designated as being distinguished by bliss.

By means of the passage beginning with "Kaṃ brahma" (What is Brahman?), for the purpose of establishing the locus and other attributes of the very same Supreme Being under discussion previously through its possession of excellence of bliss, [the text proceeds]. (158)
Because of the designation "He who is this," the person within the eye here is the Supreme;
and for that very reason, He is Brahman.
How is that which was declared by the words "What is Brahman? and so forth, described as "Brahman"? || 159 ||
If it is argued that the method of perceiving Brahman as "Ka" and "Kha" would be different, that is not so;
for that which is indeed "Ka" is the very same as "Kha," since the entity of space (kha) is present therein.
Therefore, the teaching on the excellence of bliss is here designated by the word *kha*;
for the supreme Brahman is space (*ākāśa*), whose nature is unlimited bliss. (161)
It has been stated at the end that they spoke to him of both the vital breath (prāṇa) and that space (ākāśa);
therefore, Brahman—which is the subject under discussion—is of the nature of unlimited bliss.
Because it is heard here as well that [the Self] has the eye as its support, the Supreme is located in the eye;
and because there is a description of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads.
That destination which is to be reached by those who have realized the true nature of Brahman.
Elsewhere, the path beginning with light (arcirādi) is heard as leading to the attainment of Brahman;
here, however, it is recited as the destination to be reached by the Person in the Eye who has been heard [in the Upanishads].
It is certain that the Supreme Self is the one who dwells within the eye as the Atman;
it is not any other, because of the impossibility [of others] and because of the lack of stability.
Because neither the living soul nor the reflection of the sun remains stable. || 165 ||
Because qualities that possess the nature of being free from limiting adjuncts cannot possibly exist in the eyes by necessity, the person within the eye is none other than the Supreme Self. 166.
Thus concludes the section on the intermediate state.
The Section on the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa)
The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) [is Brahman], because His attributes are designated in relation to the deities, the worlds, and so forth.
Having first established the opponent's position regarding the existence of the eye, the argument here is refuted that the existence [of the eye] belongs to the soul alone. (167)

In the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa, that which is heard as the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) through the statement "He who is within the earth," may be the individual soul (jīva), because of its possession of seeing and other such qualities. (168)

Furthermore, this doctrine is not accepted because it negates another seer; for such a view contradicts the scriptural texts marked by terms such as "with reference to the deities" (adhidaiva) and "with reference to the worlds" (adhiloka). || 169 ||
The inner controller (antaryāmī) is indeed the Supreme Self, because of the designation of His attributes;
likewise, He possesses the state of having the universe as His body and the nature of being the inner controller of all. (170)
In this very context, such qualities as these are taught as being dependent upon Nārāyaṇa;
for the perception [of Him] and so forth is the direct realization of form and the rest, and not otherwise.
The statement "There is nothing else besides this" negates any other seer equal [to it];
nor is the embodied self [the one referred to], because its attributes are not described there.
Likewise, neither the Pradhāna nor the Jīva is the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmī) of those two.
Because they repeatedly express doctrines that are impossible, just as an insentient thing is unfit [to speak], so too are these [teachers] unfit [to speak]. 173.
For both [schools] indeed study this [text] with a distinction.

Since the Kāṇvas and Mādhyandinas study the Inner Controller as distinct from the individual soul (jīva), ending with the words, "He who is in knowledge, he who is in the self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22).
Therefore, this Supreme Person, the Inner Controller, is distinct from the individual soul;
He is the Self beyond all, free from sin, established as Nārāyaṇa. (175)
Thus ends the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmi-Adhikaraṇa).
The Section Concerning the One Possessing Qualities such as Invisibility.
The one characterized by qualities such as invisibility [is Brahman], because of the statement of its attributes.
The doubt that "where the state of being the supreme self is not present through [the possession of] the nature of a seer and so forth, there must be the Pradhāna alone" is hereby dispelled. (176)
That which is heard in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad in passages such as "that which is invisible," and "the source of beings," and also "higher than the high Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.5–6); || 177 ||
In this context, "dense" (ghana) refers respectively to the cowherd and the dense [cloud];
because of the negation [of consciousness], and because it exists as non-consciousness and is an object of perception, it is insentient. (178)

The primary cause (pradhāna) would be of the same class [as the effect], as would the imperishable source of beings (bhūtayoni); furthermore, the claim that "beyond the imperishable there is the mass of individual souls (jīvaghana), which is higher" is incorrect. (179)

In this context, that which possesses qualities such as invisibility and is higher than the Imperishable (akṣara) is the Supreme Self alone, because of the scriptural revelation of its attributes, such as omniscience. (180)
The word "akṣara" ending in the fifth case denotes the subtle element (bhūtasūkṣma); that akṣara possesses qualities such as invisibility and so forth, and it exists everywhere.

Because it is "other" than that [world], and because being "other" than that is impossible for anything else, this [Brahman] is indeed distinguished by such attributes as omniscience and being the source of the world. (182)
And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, it is neither of the other two.

And here, by means of the great context, the promise of omniscience, and other such arguments, [the text] distinguishes the Imperishable (akṣara) from both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
By these two terms, "the further" and "the beyond," his distinction is taught;
therefore, it is said here that the Lord Nārāyaṇa is beyond those two.
And because of the presentation of form.
The form described by the verse beginning with "Agnirmūrdhā" belongs to the Supreme Self alone, who has the three worlds as his form; therefore, this is the Supreme Person. (185)
Thus concludes the section concerning the one characterized by qualities such as invisibility.
The Section Concerning Vaiśvānara.
Vaiśvānara [is the Supreme Self], because of the distinction of a common term.
The supreme nature [of the Lord] has been established by virtue of His possessing the form of the three worlds;
here, the doubt that this same [nature] might belong to another as well is dispelled. (186)
In the passage concerning Vaiśvānara as having a universal nature, it is by no means possible to determine that Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self. (187)

Because these [words] are applied to the digestive fire, to that state, to a being, to the divine, and to the Supreme Self—in all four cases—due to the perception of their indicative marks (liṅga) in this context. (188)
It is not so; the Supreme Person is indeed denoted by the term Vaiśvānara, because this common word [is applied] to Him through His attributes that are unique to the Supreme. (189)
Because it is being qualified here by many attributes such as "being the self of all" and so forth,
that which is being remembered would constitute an inference.
The form of the Vaiśvānara Self, characterized by having heaven as its head and so forth, has thus been described. (190)
And here, that very same [Self], well-known from the Śruti and Smṛti, being recognized as "this is that indeed," belongs to this Vaiśvānara Self. (191)
This is a mark [indicating] that the Supreme Self is meant; therefore, Vaiśvānara is the Supreme.

If it be argued that He is not [the Supreme] because of the mention of "sound" and so forth, and because of His being established within, we say no, because there is instruction for viewing Him as such, because [those attributes] are impossible [in the Supreme], and because they also study this one as the Puruṣa.
"Agni Vaiśvānara" [is established] through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). || 192 ||

From the conception of it as the threefold fire (tretāgni), from its location, from the oblation of breath, and from its abiding within the body, its nature as the digestive fire (jāṭhara) is understood. || 193 ||
If it is argued that, for this reason, he cannot be the Supreme Self, we say no;
for such is not the case here, because Vaiśvānara has the fire within the belly as his body.

Because there is an injunction for meditation upon that [Supreme Self] as qualified [by the gastric fire], whereas for the mere gastric fire alone, it is impossible for it to have the three worlds as its limbs. (195)
In this way, some Vājasaneyins record the Vaiśvānara as the Self and as the Puruṣa, according to the statement: "He is this very fire. (196)
Indeed, this Lord Nārāyaṇa alone, whose nature is Vaiśvānara, is to be meditated upon, for he is designated by the term "the Person who has emerged beyond all limiting adjuncts. (197)
For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an elemental being.
Since this person is the Vaiśvānara Self, free from limiting adjuncts,
and has the three worlds as his limbs, he is therefore neither an element nor a deity.
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even with direct perception.
In this context, even the word "Agni" denotes the Supreme Self by virtue of the quality of being the first to attain [the goal], just as the term "Vaiśvānara" does. (199)
Therefore, the designation of Vaiśvānara by the word "Agni" is not sublated;
the sage Jaimini considers this to be the case in the determination of its supreme nature. (200)
"Because of manifestation," says Āśmarathya.

Regarding this, Āśmarathya says that the teaching concerning the limited size of the celestial chariot (vimāna) of the Supreme Self is intended to manifest [the status of] the lay follower (upāsaka). 201.
Bādari [holds that the soul's departure] is for the sake of recollection.
The venerable seer Bādari has stated that the conceptualization of the body here, from the head down to the feet, is for the purpose of meditative worship.
"Jaimini [holds that the fruit arises] from attainment; for thus the scripture shows."

The analogy of the householder’s fires, such as the *gārhapatya*, is applied to the constituent parts of the lay follower (*upāsaka*) with respect to the rite called the "oblation of breath" (*prāṇāhuti*), which is performed daily. (203)
Jaimini declared that this is for the sake of accomplishing the status of the Agnihotra; and he shows that accomplishment in the passage beginning with "He who [performs it] thus. (204)
And they record this [Self] in this [body].

Within this body of the lay devotee (upāsaka), [he should meditate upon] this Vaiśvānara, the Supreme Self, whose body consists of heaven, earth, and so forth, by means of the oblation of the vital breaths into the fire.
The introductory passages, such as "They proclaim his words for the sake of worship," establish that Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Person, Nārāyaṇa. Thus it is proven. (206)
Thus concludes the section concerning Vaiśvānara.
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter.
Now begins the third quarter of the first chapter.
The Section Concerning Heaven, Earth, and the Other Elements (Dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa)
The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word.
In the preceding [pāda], passages containing signs and statements that were either very indistinct or indistinct regarding the marks [of Brahman] were examined;
in this pāda, passages containing clear signs and statements regarding the individual soul (jīva) and so forth are now investigated.
The supreme self-nature of that which has heaven, earth, and so forth as its locus has been established; that very point is now challenged in this section and firmly reaffirmed. (208)
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad it is heard: "In whom heaven and earth are contained.
Here, it is the individual soul (jīva) that is the locus of the instruments and the subject of manifold births. (209)
And [the opponent argues] that the yoga of the channels (nāḍīyoga) and so forth is taught as the accumulation of the qualities of the individual soul (jīva);
[we reply: it is not so, for the abode of heaven, earth, and so on is the Supreme Brahman, because of its own specific term [in the text]. (210)
The word "own" (sva) here refers to such passages as "This is the bridge to immortality";
it is declared that this very [Self] is the cause for attaining immortality. || 211 ||

And here, the word "Self" (ātman) refers to the Supreme Being without any limiting adjuncts; omniscience and other such qualities mentioned here are perfectly consistent with that very Being alone. (212)

And its being the substratum of the channels is stated based on the continuous scriptural passages, such as the Śruti beginning with "unborn" (ajāyamāna), and from the Smṛti which says "He is also unborn" (aja). || 213 ||
It is established that he manifests in many ways by his own will;
it is logical that he, who is the substratum of all, has the mind and other faculties as his locus. (214)
And because there is the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated.

Then, from such scriptural statements as "the wise man [transcends] merit and sin," and because the Supreme Person is designated as that which is to be attained by those liberated from bondage, [He is established]. (215)
Nor is there inference [of a creator], because of the word "that" and because of the mention of "living beings."
Just as it is said that the Pradhāna is not the primary subject here due to the absence of a word denoting it,
so too this living being (prāṇabhṛt) is not to be understood from the sentence.
On account of the designation of difference.
By the statement beginning with "In the same tree," the Lord is designated as an ocean of majesty, distinct from the individual soul. (217)
From the context.

By means of the multitude of scriptural words such as "the highest" and "beyond this," and because it is the subject under discussion, that which is heard in this context is indeed the Supreme Brahman alone. (218)
And on account of abiding and eating.

In the mantra beginning with "dvā suparṇā," the state of being an enjoyer of the fruit is stated for one [of the two birds], while for the other, only its mere existence within the body is demonstrated. (219)
In that state, not eating yet shining brightly, he becomes the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth;
he is not the enjoyer of those things. Therefore, the Supreme Person is the one who has heaven, earth, and so forth as his abode.
Thus concludes the section concerning "Heaven, Earth, and so forth."
The Section on the Abundance [of Bliss] (Bhūmādhikaraṇa)
The Infinite is [the Self] because it is taught as being superior to the state of perfect serenity.

The identity of the Self with the Supreme has been established previously through the continuity of the context; now, by that very same reason, the notion that "the individual soul (jīva) is merely the plenitude (bhūman)" is cast aside. 221.
The statement "where one sees nothing else" is recited in the Sāman;
there, the Bhūman is the inner self (pratyagātman) denoted by the word "Prāṇa."

Because the instruction on the Self as name and so forth has reached its conclusion immediately thereafter, and because there is an absence of further questions and answers, as well as the end of the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa). || 223 ||
If it is argued that the "plurality" (bhūman) here refers to the inner self (pratyagātman) because of its uninterrupted continuity, that is not so;
for the plurality is the Supreme (para), as it is taught to be superior to the state of perfect serenity (saṃprasāda).
It is determined by another scriptural passage that "the serene being" is the inner self;
for it is stated that this knower of the vital breath speaks of the superiority of his own object of worship. (225)

With the word "but" (tu), [the author] introduces another proponent of the "exceeding speech" (ativādin) himself, setting aside this proponent of the breath as the True (satyopāsituḥ) who speaks beyond [the breath]. || 226 ||

Because of the statement of superiority, because of the interruption, and because of the context of the vital breath (prāṇa), that which is denoted by the word "Truth" (satya) is declared to be a different entity from the vital breath. || 227 ||
This Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Infinite (bhūman), is of the nature of absolute bliss; for [only in Him] is dharma logically possible.
And innate immortality is abiding in one's own majesty alone. || 228 ||

Furthermore, those attributes such as being the self of all and so forth, which are heard in the context of the "Full" (Bhūman), are logically possible only in the Supreme; therefore, the Full is the Supreme Person.
Thus concludes the section concerning the Infinite (Bhūma).
The Section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa)
The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the ether.
It was previously established that Brahman abides in its own majesty; this [present verse] refutes the notion that such [abiding] exists in anything other than that Supreme.
In the Gārgī-praśna, the passage beginning with "He said, 'This indeed... is recited.
