Here, the Imperishable (akṣara) must be the Pradhāna, as it possesses attributes such as being neither gross nor subtle. (231)
Because the word "akṣara" is used for the Pradhāna [in the phrase] "from the akṣara," [it refers] to the cause even of the ether (ākāśa), which serves as the substratum for all effects. || 232 ||
If that which is spoken in response to a question were "unexplained," it would be [merely] the syllable;
but it is not so here, for the Supreme Person is what is denoted by the word "syllable" (akṣara).

Because it also sustains Pradhāna, which is as boundless as space, [the scripture] begins with the words "That which is above" and [describes] that which exists throughout the three periods of time. (234)
The ether (ambara) is not said to be the wind, but rather it is declared to be the substratum for all that is born of modification;
however, it must be the unmanifest (avyākṛta) that lies beyond that.
That Imperishable, described as the support of that [world], is not the Pradhāna;
and it is so because of its presiding over [the world].
In that case, the individual soul (jīva) is the Imperishable (akṣara), distinct from the entire category of insentient things.
This doctrine—that [the ether] is established as a substratum—is refuted by the passage beginning with "Of this very syllable," which establishes that [ether] belongs to this syllable. (237)
It is taught that steadfastness arises precisely from his command;
for such a command could not possibly belong even to those who are bound or already liberated. (238)
And because of the exclusion of other states.

The supplementary portion of the text beginning with "the unseen seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11) [establishes] that it is other than the Supreme Self; furthermore, the subsequent passage excludes any difference between this [individual self] and the Imperishable (akṣara). // 239 //
Or rather, it excludes the existence of any other [being] characterized by such qualities;
therefore, there is a Supreme Person who is the sustainer of all, dependent upon His own teaching. (240)
Thus concludes the section on the syllable *Om*.
The Section Concerning the Object of the Act of Seeing.
He is that [Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing.
It was previously stated that another [entity] cannot be perceived by others;
therefore, it is now refuted that what is described as being "perceivable" could not be another. (241)

Furthermore, regarding the question, that which is recited beginning with "him who consists of three measures" (*trimātra*) refers here to the four-faced one (*caturmukha*), designated as the "Supreme Person" (*paraṃ puruṣam*). (242)
For those who worship the Praṇava mantra consisting of one or two mātrās,
the respective fruits consist of attaining the world of mortals and attaining the world of the intermediate space.

Having been described as that which is attained by one who meditates on the three *mātrās*, the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) is [understood] to be beyond the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) by virtue of its association with that. (244)
The world of Viriñca is indeed seen by that very [Being] residing there;
however, it is not so, for in this context, the Supreme Person alone is the object of his vision. (245)

In the final verse of the passage beginning with "Beyond the sun," there is the teaching that the object of the act of seeing is characterized by being without limiting adjuncts, peacefulness, immortality, and so forth. (246)

Thus, when the identity with the Supreme Self is established, that state of the world of Brahmā is what is described here as "that which the seers [call] 'the poets'," which is frequented by the sun-like sages.
It is understood that this refers to that very abode of Vaikuṇṭha;
nor is there any world of the Creator (Brahmā) separated from the intermediate space.
Because many worlds such as heaven and others arise in the midst [of this], the Lord Nārāyaṇa is heard here as the object of the act of seeing. (249)
Thus concludes the section concerning the object of the act of seeing.
The Section on the Subtle Space within the Heart (Daharādhikaraṇa)
The small [ether] is [Brahman], because of the subsequent [scriptural passages].
Previously, the supreme nature of that which lies within the city (the heart) was established;
here, the supreme nature of that which is designated by the term "ether" is being firmly established. (250)
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the passage beginning with "Now, that which is within this" is recited; here, the small ether heard in the text is determined to be the elemental ether. (251)

If it is argued that this is because the word "space" (ākāśa) is preeminently well-known in that very sense, and because it is perceived as the substratum for that which is to be sought, we say: no, that is not so.
The inner space (daharākāśa) is the Supreme Self (parātmā), because of the attributes stated in the subsequent passage:
its being the essential nature of the self (svābhāvikātmatva) and its freedom from sin (apahatapāpmatva). || 253 ||
Furthermore, "having true resolve" and "having true desires"—these are the exclusive attributes of the Supreme Self, as recited in the subsequent passage. (254)
Furthermore, there is another thing to be sought here: the group of eight qualities residing within that [small space].
Having introduced both the small space and the collection of qualities, [the text proceeds] with respect to both of them. (255)
Thus, by such statements as "That which is as vast as this space," it is enjoined that [Brahman] is to be meditated upon as something to be sought after. (256)
Furthermore, a clear distinction is perceived between the small space and [ordinary] space;
therefore, the small space must be the Supreme Self and cannot be the physical ether. (257)
On account of the movement and the word; for thus is the mark seen.
And in this small space, there is the daily departure of conscious beings who do not know [the truth], as well as the destination to which they go. (258)
The mention of the "abode of Brahman" and [the mention of] "immortality"—both of these indicate the supreme nature of this small space (dahara);
that pair is seen elsewhere as well.
"Having attained [the state of] existence, one goes to this world of Brahman," according to the Śruti;
what else could there be here than these two things being heard? (260)
Indeed, there is sufficient evidence for the fact that the "Child" (Dahara) is the Supreme Self,
because its supporting and its greatness are perceived within it.
And [this is so] because Brahman alone is the exclusive object proclaimed by all the Vedāntas. || 261 ||

Because the Infinite One, known as the Sustainer of the World, is proclaimed even within this small space, the glorious Supreme Nārāyaṇa is declared to be the Space within the Small (daharākāśa). || 262 ||
And because of common renown.

For in such passages as "Who indeed shall breathe? and so forth, since this term "ether" (ākāśa) is well-established as referring to the Supreme Self, the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is the Supreme Person.
If it be argued that "He" refers to the other [the individual soul] because of the reference to it, we say no, because of impossibility.

If it is argued that the one described as "this serene being who departs from here" is the individual soul (jīva) distinct from the Supreme, and that this must be the "small ether" (daharākāśa) mentioned here—no, that is not so. (264)

Because the aforementioned qualities residing in the small [space] are impossible in this [state], [it is argued that the soul is not the agent]; if it is argued that [the soul is the agent] because of the subsequent [scriptural passage], [we reply]: "But [it is so] when its true nature has become manifest."
In the subsequent statement regarding Prajāpati, the individual soul (jīva) is likewise such.

Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the small [space] is He, on account of its being described as having its evil destroyed and so forth; for previously its qualities were concealed, [but they are revealed] thereafter through the meditation upon Brahman. (266)

But the individual soul (jīva) is proclaimed there as one whose true nature has become manifest; however, because the small [space] possesses its natural qualities, there is no notion of a "living being" here. (267)
And the reference has another purpose.
In this context, the individual soul (jīva) is mentioned for the purpose of indicating the Supreme, which is the foremost attainment known as the manifestation of the soul's true nature. (268)
If it be argued that this is because [the scripture] has little to hear, that has already been answered.
If it is argued that here the possession of limited knowledge and learning is appropriate for the individual soul (jīva) alone and not for the greater [Self],
the answer to this has already been stated previously.
And because of the imitation of that.
For one who is liberated from imitation of others, there is the possession of the eightfold qualities;
therefore, the object of imitation (the *dahara*) is superior to the living self (*jīva*), which is the imitator. || 270 ||
It is also recorded in the Smṛti.
Through the worship of the other, it is said that this individual soul attains identity with Him;
according to the Smṛti, "This is knowledge," that which is other than the individual soul is the Supreme. (271)
Thus concludes the section on the "Small" (dahara-adhikaraṇa).
The Section on the Measured [Object] (Pramitādhikaraṇa)
"He is known from the word alone."
The magnitude of the Supreme Self has been described as being vast;
here, it is stated that He possesses the measure of a thumb. (272)
The verses beginning with "thumb-sized" are heard in the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad;
therein, the conclusion is that this being of thumb-measure is indeed the individual soul (jīva). (273)
From scriptural statements such as "The lord of the vital breaths is the size of a thumb," it is understood that the individual self (jīvātman) possesses the measurement of a thumb. (274)
Do not think so; for by the absolute term "the Supreme Person, the Lord of what has been and what is to be," it is measured here as being the size of a thumb. (275)
But with respect to the heart, [the meditation is] for humans, because the qualification belongs to humans.
Because the heart of a lay devotee is the size of a thumb, and because the Supreme Self resides therein, the [Self] is said to be the size of a thumb in relation to that [heart]. (276)

However, since the scripture has human beings as its intended audience, the statement that the Supreme is the size of a thumb is made with reference to them; other justifications for this will also be stated.
The Section on the Deity in the Center.
"Even beyond that [the world of Brahmā], Bādarāyaṇa [maintains it is possible], because of the possibility."
The scripture concerning the meditation on Brahman previously taught was intended for mortals; it is now considered whether or not gods and others possess the qualification for this practice. (278)
Deities and others who are bodiless have no qualification for worship; they lack the capacity for this worship which is to be accomplished by an embodied being. (279)
"Let it not be so; for such worship of another may even occur among the immortals.
Thus does the venerable Vyāsa Bādarāyaṇa consider.
Because in them both the desire and the capacity exist, that longing is directed toward the Supreme Self—the ocean of auspicious qualities—with the thought of Him as the object of enjoyment. (281)
Furthermore, their own capacity also exists;
by virtue of possessing bodies, sense organs, and so forth, all the gods likewise possess that [capacity]. (282)
In the Vedānta, [the Self] is heard of both in the context of creation and in the context of meditation;
therefore, because those two exist for them, they possess the qualification for meditation.
If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe the attainment of multiple [bodies].

Even though the gods possess bodies, there would indeed be a contradiction regarding ritual action, since they are summoned simultaneously at many sacrifices while possessing only a single body. (284)

If it is argued that [the Lord] cannot be present everywhere because of the impossibility of such presence, we say no; for by His own power, this assumption of multiple bodies is observed in cases such as Saubhari and others.
If it be argued that [the world] is [produced] from the Word, we say no; because [the world] originates from this [Brahman], as is known through perception and inference.
There would be a contradiction regarding Vedic words due to their connection with impermanent objects,
because the bodies of deities such as Indra are impermanent owing to their birth.
If it is argued that these words existing in the Veda are either devoid of meaning prior to their destruction or after [their production], or else that they are impermanent— that is not so.
Furthermore, because the referents such as Indra originate from the very words "Indra" and so forth,
the Vedic words "Indra" and the like do not apply to mere individuals.
Just as in the case of words such as "cow" and others, because they denote the generic form (ākṛti),
when a single individual instance has perished, [the word continues to function] through that specific Vedic term.
It is understood that Prajāpati, having perceived the respective objects from the mind's state, creates another Indra of similar form. (290)
Therefore, there is no contradiction regarding the scope of the word as established by both Śruti and Smṛti;
for this very reason, it is eternal.
For from that [Veda] and from Vedic words, the recollection of the meaning arises for the Creator.
Furthermore, having reflected upon the forms, powers, and other attributes of the sages who composed the mantras and so forth,
[the Lord] then and there [manifests them] endowed with those very forms and powers.
Having created them, he impels those very beings toward the composition of their respective mantras;
therefore, both the eternity of the Vedas and the status of these beings as mantra-composers are established.
And because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of repetition, as is seen from scripture and from tradition.

Even though there is a complete destruction followed by the recurrence of the creation of the world, non-contradiction should be understood according to the method already stated, because names and forms are the same. (294)

Furthermore, that Blessed One, having directly created the cosmic egg and the four-faced Brahmā, [reinstated] all the Vedas exactly as they were before, which had been held within his own heart. (295)
Having instructed the Four-faced One (Brahmā) regarding the work of creation as before,
and having appointed him to that task, He Himself remains as the Controller.

By recollecting that very same prior sequence through firm mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the Veda is uttered by means of that [sequence] alone; this constitutes its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatā*). (297)
Since such a meaning as this— eternality— is understood from the Śruti and Smṛti,
therefore gods and others indeed possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.
Thus concludes the section concerning the deities.
Now begins the section concerning the Madhu-vidyā.
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no entitlement [to the knowledge of Brahman] for those such as the Madhvas, because [the requirements for it] are impossible in their case.
It has been stated that gods possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman;
and any doubt regarding the impossibility of that [qualification] is refuted in this specific section. || 299 ||

For the Vasus, Ādityas, and other gods who have already attained the status of Vasus and so forth, there can be no desire for the means of attaining those states, such as the Madhu-vidyā and others. || 300 ||
The teacher Jaimini considers that there is an absence of qualification here;
for those who are to be meditated upon in various vidyās do not have the right to them in this case. (301)
And because of the existence [of the term] in the sense of light.

In this context, the term *brahmopasti* (service to Brahman) has been mentioned; for among the inhabitants of heaven, that [service] is established as common to both gods and mortals by the words "taṃ devāḥ" (that which the gods [desire]). 302.

However, the specific scriptural hearing (śravaṇa) of these [passages] precludes the performance of meditations on Brahman other than those [specified]; therefore, they have no qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and similar practices. (303)
But Bādarāyaṇa maintains that there is indeed an actual state of existence.

Regarding the Vasus and others [in the context of] honey and so forth, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that these deities, the Vasus and the rest, possess the qualification for ritual engagement. (304)

Even after attaining the state of the Vasus and others in the midst of other kalpas, those desiring to attain Brahman at the end [should practice] this [knowledge] whose essence is the Madhu-vidyā. (305)
Having taken recourse to the knowledge of Brahman, they are always worthy of meditating upon Brahman as abiding within themselves; therefore, they possess the qualification for this. || 306 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning honey.
Now begins the section concerning those who are not Śūdras (the *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*).
For it is indeed indicated by the hearing of that disregard toward Śuka and by his subsequent rushing [to him].
It has been stated that the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman belongs to the gods due to their possession of fitness;
however, the objection that the Śūdra should also possess this qualification because he likewise possesses that [fitness] is now being refuted. || 307 ||
The Śūdra also possesses the qualification for these knowledges of Brahman;
even in the absence of Vedic study, he may attain it through such means as listening to the Purāṇas.

Because the knowledge of the nature of Brahman and the method of meditating upon it arises, and because the desire for liberation arises, as well as the capacity and the sense of seeking [instruction] arise. || 309 ||
Therefore, the claim that Raikva addressed Jānaśruti as "Śūdra" and instructed him in the knowledge of Brahman is inconsistent.
From his hearing the words of the swan’s censure of Jānaśruti, and from his very immediate rushing toward the teacher Raikva at that very moment, his purity (śukra) is indicated.
The term "Śūdrā" used by the Guru refers specifically to her [as a spiritual disciple], and not to her caste;
for it is only one who possesses the wisdom born from the Vedāntic statements that is entitled to this knowledge.

Because it is heard that he [the teacher] possesses the requisite skillful means, and because such skillful means cannot exist in one born of the Śūdra caste; and even if he possessed the desire for knowledge, he would lack the necessary capacity. (313)
Permission to listen to the Purāṇas has been granted for the sake of pacifying sins;
therefore, a Śūdra has no qualification whatsoever for the worship of another [deity]. (314)
And because of the attainment of the status of a Kṣatriya.
From the statement that he was "one who gives much" to Jānaśruti, who desired to hear [the teaching], and because his status as a Kṣatriya is perceived, that address was not based on caste. (315)
And later on, [the identity of the two passages is established] by means of the indicative mark of Caitraratha.
In this Saṃvarga-vidyā, at the point where the subsequent narrative occurs, the connection belongs specifically to a Kṣatriya among the castes other than Brāhmaṇas. (316)
It is understood that Abhipratārin was the one named Caitraratha;
therefore, Janaśruti is considered here to be a different Kṣatriya from Raikva.
Furthermore, from his association with Kāpeya, it is known that Abhipratārin was also a descendant of Citraratha and a king, as seen in other scriptural passages. (318)
Because of the misapprehension of mental formations and because of the expression of their non-existence.
Because refinement is required for the statements concerning the instruction of knowledge,
and because that refinement is absent in the case of a Śūdra, no eligibility exists for him here.
And because activity proceeds when there is a determination of the non-existence of that [object].
And since it is certain that Jābāla lacks the status of a Śūdra because he was intent on service, his fitness for instruction does not exist while that certainty remains. (320)
Because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda].
For a Śūdra, the hearing, study, and so forth of the Vedas are prohibited in every respect; therefore, he has no entitlement to meditative worship (upāsana).
And because of Smṛti.
Furthermore, because of Smṛti passages such as "one should not teach him the Dharma," the prohibition of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth is explicit; therefore, he lacks the requisite fitness.
Thus concludes the section concerning those who are not Śūdras.
Now follows the supplement to the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramitādhikaraṇa*).
Because of trembling.
Having concluded the incidental discussion, the reasoning is now presented to explain how that which is the size of a thumb is indeed the Supreme Self.
From this fear— which is expressed here in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad by the words "whatever there is" and so forth—
there has always arisen that which is denoted by the term *prāṇa* (vital breath) as being the size of a thumb.
Because all the gods tremble violently at the mere raising of his vajra and other weapons, the Supreme Person is of such a nature that he is measured by the size of a thumb. (325)
Because of the observation of light.
In this place, as well as in the passage beginning with "There is no sun there," [it refers] to that which is the cause of all lights and is uniquely supreme.
Because he is perceived through the light and because he is eternally free from all excellence [of worldly attributes],
the glorious Nārāyaṇa is described as being the size of a thumb.
Thus concludes the section concerning that which is measured by the thumb.
The Section Concerning the Designation of Being a Different Entity and So Forth.
Space [is distinct from the Self], because it is designated as being a different entity and so forth.

Having raised the doubt that the meaning of the word "ether" (ākāśa), heard here in its general sense, might refer to the individual soul (jīva) in proximity to the small [space], it is established that it refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 328 ||
It is recited: "The ether, indeed, [is the revealer] of name and form.
Here, "ether" refers to the liberated soul (muktajīva), because it is that very one which is under discussion. (329)
The claim that the word "dhūtvā" (having shaken off) refers to the subsequent sentence is not tenable;
here, the Supreme Person is the bearer of name and form, who is like space. || 330 ||

Because it is taught that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and contact (sparśa) are distinct from its own form, its agency regarding name-and-form consists in being of the nature of both the bound and the liberated. (331)
The bound soul is said to be distinct in nature from Him due to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) associated with that state;
however, even the liberated soul, though far removed from the worldly activities of the universe, is not its sustainer.
By such passages as "with this living self," the fact that the Supreme Self is the sustainer of those two—
name and form— is established.
In the verse beginning with "dhūtvā" (having shaken off), the Supreme Being is the subject under discussion precisely because He is the one to be attained;
therefore, the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the one denoted here by the word "ether" (ākāśa).
On account of the difference between deep sleep and departure.
Because of the teaching of identity and because of the negation "not this,
not that," the doctrine that Brahman is an entity other than the individual soul (jīva) is refuted.

In the two scriptural passages beginning with "by the Prājña," which speak of the embracing and the ascending of the individual soul (jīva) by the inner Self (pratyagātman) at the times of deep sleep and departure, [the soul is described as being embraced]. || 336 ||
Furthermore, because the act of embracing another is mentioned as distinct [from self-embracing], there exists another person besides oneself;
for such acts as embracing another could not occur while one is asleep by oneself alone. (337)
[The word Brahman is derived] from words such as "Lord" (pati).
In this context, regarding the statement "the lord of all," [it refers] to the Supreme Self;
for from the words such as "lord" heard in the scriptures, [He is understood] as distinct from the individual self (pratyagātman). || 338 ||

It has been established that this statement of identity, as well as the speech denying difference, is characterized by a distinct nature because it is prompted by the fact that everything is an effect of Brahman. (339)
Thus concludes the section concerning the designation [of Brahman] as being something other than the object and so forth.
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter.
Now begins the fourth quarter.
The Section Concerning Those Based on Inference (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa)

If it be argued that for some [the Self] is also inferential, we say no; because [the scripture] shows that it is apprehended as presented in the allegory of the body. And it further demonstrates this.

In the preceding section, a passage containing clear indicative marks (liṅga) such as the individual soul (jīva) was examined; here, a passage containing extremely clear indicative marks of the individual soul is being investigated. (340)

And here, by means of an investigation into scriptural passages containing extremely clear indicative marks of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, the over-extension of the definition to that which is distinct from Brahman is avoided. (341)
Previously, the doctrine that there is no entity other than the living soul was refuted; here, that same [objection] is being countered by means of another method. (342)
In the Kaṭha Śruti, according to the mantra "Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest," that which is called by the word "Unmanifest" is also the causal Pradhāna. (343)

Because of the recognition of that very system [of Sāṃkhya], because of the [Sāṃkhya] principle that "there is nothing beyond the twenty-fifth person," and because of the exclusion of anything else by the statement "there is nothing higher than the person. (344)

If it is argued thus, [we reply]: since the body has been characterized as being "like a chariot," therefore the word "manifest" (vyakta) refers to that which is perceptible; hence, that which is imperceptible is not the cause. || 345 ||
From the previously mentioned mantra beginning with "Know the self as the rider of the chariot," the self, the body, and so forth, serve in succession as the means for meditation.

Furthermore, because they can be brought under control by means of charioteers and so forth, these [objects] are said to be "superior" to the sense organs, according to the mantra beginning with "Superior to the senses... (Katha Upanishad 1.3.10). || 347 ||
In this context, the faculties and so forth are expressed by their own respective terms;
however, the body is metaphorically described as a chariot, rather than being denoted by its own specific term.

By process of elimination, that very [principle] previously mentioned by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) is what is understood here; therefore, there is no recourse to the [alternative] system (tantra). || 349 ||
Therefore, the Puruṣa is not declared to be the twenty-fifth;
rather, the Supreme Person is the one to be attained, having reached the ultimate limit of that which is to be brought under control. || 350 ||
The remainder of the passage clearly demonstrates this point:
"The wise man should restrain speech and mind; he should restrain those two in knowledge. (351)
But that [knowledge] is subtle because of its fitness for such a state.
Since that which exists in the state of the body is indeed unmanifest and capable of producing effects,
it is for this reason that the body alone is understood here by the term "unmanifest" (avyakta).
Because it is dependent on that, it is purposeful.
Because it is the body of the Supreme Self and is dependent upon Him, it is purposeful;
for here, the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) refers to the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma). (353)
And because it is not stated that [the Self] is an object of knowledge.
If this were the system of Tantra, then its terminology—such as "the manifest" (vyakta) and "the unmanifest" (avyakta)—would have to be mentioned;
yet its knowability has not been stated here, and therefore that [Tantric system] is not intended [by this text].
If it is argued that [the Self] speaks, we say no; for the wise one [is meant], according to the context.
By the statement "soundless," it is taught that the unmanifest is the object of knowledge;
it is not so for the conscious one (prājña), because he is mentioned there [in that context] and he alone is the subject under discussion.
And thus, there is both the presentation and the question regarding these three alone.

In this section, beginning from the words "yeyam" [and] continuing until the end, there is an extensive [discussion] regarding the object of worship, the act of worship, and the worshippers, insofar as they are to be known. (356)
Thus, both the presentation and the inquiry are seen to concern only three [entities];
therefore, there is no inclusion here of the "unmanifest" (avyakta) as taught in the Tantras. (357)
And like the Great One (mahat).

Just as the "Great Self" (mahān ātmā) mentioned in the phrase "the Great Self of the intellect" is not understood [as the technical sense of the Self] because of the word "Self," so too it is not the technical [Sāṃkhya] principle when referred to by the word "Unmanifest" (avyakta). 358.
The Section on the Chamasas (Cups)
It is like the cup, because there is no distinction.

The independence of the Pradhāna, which is designated as the Unmanifest, has been refuted; now, having raised the objection that its existence is established by the *ajā* mantra, it is being rejected. (359)

In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, the passage beginning with "ajāmekām" (the one unborn) is recited; therein, the term "ajā" (unborn) refers to the Tantric goddess, because of the scriptural statement regarding her being uncreated.

Furthermore, because it is heard in scripture that [the Unborn] is the creator of living beings through its own independence, it is not the case that this non-Brahman Unborn is not stated to be the cause. (361)
There is no restriction [on the meaning] simply because of the scriptural mention of the impossibility of birth;
for instance, in passages such as "upward-turned mouth" and so forth, even though the means is called a *camasa* (a wooden cup).
Even when the remainder of the sentence is heard, the understanding that the head is a *camasa* arises;
likewise, in this case, the mention of "born" (*ajā*) established by the *tantra* is not a restrictive factor.
Only the state of being the cause of creation has been stated here; independence is not asserted.
For it is thus studied by some: "But [the soul] begins with light, for so it is taught."
This unborn [nature] is indeed based on Brahman as the cause; likewise, the followers of the Taittirīya school [hold this view]. (364)

In the context of the collection of mantras beginning with "aṇoraṇīyān" (smaller than the small) and extending up to the Supreme Self, it is taught that [the individual soul] arises from everything because its essence is that [Supreme Self]. 365.
The one unborn (ajā) mentioned in the verse "the one unborn" is indeed the Supreme Self;
and because it is taught as a figurative designation, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and other such examples.
Because of this statement, "The Illusionist [creates]," and because of the teaching regarding creation here [in this context]. (366)
There is no mutual contradiction between the two properties of being unborn and being an effect of Brahman; however, at the time of dissolution, it [the world] abandons name and form.
Therefore, by virtue of existing as the body of Brahman, the insentient substance is unborn;
yet at the time of creation, those unborn things, having Brahman as their cause, become subject to change.
Just as the state of being honey and the state of being an effect belong to the sun at the time of its creation, so too,
at the time of its dissolution, its subtle state is the state of being a non-effect.
Thus concludes the section concerning the cups.
The Section Concerning the Comprehension of the Number [Five] (Saṅkhyopasaṅgrahādhikaraṇa).
Nor [is the Sāṃkhya doctrine established] even by the inclusion of a specific number, because of the diversity [of the principles] and because of the excess [over that number].
The claim that the unborn [Prakṛti] lacks the nature of Brahman has already been set aside due to the absence of any reason;
now, the argument that "in that [which is eternal] there exists its characteristic mark" is being refuted.
The mantra beginning with "yasmin pañca," which exists in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, is held to be the indicator of the principles of the Sāṃkhya system. (371)

Because they consist of the realization of the reality of the tantra comprising twenty-five categories, and because they pertain to the domain of liberation, it is certain that these are Tantric. || 372 ||
Not so; for from such statements as "In whom the five groups of five persons [dwell]," because the number twenty-five is included therein, that word [refers to the Sāṅkhya principles]. (373)
There can be no understanding of the Tantra here [in this context], because these [elements] are distinct from them;
for [the Self] always has Brahman as its locus, as expressed by the word "in which" (yasmin).
For their nature as Brahman is indeed known through the principle of excess;
for that which is denoted by the word "Space" is in excess of the twenty-five [tattvas]. (375)
By the word "even" (api), it is made known that there is no inclusion of a specific number here;
rather, it is stated that there are five [beings] designated as "pañcajanāḥ. (376)
The vital breath and the others [are the objects of meditation], because of the supplementary statement.
The five "people" (pañcajana) are the five beginning with breath (prāṇa), which have Brahman as their support;
this is understood from the supplementary passage, "the breath of breath," and so forth. || 377 ||
According to some, there is light when food is absent.
Even if the reading of the Kāṇvas does not contain the word "food," one should understand that these five persons are the sense organs, because of the word "light" mentioned previously.
Having stated that Brahman is the illuminator,
and immediately thereafter [stating] "five-fives," it follows that the sense organs must indeed be of that same nature.
Therefore, because it is taught that [the senses] abide as the indriyas within the Supreme Self by means of the passage beginning with "five, five," this is certainly not a Tantric teaching.
Thus ends the section concerning the inclusion of the number.
The Section on Being the Cause (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa)
And because, in the case of ether and so forth, it is taught as the cause exactly as it was previously designated.
It has been stated that the causality of one for whom Brahman, the Self, or Pradhāna is not primary is non-Vedic; in that regard, the assertion of the unanimity of the Vedas is now set forth. (381)
In some cases, it is likewise left undeclared whether [the world] is eternal or non-eternal;
thus, the causal reality is expressed through statements that awaken one to the cause. (382)

If Brahman were the cause, however, there would be no uniformity of voice among all scriptural statements due to the contradiction regarding its existence, non-existence, and so forth; but this is not the case when [the cause] is taught according to the Tantras.
Existence, non-existence, and the indeterminate state abide according to the distinction of time;
likewise, due to beginninglessness and transformation at the time of creation. (384)
The argument that "because it is unmanifest due to the separation from name-and-form at the time of dissolution,
that cause must therefore be Pradhāna" is inconsistent.
Because [the Lord] is always proclaimed as the cause of effects such as space, being distinguished by qualities such as omniscience that are logically consistent with Him. (386)

The conclusion reached by all scriptural statements is that Brahman alone is the cause; this refers to the "All-knowing One" (Vipaścit) under discussion in the Śruti passage, "Truth, Knowledge... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
In all subsequent statements, a connection is observed;
for it is exactly thus everywhere, therefore Brahman alone is the cause. || 388 ||
Because of the drawing together.
In the passage "In the beginning, [Brahman] desired," regarding Brahman who is creating the world;
and in the passage "Non-being indeed was this," regarding that which was spoken of subsequently by the words "Then, indeed" (tad dha). || 389 ||

And in the statement "This is that," because of the drawing together [of the two referents], the word "non-existent" (asat) and the word "unmanifested" (avyākṛta) denote Brahman whose body is the unmanifested. (390)
Likewise, the two words "Brahman" and "Self" do not denote the Pradhāna;
therefore, there is no possibility of the Pradhāna being the cause. (391)
Thus concludes the section concerning the status of being the cause.
The Section on the Denotation of the World.
Because of the mention of the world.

It was stated previously that the causality of the world is attributed to consciousness alone; and that consciousness is the living being who performs actions (karmī-jīva), and not anything else. (392)
Therefore, this primary matter (pradhāna), being presided over by that [Self], is accepted as the cause;
thus, this Sāṃkhya doctrine is refuted here in this context. || 393 ||
In the Kauṣītakī Śruti, that which is recited as "O Bālāka," refers to the Puruṣa who is distinct from Prakṛti and is declared here as the object to be known. (394)
Since the scripture states "of whom this [is the fruit]," it declares that karma is connected to the individual soul;
however, Brahman has no connection with such karma consisting of merit and demerit.
Because the word "karma" is used here in its conventional sense, it is that [primordial matter] alone which is spoken of;
therefore, the claim that this primary matter, presided over by the individual soul (jīva) who possesses karma, is the cause is incorrect. (396)

Regarding the phrase "he whose work this is," because the word "work" (karman) refers to the world that is the effect of Brahman, there is no inclusion of the *puruṣa* as asserted by the Sāṃkhya school. || 397 ||

Having refuted the reality of those who perform rituals, such as Āditya and others, as being Brahman as asserted by Bālāki, [the Upanishad] spoke solely for the purpose of making known the Supreme. || 398 ||

In this sentence, the word "action" (karman) does not denote merit, demerit, and so forth; for [if it did], the function of making known what was previously unknown would not be established, since it is that which is to be done which is called "action. (399)
Furthermore, this entire world was previously introduced as being denoted by the face of the Sun;
therefore, this whole universe is the effect of that Supreme Self. (400)
It is Nārāyaṇa alone who is to be understood here;
if it be argued that this is not so because of the characteristics of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), that has already been explained.
In this very sentence, "evam eva," the individual soul (jīva) who is the enjoyer is indicated by its characteristic mark. || 401 ||

If it is argued that this [Self] is not the Supreme Self because of its connection with the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) in the passage beginning "Now, in this breath," the refutation of this has already been shown previously.

Once it has been determined that [the passage] refers to Brahman through the application of interpretive methods and so forth, everything must be interpreted in accordance with that; this is what is meant by the term "indicative mark" (liṅga). || 403 ||

It has been stated that the proclamation of the characteristics of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) in the Prātardana section is for the purpose of the meditation on Brahman as having those as its body. (404)

And here, by virtue of the grammatical coreferentiality in the expression "in this breath," the mention of "breath" is appropriate for the purpose of meditating on the inner ruler (antaryāmin) who dwells within the breath. (405)
Jaimini, however, [holds that the mantras] have another purpose, on account of both questions and explanations; and some [teachers] also agree with this.
Jaimini maintains that the demonstration of the existence of a soul distinct from the body is intended to make known the existence of the Brahman who is other than that [body]. (406)

From the question, "Where was this then? and from the subsequent answer, "In this prāṇa, my dear," which serves as a meaningful response to the statement beginning with "Being, my dear... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1), [it is established]. || 407 ||
Moreover, certain followers of other recensions indeed recite in this dialogue a scriptural passage concerning the Supreme Self, which concludes with the words, "In Him He lies. (408)
Thus concludes the section concerning the designation of the world.
The Section on the Connection of Sentences (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa)
On account of the syntactical connection of the sentence.

In the preceding case, because the word "karma" was taken to mean the world, the sentence's reference to the enjoyer was rejected; however, here in this [context], it refers to the qualified person (adhikṛta).

It is established that the direct subject matter to be conveyed is precisely the attainment of the fruit produced by karma; and it is argued that it is logical for the sentence to have that as its primary purport—this is what is being set forth here. (410)
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti, it is stated: "Verily, not for the sake of the husband [does a wife exist]," and so forth;
the Puruṣa spoken of there as the object to be seen is considered by the Tantrikas to be that very one. (411)

Because of the continuity of affection for one's husband, wife, children, wealth, cattle, and so forth, the perception of a living being exists at the beginning, as well as in the middle and at the end. (412)

For it is precisely the knowledge of the nature of the individual soul (jīva) as distinct from the attributes of the insentient (acit) that is declared in the Tantra to be the cause of immortality; therefore, such [knowledge] is what is intended here.
The true nature [of the Self] is declared as that which is to be seen for the sake of immortality;
therefore, it is incorrect to say that the Pradhāna is the primary cause of the universe. (414)
Because the entire passage is consistent in its application to the Supreme Self, it is that very Supreme Person who is designated as the object to be seen. (415)

Since husbands and other such relations are dear to the living being for the sake of attaining their own desired ends, one should therefore meditate upon that form which is devoid of them, having abandoned those objects of affection. (416)
This statement would be inconsistent, for that which is to be sought after is indeed what is dear;
for one's own desire, husbands and the like would not be dear to husbands and the like themselves. (417)
Having stated, "But for the sake of one's own self," [the text continues] with "Verily, the Self, my dear";
that which is indicated as the object to be seen is indeed the Supreme Self, distinct from the individual soul. (418)
And since the husband and others feel affection for their own [wives] by His will, He—the Supreme Person, whose resolve is true—is exceedingly dear. (419)
Āśmarathya [holds that] the inferential mark [is the means of proof] because it establishes the proposition.
This is considered a sign for the establishment of the claim to omniscience:
that the Supreme Self is addressed by words denoting the individual soul. (420)
If the individual soul (jīva) were indeed the supreme self itself and not its effect, then knowledge of the individual soul would not be possible through knowledge of the supreme self. || 421 ||
Both its origination and its dissolution are known to proceed from the Supreme Self;
therefore, the statement [in scripture] using the term "individual self" (jīvātman) refers to that [Supreme Self], according to Āśmarathya. (422)
Auḍulomi [holds that this occurs] because of the very nature of one who is about to depart.
Because the view that the individual soul (jīva) is an effect of Brahman entails many logical defects, and because its eternity is established by the scriptural text, "It is not born. (423)
"What was stated previously is incorrect; for it is only one who is about to depart [from the body] that is designated by the word 'jīva' due to its identity with Brahman—so says Auḍulomi. (424)
"Because of the abiding [of the Self in all beings], so says Kāśakṛtsna."
Because it is tainted by many defects, this too is inconsistent:
[the claim] that the Supreme Self exists as the self within the individual self, which has become a body. (425)
This [Self] is designated by the word "jīva" because of its abiding [within];
likewise in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa and elsewhere in the Śruti.
"The fact that Brahman has the conscious and the unconscious as its body is proclaimed repeatedly;
thus speaks Kāśakṛtsna, who holds this view dear to the author of the Sūtras. (427)
Thus concludes the section on the syntactical connection of the sentences (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa).
The Section Concerning Primordial Matter (Prakṛti)
And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples.
That which was previously accepted regarding the Supreme Self as the material cause (upādāna) of the world—that this [notion] would not be tenable—is here refuted. || 428 ||
The other [the Supreme Being] could be only the efficient cause (nimitta) of the world, not its material cause (upādāna),
because in the world one observes a necessary distinction between those two types of causes.

This is incorrect because difference is established by such statements as "The Illusionist [creates] from this," and because it would contradict the scriptural texts concerning the changelessness of Brahman. (430)
Because it would contradict the propositions and illustrations regarding omniscience, Brahman is neither merely the efficient cause nor the material cause of the world. (431)
Likewise, by means of the knowledge of Brahman, through the proposition that "by knowing one, all is known," as understood from the statement, "By which the unheard becomes heard. (432)

Just as, through the illustration of clay and its products stated in the passage beginning with "O Somya," it is understood that Brahman alone is the material cause, so too is that Brahman [the cause]. (433)
The cognition of the world would be caused solely by its efficient cause (nimitta-hetu) and not by the cognition of that [cause];
for the cognition of an effect such as a jar does not arise from the cognition of the potter and so forth.
Of the Supreme Self, which is distinct from everything, all-powerful,
and accessible through scripture alone, [and] of the two forms of cause and effect— (435)
Even in the two states, the embodied one is always both the efficient cause and the material cause of the conscious and the unconscious; for this single status is indeed uncontradicted. (436)
For modifications are indeed attached only to the insentient entity within the body;
therefore, even in the state of being an effect, its immutability remains unimpaired. || 437 ||
Even though He is the material cause of this world, His freedom from all defects is understood through the passage beginning with "the Illusionist" (māyī) and so forth. (438)
And because of the teaching regarding covetousness.

This is because of the teaching that the desire for multiplicity belongs to Brahman itself as the creator, based on such scriptural passages as "He desired, 'May I be many'" and "That [Being] reflected. (439)
It is understood that Brahman alone is both the material cause and the efficient cause of the universe,
because both are directly declared [in scripture].
The Supreme is directly revealed by such [Vedic] passages as "What forest? and "Who is He? (RV 1.164.39).
Because it creates itself, that which consists of both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*) is Brahman alone.
Then, [the phrase] "himself as the self" refers to the aforementioned Supreme Self (parātman). || 441 ||
In the act of creation, both the state of being the object and the state of being the agent are perceived; yet that [Brahman] is the other [transcendent].
It is the effect that is the locus of name and form, while the agent is not dependent upon that.
Because of transformation.
In this regard, for the transformation being taught here, there is no possibility of defect whatsoever; rather, it brings about supreme sovereignty in an extreme degree.

In the Śruti, that which is not distinct from name, form, and so forth, and consists of subtle non-consciousness and the individual soul (jīva), appears as having distinct name, form, non-consciousness, and the individual soul as its body. 444.
For the teaching of transformation is indeed based on the statement "this [world] was that";
therefore, defects such as the failure to achieve the goals of human life, which reside in the body and in consciousness and non-consciousness, [do not apply]. (445)
In both states, Brahman is the very self, free from all evil;
for Brahman constitutes the body of the entire reality, whether in its gross or subtle condition.
That Brahman is the very self [of all] is frequently recited in the Vedānta;
therefore, O sinless one, the Supreme Self alone is the cause of both here.
For it is indeed sung as the womb.
The Ṛgvedic verses describe Him as the source of all beings, the agent, the Lord, and the Puruṣa;
for He is indeed praised as the source of the entire universe. (448)
It is understood precisely here that the word *yoni* denotes the material cause (*upādāna*);
thus, by means of the statement regarding the spider, the twofold nature of the cause [as both efficient and material] is established beyond this. (449)
Thus ends the section concerning the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The Section on All Explanations.
By this, all [remaining cases] have been explained; they have been explained.
Indeed, it has been stated that Nārāyaṇa is the cause and the object of worship;
however, this is incorrect, for Rudra is mentioned in some Vedic branches as being so. (450)
This section is undertaken to make it known that the doubt concerning [the self] being the cause has been refuted by the collection of arguments stated previously. (451)

By the words "When there was darkness" and so forth, it is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad that the one Rudra remains established during the dissolution of the world; therefore [he is the cause]. (452)
It would follow that only that [consciousness] is the cause; this is untenable.
By the collection of arguments already stated, all proponents of causality [are refuted]. 453.
The Vedāntas have been established as being devoted to the illustrious Nārāyaṇa alone, through such means as the conceptualization of Nārāyaṇa’s own manifold manifestations. (454)

When His status as the cause has been firmly established by means of unique attributes, words such as "Śiva" and others must be understood as referring to Him alone, even if this requires setting aside their conventional meanings. (455)
The doubt as to why there should not be a reversal here cannot arise,
because this term "Nārāyaṇa" is established either through conventional usage (rūḍhi) or through etymological derivation (yoga).

Because it is impossible for it to have any other purpose, because the substitution of *ṇ* is otherwise unattainable, because the rule for *ṇatva* applies specifically to technical names (*saṃjñā*), and because the status of being "Śrī" is likewise impossible [in that context]. (457)
Therefore, the causality and other attributes belong exclusively and permanently to Nārāyaṇa;
for this reason, one should always meditate upon Nārāyaṇa without agitation. 458.
Thus has been stated in the Veda and by the authors of the Sūtras in the fifth [chapter];
here, the repetition serves as an indicator of the completion of the chapter. (459)
Thus concludes the section concerning the interpretation of all [scriptural passages].
The first chapter is completed.
The Glorious Garland of Verses on the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā]
Now begins the first quarter of the second chapter.
The Section on Smṛti (Tradition)
If it be argued that this leads to the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis, we say no, because that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis [that are not in conflict].
In the first chapter, it was declared by the wise that Brahman alone, known as Nārāyaṇa, is established in the Śruti as the cause of the universe.
Having refuted the opposing positions through the method of driving in a pillar, this chapter proceeds in order to strengthen the meaning previously stated. (2)
Previously, two Sāṅkhya proponents were refuted by means of elucidating the meaning of Vedānta;
here, the one who follows the Smṛti of Kapila and maintains that there is no Lord (nirīśvara) is refuted. (3)

The determination of the meaning of the Vedānta must be made by those of little learning and dull intellect through the Smṛti composed by a trustworthy authority alone; for that [Smṛti] is equal to what is spoken in the Veda, as spoken by Kapila.
The determination of the meaning of the Veda is justified by means of Smṛti, which has the single reality as its object;
otherwise, there would be no scope for it. Therefore, [the Veda] is the cause of everything.
It is indeed logical that the Pradhāna alone is what is to be known through the Vedāntas;
nor can it be argued that the Pradhāna is not the cause because of its irrationality. (6)
For when there is a contradiction with scripture, logic does not apply at all.
Therefore, if it is argued that the cause of the world is that Pradhāna, it is not so.
Therefore, even the Veda, when reinforced by a Smṛti that is not contradicted by logic, is weaker than one that is reinforced by a Smṛti contrary to it. || 8 ||
The expansion [of the Veda] performed by Manu and others, who are most authoritative due to the declarations of the Vedas and their praises, is indeed to be accepted;
otherwise, there would be great fault.
The defect of these [scriptures] being devoid of scope would ensue;
for they could not possess scope if they were augmented by dharma. (10)

For those dharmas have the nature of propitiating another, as stated by the Śruti in the passage "sacrifices and works of public utility" (iṣṭāpūrta) and by the Smṛti in the passage "by sacrifices, however" (yajñaistvam). || 11 ||
Therefore, it is understood that the supplementation by the words of Kapila is inconsistent;
for "supplementation of the Veda" means the illumination of the meaning already stated therein. (12)
Because it is contradictory to that [Vedic authority], Kāpilya does not deserve to be considered a possibility;
by the statement "having brought forth the Sage," he cannot possess the status of being most authoritative. (13)
And because others are not perceived.

And [the teachings] of Manu and many others, who were the most eminent among the knowers of the Vedanta and who, through their own spiritual yoga, had directly realized the entire range of supersensuous objects. (14)
Since reality is not apprehended in the manner described by Kapila, this tradition is rooted in error; therefore, no determination of the object can be made on its basis. (15)
Thus concludes the section concerning Smṛti.
The Section on the Refutation of Yoga.
By this, Yoga is refuted.
Even though Kapila’s teaching might be rooted in error, that is impossible in the case of the Yoga system taught by the Vedic proclaimer through his injunctions; for that reason, indeed. (16)
The doubt that it is logical for [the Purāṇas] to be supplements to the Vedas is dispelled, because Yoga was indeed taught by the very speaker of the entire Veda. (17)
Furthermore, because the Lord is accepted [as the author], it is logical that the determination of the meaning of Vedic statements is made through the Smṛti of Yoga;
therefore, the claim that the Vedas have Primordial Matter (pradhāna) as their primary purport is incorrect.
The Yoga-tantra is also refuted by the rejection of Kapila’s words, because there is no difference in their being contrary to the Vedas, just like the Smṛti of Kapila. (19)
Furthermore, the yogic memory that is ungraspable in every respect has delusion as its cause;
for since it arises from the speaker’s status as a knower of the field (kṣetrajña), could there not indeed be error and the like? (20)
Thus concludes the section on the refutation of Yoga.
The Section on Being of a Different Characteristic.
Not so, because this [world] has different characteristics; and its being thus [as described by scripture] is due to the word [of scripture].
The Smṛtis of Manu and others are extremely weak because they contradict reasoning; therefore, it is rejected that the system of Kapila, which follows reasoning, should be accepted. (21)

Because of its being subject to transformation, its lack of consciousness, its failure to achieve the human goal, its impurity, and other such qualities, the world is of a different nature [from Brahman]; therefore, it cannot be the effect of Brahman. || 22 ||
Furthermore, a distinction [from the Self] is understood from the Vedic text, "And consciousness...
Therefore, that which is the cause of the world would be the Pradhāna, possessing similar characteristics [with the individual soul]. || 23 ||
From such scriptural statements as, "The earth said to him," and "The waters [said to him]," it is clearly understood that even the earth and other elements possess the yoga of knowledge. (24)
Therefore, there can be no difference between the world and Brahman; to resolve this objection, the subsequent Sūtra is recited. (25)
But there is a designation of the presiding deities because of specification and following after.
This designation as the "effect of intelligence" (dhīkārya), namely, "The earth spoke to him," is understood to refer to the deities presiding over those respective objects.

Because of the qualification that the deities of earth and so forth are [the agents] in the passage, "Let me slay," and because of the entry of Agni and others into speech and so forth in the passage, "Agni is indeed speech. || 27 ||
Therefore, this world does not possess the characteristics of being created by Brahmā;
consequently, let it be that its material cause is Pradhāna, as is agreed upon by the scriptures. (28)
But it is indeed seen.
To this it is replied: because we observe the emergence of worms and the like from honey and so forth, the relationship of cause and effect exists even between things that are highly dissimilar. (19)
If it be argued that [the world] is non-existent, we say no, because [your statement] is a mere negation.
If it is maintained here that the effect is distinct from its cause, then the effect does not exist within the cause; thus, there is the arising of what was non-existent. (30)
If it is argued that [this] would follow as an undesirable consequence, we say no; for we are merely negating the rule that cause and effect must possess identical characteristics.

The identity of substance between those two has indeed been established; it is one and the same thing that, having attained the state of an effect, possesses both similar and dissimilar characteristics.
Therefore, it assumes various states; hence, no fixed rule exists in this regard.
Consequently, despite these differences in characteristics, the world has Brahman as its cause.
[The doctrine] is untenable because, upon dissolution, it would entail the same [absurdities].
If [the cause] were Brahman, the cause of the world, then undesirable consequences such as being subject to modification would follow for the Supreme Self, just as they do for the world. (34)
If it be argued that the Vedānta statements would thus be inconsistent,
we say no, because there exist supporting illustrations.
This is not logical for this Brahman, who possesses a body composed of both conscious and unconscious entities.
And because there is no contact between the cause and the effect regarding merits and defects, an illustration exists, as in the case of the embodied soul. (36)
The states of childhood, youth, and old age certainly exist in the body;
likewise, knowledge, happiness, and so forth exist in the self alone, as they do in the Supreme Self.
The defects residing in the body, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, are directed downward;
whereas omniscience, the power of true resolve, and other such qualities reside in the Supreme Self. (38)
And because of the defects in one's own position.
The inclusion of the doctrine of Brahman as the cause is not merely because it is faultless; for there are indeed faults in the view that Pradhāna is the cause. (39)

For in the doctrine that Pradhāna is the cause, since the person (puruṣa) is eternally changeless and there is no proximity of the Unborn (Māyā), the mutual superimposition of attributes would not be possible.
For superimposition (adhyāsa) is indeed the attribution of the qualities of one thing to another object that is distinct from it;
such superimposition could not possibly occur in the case of the changeless non-conscious (acit) principle. (41)
Because [the world] arises from primordial matter (prakṛti), the emergence of the universe and its effects as rooted in that [matter] would be impossible;
therefore, due to its extreme fallacy, that position is not accepted.
Also because of the non-establishment of reasoning.

Because this [system] is unstable and its reasoning has been refuted by others, those who rely on authoritative means of knowledge should utterly abandon this tantric doctrine which is rooted therein. (43)
If it is argued that the object of inference is otherwise, even so, there follows the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation.
If it is argued that the object of inference is inferential by a mode other than the established modes [of perception], even so, it is subject to the faults already mentioned. (44)
Furthermore, the consequence of the impossibility of liberation would certainly be difficult to avoid, since there exists even more fallacious reasoning than the logic you have stated. (45)
Thus concludes the section on the difference in characteristics.
The Section on [Theories] Not Accepted by the Learned (Śiṣṭāparigrahādhikaraṇa).
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained.
Although the proponent of Brahman as the cause cannot be shaken by unstable reasoning, he can be shaken by the arguments concerning atoms as the cause; this is what is being set forth here.
By the refutation of the Sāṅkhya system, those learned ones who do not accept the Vedas are also refuted;
likewise, the Smṛtis of Kaṇabhakṣa and others, being unstable, are likewise rejected.
There is no fault in the atomic theory due to excessive doubt, because it is supported by many [scriptural] apprehensions;
yet there is instability in this [theory] as well, because its foundation is reasoning (tarka). || 48 ||
Thus concludes the section [refuting] the doctrines not accepted by the learned.
The Section on the Attainment of the Nature of the Enjoyer.
If it be argued that there is no distinction because of the eater’s becoming [the food], we say: it may be so, as in the world.

Even in your view, by virtue of the relationship between the world and the body, defects such as being an enjoyer and so forth would belong to Brahman just as they do to the individual soul (jīva). (49)
In this regard, the Sāṅkhya counter-argument is again considered:
that the embodied soul and the Supreme Self [are distinct] from the world consisting of conscious and unconscious forms. (50)

Because it would result in this [Self] becoming an enjoyer of pleasure and pain produced by its connection with a body—just like the individual soul (jīvātman)—there would be no distinction between it and the living being. || 51 ||
If it is argued that there would be no distinction [between the self and the body] because [the self] is the opposite of that which is to be abandoned, we reply:
the experience of pleasure and pain is not caused by the state of having a body. (52)
The phrase "na ha vā" indicates that [the body] has karma as its root; thus, it refers to the nature of the body as being rooted in karma.
From such statements as "sa ekadhā," even for the liberated one, there exists embodiment.
Therefore, it is heard that this Supreme Being possesses no capacity for enjoyment whatsoever,
just as in the world there is a difference between those who abide by the king's commands and those who transgress them.
Even though pleasure and pain follow this king, he would not be their experiencer merely by virtue of possessing a body, because of his independence from anything else.
Therefore, the doctrine that Brahman—the sovereign ruler of all and the body of the universe—is the material cause of the world is entirely free from even a scent of defect. (56)
Thus concludes the section concerning the attainment of the state of being an enjoyer.
The Section on Origination (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa)
The non-difference of that [effect] from that [cause] follows from such terms as "originating" (ārambhaṇa) and others.

Having relied upon the non-difference between the effect and the cause—the universe and the Supreme Self—his status as the cause of the universe has been stated; that non-difference is now established here.
The non-difference between the two lords can never be logically established;
for it is impossible for the effect-entity to be non-different from its cause. (58)

Because one observes distinctions in name, form, function, time, and cognition, and because it would otherwise follow that the collection of causal factors and their activities would be rendered purposeless. (59)
Therefore, the world is the effect of Brahman; it would certainly be something other than Brahman.
If it is argued that this is not so because the scripture teaches non-difference (*ananyatva*), we say: no, that is not the case. (60)
Therefore, from such statements as "the world is a mere modification of speech" (vācārambhaṇa), the non-difference of the effect—the universe—from its cause, the Supreme Self, is understood. (61)

For the sake of establishing linguistic convention preceded by speech, there is a modification such as having a broad base and a large belly through clay and other materials, which is also called "a jar. (62)
And because the name is touched [by the cognition], even an effect such as a jar is perceived by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) as nothing other than the substance clay. (63)
But they do not exist as separate substances, such as distinct cognitions or words;
rather, they are established in various ways through the different states of a single [entity], just as in the case of a person. (64)

The distinctions such as "child," "youth," and "old man," as well as differences in cognition and terminology, and the various observed differences in their functions—there is no contradiction whatsoever in this regard. (65)
Because they bring about that state, even the activities possess purpose;
for that which is the subtle aggregate of consciousness and non-consciousness remains untouched by name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
That Brahman which exists in the causal state as the subtle body of consciousness and matter is, from this cause, the world in its state of effect; thus the world arises from Brahman.
The form of the effect would be non-different even in both states;
thus the distinction between qualities and defects has been stated for both the body and the embodied self.
And because [the self] is perceived when there is existence.
Even when there is an effect such as a jar, that very same substance, such as clay, is perceived; therefore, the effect is indeed the cause itself. (69)
And because of the existence of another.
"All this, such as a jar and so forth, was previously nothing but clay," as it is said in the world and in the Śruti: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. (70)
Because this other effect exists within its cause, there is non-difference between the two; therefore, the effect is described by way of its causality. (71)

If it be argued that [the soul] does not exist because of the designation of non-existence, we say no; for [its existence] is established by means of another attribute, on account of the remainder of the passage and logical reasoning, and from another scriptural word.
In passages such as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," because there is a designation of the non-existence of the effect in the cause, that aforementioned meaning is not tenable. (72)
If it is argued thus, [we reply] no, because a substance is designated by means of another property, due to its association with other properties such as grossness and its opposite, subtlety. (73)

The statement "it is non-existent" has this meaning, which is established by the remainder of the passage and so forth; and that remainder of the passage is: "that which is non-existent is indeed the mind. (74)
In this context, an unreal object is held to be something other than a mere void, such as mental attention (manaskāra) and so forth;
and the reasoning regarding existence and non-existence is that which establishes their status as properties of real entities.

The fact that clay possesses some degree of persistence is the cause for saying "the jar exists"; its association with a form contrary to that [persistence] is the cause for saying "it does not exist. (76)
There is no other category of object here designated as "non-existence"; rather, it is simply another word for that which was previously described as "being" and so forth. (77)
And like a cloth.
Just as many threads, through a particular kind of interweaving, assume different names and forms as distinct objects, so too does Brahman.
And as, for example, the vital breath and so forth.
Just as the single wind within the body, through its various modes of activity, assumes different names, forms, and functions such as prāṇa, apāna, and so forth; || 79 ||
In that very same way, the one Brahman manifests as the world of moving and non-moving beings;
thus, the variegated universe comes into existence, and for this reason, the world is not other than the Supreme.
Thus concludes the section on "the origination" (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa).
The Section on Designation as Something Else (Itaravyapadeśādhikaraṇa).
Because of the designation of [the Self] as other [than the body], there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial and so forth.
The contradiction regarding the status of another as a material cause (*upādāna*) has been set forth by the opponent;
here, that which is based on [the opponent's claim of] being a causal condition (*nimitta*) while [the two are] non-different is refuted. (81)

Because the individual soul (jīva), which is other than Brahman, is designated as being Brahman, there would be the fault of its failing to act for its own benefit, as well as its performing what is not in its own interest. (82)

In that regard, [the objection] is difficult to ward off; for by such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), the identity of the individual soul (jīvātman) and this Brahman is indeed asserted. (83)
Since numerous qualities such as omniscience and others are accepted [in Brahman], the creatorship of such a Brahman is indeed not tenable. (84)
This world is seen to be intensely painful and contrary [to our desires];
therefore, it is inconsistent for Brahman, which is non-different from individual souls (jīva), to be its cause. (85)
But it is more [than that], because of the specific designation of its divisions.

From the scriptural indications of distinction, such as "the Knower and the Unknower" and "that which is in the self," it is determined that Brahman is indeed an entity distinct from the individual soul (jīvātman). (86)

The identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) is heard in the scriptures through such texts as "That thou art" (tattvamasi); this is due to the relationship of body and self, and therefore [it applies] to the creator and the created who are mutually related. (87)

Therefore, a difference in essential nature is established for the Supreme Self, even though He is the creator of that manifold world which is undesirable to Him, in accordance with the karma of individual souls. (88)
Therefore, this fault does not exist, and its status as the cause of the world is established;
nor is it untenable, just like the case of stones and other such things.
Just as [the nature] is always [present] in discardable objects such as stones, wood, and the like. (89)

The nature of Brahman, which consists of infinite auspicious qualities that oppose all that is to be abandoned, could not possibly exist [as such] for one of meager intellect, who is powerless and afflicted by suffering. (90)

The Brahman-nature of the individual soul (jīva) would also be impossible in every respect; therefore, the statement of grammatical coreferentiality between the two is based on their relationship as body and self. (91)
The world's being an effect of Brahman and its non-difference from Him; and the established distinction between the qualities and defects of the insentient, the individual soul, and Brahman. (92)
There is no contradiction with any scriptural revelation, and everything here is consistent;
therefore, the Lord Nārāyaṇa is also the efficient cause.
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of the other.
The Section Concerning the Observation of Withdrawal (Upasaṃhāradarśanādhikaraṇa).
If it be argued that [the Lord] is not [the cause] because we observe the withdrawal [of the world], we say no; for it is like milk.
The distinction of the Supreme Being has been stated through such qualities as the possession of true volition; the objection that creation by mere volition is not logical is now being set aside.
Since we observe that an instrument is brought forth for the production of an effect, this Brahman, being without assistants, cannot be the cause of the world. (95)

If it is argued thus, [we reply]: no; for just as milk, though lacking any other assistant, possesses causality toward the state of curd, so too could this [Primal Matter] possess causality toward the universe. (96)
And as in the world, [the case] of the gods and so forth.
Just as the gods and others, by mere volition, create within their own respective worlds whatever they require for themselves, so too does this Supreme Person.
By his own volition alone, he creates the entire world and remains its master;
the mention of an illustrative example here is for the sake of facilitating easy comprehension of Brahman.
Thus ends the section concerning the observation of reabsorption.
The Section on the Consequence of Totality.
Either there would be the consequence of the whole [Brahman] being affected, or else there would be a contradiction of the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness.
The [agency] of the Lord in initiating the universe was previously stated by means of the analogy of a flowing stream;
here, the suspicion that there is a dissimilarity between the two analogies is being refuted. (99)
If this Brahman, which is devoid of constituent parts, were to undergo transformation into the form of the world, then its entire essential nature would become involved in the effect. (100)
If, however, there were transformation into parts, then words that convey partlessness would be contradicted; therefore, causality is untenable.
But it is based on scripture, because [the knowledge of dharma] has its root in the word [of the Veda].
On account of the authority of the Śruti, such an inconsistency would not arise;
for the Śruti itself declares both the partlessness of Brahman and its creation of the universe. (102)
In this case, the connection with manifold powers of this extraordinary reality, which is cognizable solely through scripture, is not contradicted by the Veda. (103)
An objection based on general observation can never apply to Brahman, who is of a different nature from all objects and possesses all powers. (104)
And likewise within the self, for [the qualities] are indeed manifold.

Precisely because they belong to a different class from the insentient, the qualities residing in the insentient do not attach themselves to the sentient, nor even to other insentient things that are of a different class. (105)
Thus, wonderful powers reside within fire, water, and so forth;
likewise, the Supreme Self always possesses diverse powers.
And because of the defect in one's own position.
And because causes such as *pradhāna* are of the same nature as worldly objects, the multitude of defects observed in the world would consequently apply to them as well. (107)
Only that Brahman, being of a distinct nature, is capable of being the cause;
because it is corrupted by manifold defects, the Pradhāna and other such principles cannot be the cause. (108)
And she is endowed with all [qualities] through the vision of that.
For this supreme deity is always endowed with all powers;
the scripture beginning with "His power is supreme" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8) declares this very meaning.
If it is argued that [the Lord] cannot [be the cause] because He is devoid of organs, that has already been answered.

If it is argued that there is no undertaking of action because of such scriptural texts as "There is no work for him," due to his being devoid of body and senses, the answer to this has already been stated previously.
And regarding the passage beginning with "Because scripture has its root in the Word," the Śruti says:
"He sees without eyes," and so forth; therefore, Brahman alone is the cause. || 111 ||
Thus concludes the section on the consequence of the whole [of Brahman] being affected.
The Section on the Possession of Purpose.
Not so, because it possesses a purpose.
It was previously stated that the Supreme Self creates the world solely by its own will;
however, the objection that this cannot be so because there would be no purpose for creation is now being refuted. (112)
Because creation is inseparable from its fruit, that Supreme Self, having attained all desires, is indifferent toward the purpose of that [creation]. (113)
