There is no creatorship; for when undertakings are begun, there are two kinds of results:
for one's own sake and for the sake of others. And for this Perfect One, the former does not exist. (114)
For a compassionate being, there is no finality [to suffering], because the creation of the world does not cease.
Therefore, the status of being the cause of the world would not be possible for this Brahman.
But as in the world, [the Lord's activity] is mere sport.
For this Brahman who is completely full, the sole purpose for creation would be mere sport, just as it is for a person of great prosperity in the world. (116)
Just as for a king, games such as ball-play have as their sole fruit mere sport,
even so for Brahman, the purpose of creation is indeed nothing but sport.
"Inequality and cruelty [cannot be attributed to the Lord] because He has regard [for karma]; for thus [the scripture] shows."

Due to the creation of gods and others in superior and inferior states, there would be partiality on the part of the Supreme Self; and because of causing them to undergo suffering, even cruelty would be possible. (118)

If this is argued, it is not so; for those who are the souls of all that is being created, there would be no such [uniformity], because each specific creation depends upon its respective karma; thus says the Śruti.
The *Pārāśarī Smṛti* likewise states: "He who performs good deeds is a good man," and so forth;
it expresses this meaning in such passages as, "He is merely the instrumental cause. (120)

If it is argued that [the distinction between the soul and the body] arises from the non-separation of karma, we say no; for it is established by its beginninglessness, and it is both logically consistent and observed in experience.

And since non-differentiation is heard in such passages as "with the gods" (*sadeva*) at that time, individual souls (*jīvas*) would not exist; how then could there be karma? How, then, can it be said [that they existed] prior to creation? (121)

If it is argued that there would be an inequality in creation, we say no, because both the living beings and their karmas are beginningless; at the time of [dissolution], the essence of the living beings resides within the Supreme Self.
Since there exists karma and so forth that is undivided and extremely subtle, non-distinction is therefore established; otherwise, this would not be possible. (123)
The two faults—the arrival of what was not done and the loss of what was done—are avoided by the permanence [of the soul];
the eternity of the living being is obtained from the Śruti text, "It is not born. 124.
Therefore, it is well established that Brahman alone is the cause of the world,
because all attributes are logically consistent with it.
For those [arguments] that establish the primacy of the Pradhāna, atoms, and so forth as causes are indeed refuted.
And since all these phenomena arise within Brahman alone,
Brahman indeed, known as Nārāyaṇa, is the sole cause of the universe.
Thus concludes the section concerning the possession of a purpose.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter.
The second quarter of the second chapter.
The Section on the Impossibility of Creation (Racanānupapattyadhikaraṇa)
And because the formation [of the world] is untenable, and because of [the nature of] activity, there is no inference [of a creator].
The faults urged by others against the position that Brahman is the cause have been set forth; now, for the sake of defending our own position, the multitude of other doctrines is cast aside. (127)

First, the doctrine of Kapila—which, by its inclusion of the theory of the pre-existent effect (satkāryavāda) and other tenets, causes confusion regarding the true nature of reality—is refuted through valid means of knowledge and reasoning. (128)
An effect such as a body and so forth is produced from a cause belonging to its own genus;
for it is observed in the world that this is indeed the case with every effect, just like a jar. (129)

In the case under consideration, since the body, the sense organs, and so forth, consist of pleasure, pain, and the like, it is established that their cause must be of the same nature; that [cause] is Pradhāna. 130.

If it is argued that the primary cause (pradhāna) itself possesses homogeneity, being composed of substances such as existence (sattva) whose nature consists of pleasure and so forth, that is not logical.
That Pradhāna, being insentient, cannot be the cause of the universe unless it is presided over by an intelligent being who possesses knowledge of it. (132)

Because the creation [of the world] is impossible [on its own], and because we observe that it proceeds when presided over by one who knows it, just as wood and other materials [proceed to form things only when worked upon]. (133)
Therefore, this [Prakṛti], being unguided by an intelligent being, would not be capable of producing effects such as the earth and so forth; thus, Prakṛti cannot be the cause of the universe.
If it is argued that it is like water in a mirage, [we reply] that this is also the case there.

Just as milk not presided over by a conscious agent, and water released from a cloud, transform spontaneously into the state of curd and into the form of the juice of mangoes and other fruits; || 135 ||
In that case, such transformation would be possible for this [Pradhāna] alone;
but it is not so, for activity is not tenable in the absence of an intelligent presiding principle. (136)
For it has been stated that everything, such as milk, water, and so forth, is indeed made the subject of the proposition;
by the Śruti text, "He who dwells in the waters," it is understood that they are presided over by the Prājña.
And because there would be no stability for the distinction [between cause and effect], since [the cause] is independent [of the effect].

If it is said that the transformation [of the pradhāna] occurs independently of the superintendence of an intelligent being, then, because of the distinction from the creation, this must apply to the pradhāna itself. (138)
It would follow that there is an absence of stability during the state of re-absorption, because Prakṛti is independent of the Intelligent Being (Prājña) in its activity of creation. || 139 ||
Therefore, it has been stated that its creation would occur at all times; hence, the *pradhāna*, being unpresided over by the Intelligent One (*prājña*), is not the cause of the universe. (140)
And because it does not exist elsewhere, [it is] not like grass and so forth.
Just as grass and the like, having been chewed by a cow or similar animal, itself becomes milk, so too it is not tenable that the same occurs for the Pradhāna. (141)
That transformation of his occurs only through the stability of the wise;
the state of milk is not seen in the milk consumed by an ordinary bull.
If it is argued that it is like a person and a stone, even so [the objection remains].

Just as another person who is blind, but possesses the power of movement, proceeds toward a task when impelled by the proximity of a lame man who possesses the power of sight; so too [does the Self]. (143)
Just as iron moves due to the proximity of a magnet, so too does primordial nature (prakṛti) move due to the proximity of the Spirit (puruṣa). 144.
If this is argued, we reply: the activity of the Pradhāna is not tenable;
for in that case, activities such as instructing a blind man on the path are observed [to be performed by others]. || 145 ||
The lame man receives instruction, and the blind man likewise proceeds; for there is indeed an effortless approach toward the magnet by the iron.
In this case, because the Puruṣa is devoid of activity, no such modification exists;
therefore, due to his mere proximity, there would be no further engagement of Prakṛti.
Because its proximity is eternal, an eternal creation would follow as a consequence;
furthermore, because it is eternally liberated, there would be an absence of both bondage and liberation for it. (148)
And because the status of being the principal [of a ritual] is untenable.

And during the state of re-absorption (pratisarga), since the qualities (guṇas) abide in a state of equilibrium, the emergence of one [quality] as the predominant factor through its excellence is impossible. (149)

Therefore, a world-creation arising from the relationship of primary and secondary factors—which consists of the increase and decrease of those [factors]—is not possible; hence, that which is unattached to the wise is certainly not the cause.
And because, in the case of inference otherwise [than as described], there would be a lack of the capacity for knowledge.
Even if the Pradhāna were inferred by a different method than the one stated above, its defects would remain exactly as they are, because it is devoid of the power of being a knower. (151)
Even if it were accepted, there would be no object [to be negated].
Even if the Pradhāna is accepted, since there is no external object and because of this [Pradhāna],
that purpose consisting of enjoyment and liberation cannot be inferred from it.
For the unchanging Puruṣa, there can be no experience of nature (prakṛti), nor could there ever be liberation in the form of its relinquishment. (153)
If it is argued that enjoyment arises for a person solely from the presence of that [Self], then because its presence is eternal, liberation will never be achieved. || 154 ||
And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent.
The Puruṣa is changeless, a witness, and likewise an enjoyer;
for him there is neither bondage nor liberation, for both of these belong only to Prakṛti.
The activity of Prakṛti is likewise for the sake of the Puruṣa’s experience and liberation;
thus, because their statements contradict one another, the Sāṅkhya system is inconsistent. (156)
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility of the arrangement [of the world].
The section concerning the great and the long.
Or [the relation between cause and effect] is like that between the large and the long in relation to the short and the circular.
The inconsistency of the doctrine of primordial matter as the cause has already been stated;
now, the incoherence of the doctrine of atoms as the cause is being discussed here. (157)

Because of the mutual conjunction of parts, and because of the emergence of the whole [from them], as well as because of the observation of disparity among the parts due to their being few or many. (158)
If it is argued that atoms are so conceived because the limit of the diminution of their parts must necessarily exist,
and that these [atoms] are the initiators of the world in succession, that is not so.
Just as the production of dyads from atoms and triads from dyads [is asserted], so too everything else accepted by them is inconsistent. (160)
Even those atoms, when their parts such as threads and so forth are joined together by six sides consisting of their own portions, produce a gross object known as a "composite whole" (avayavin). 161.
In that very same way, dyads and other [compounds] would be joined; yet, if those atoms were partless, even a hundred atoms [could not produce a larger magnitude]. (162)
Even in conjunction, there would not be a magnitude greater than that of a single atom for those [atoms], if they are held to possess parts. (163)
Furthermore, those parts would themselves have their own parts, and those too their own parts;
thus, there would be no definitive establishment of causality, and therefore [the effect] is not real.
In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [action] does not exist.
The initial action in atoms is said to be caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa); and that unseen force may reside either in the atom or in the self. (165)
In either case, because the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is not occasional, it would follow that it produces [the effect] at all times;
thus, that [effect] could not be occasional.
Consequently, it follows that there is an absence of conjunction between actions and atoms.
If it is argued that this [action] does not produce [the effect] at all times because it depends upon maturation (vipāka), [we reply: 167.
For just as the maturation of various kinds of karmas does not occur simultaneously in a single form, so too it is by inference that [the existence of] an Īśvara is established. || 168 ||
Because [the existence] of God is unproven, a fixed order cannot arise from His volition;
therefore, the status of the atom as the cause of the world is untenable. (169)
And because of the admission of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to its being equal [to the categories it connects].
Moreover, this view is inconsistent because it accepts the inherence [of universals] and because universals and the like are established as non-separate from the substance. (170)
This inherence is also accepted [to exist] even in the absence of such [a relation];
and since the requirement for a cause is equal in both cases, an infinite regress would result. || 171 ||

If it is argued that the relation has such an existence by its very nature, then this nature would be appropriate for the universal and so forth alone; why [should it be sought] from anything else? (172)
And because it exists eternally.
If this relation were eternal, then because all things that possess the relation would exist eternally as well, this [your] doctrine would be untenable. (173)
And because they possess form and so forth, there is a reversal [of the argument], as seen from observation.

Because these collections of atoms belonging to the earth possess qualities such as color and so forth, there would follow the opposite of their intended permanence, partlessness, and other such attributes. (174)

For it is not the case that, because such a thing is observed in the case of jars and other objects possessing color and so forth, the object to be postulated must necessarily conform to one's own desired conclusion in accordance with what has been seen. (175)
And because there would be faults in either case.
If, out of fear of the faults such as impermanence already mentioned, you accept that emptiness of form and so forth resides in an aggregate of atoms,
then the effect would be devoid of form.
If, out of fear of these defects, you maintain that those qualities existing in an effect possess form because they are preceded by the qualities of their own causes,
then the previously mentioned defects, such as impermanence and so forth, would consequently follow.
Because of these faults in both cases, that [position] is indeed inconsistent. || 178 ||
And because of non-possessiveness, there is absolute lack of concern.

Even though the doctrine of Kapila is in some respects contrary to scripture and logic, there is acceptance by the followers of the Veda regarding his primary tenet, the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkāryavāda). (179)
Since this position of Kaṇāda is not accepted in any respect whatsoever, those who desire the fruit of liberation must absolutely disregard it here. (180)
Thus concludes the section concerning the large and the long.
The section concerning the aggregate.
Even if both causes were present for the collection, that [result] would not be attained.

Since the doctrine of atoms as the cause has already been refuted, the position of the Buddhists, which was proposed on the grounds of its similarity to that [atomistic theory], is now being rejected. (181)
The followers of the Sugata are of four kinds; among them, the first are called Vaibhāṣikas, and the second are called Sautrāntikas, whose view is as follows. (182)

By means of the fourfold atoms of earth and so forth, such as those consisting of odor and other qualities, the aggregates of earth and the rest are produced; and by those [aggregates], the derivative material objects (bhautika) are produced.
For these very external objects are produced as composite aggregates; whereas the internal [self], consisting of a stream of cognition, resides within another body. (184)

The self is the object of the notion "I," even though among these various entities there exists nothing but momentary things; all of this is due to ignorance, which consists of the cognition of stability and so forth.
Therefore, it follows that the arising of the world would indeed occur, as well as worldly transactional activity; thus, this [opponent's] view is incoherent. (186)

In an aggregate of earth and so forth whose causes are atoms, or in an aggregate of earth and so forth whose causes are [coarse] earth and so forth, as well as in an aggregate of the body, sense-faculties, and so forth, the arising of an aggregate is not tenable. (187)
Since you admit that atoms, earth, and so forth are momentary, at what time do these atoms—which perish in a single instant—exert their causal efficiency when combined? (188)
And when do those elements aggregate for you, and when do they become objects of your knowledge or come to be subject to worldly transaction? (189)
If all entities were distinguished by [their own] momentary nature, then neither the arising of the world nor worldly conventional practice would be tenable. (190)
If it is argued that [the existence of the world] is established because of mutual conditionality, we say no, because that is not the cause for the state of being an aggregate.

Ignorance (avidyā) is a perverted cognition; by means of it, those things called formative forces (saṃskāra)—namely attachment, aversion, and so forth—arise. Thus proceeds the succession beginning with ignorance.
Rooted in one another and beginningless, it revolves like a wheel; this is not possible without the aggregate of the primary elements and their derivatives. (192)

If it is argued that this [self] has arisen here because of its state of being a non-aggregate, this is not so, because ignorance and the other factors possess the nature of being aggregates and so forth. (193)
Ignorance consists in the notion of stability regarding that which is unstable, because it is signless;
for a momentary object cannot serve as a cause for a composite whole.

For the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell cannot be the cause for the collection of objects such as the shell; moreover, it would be so for one who perceives stability in what is momentary. (195)
Since it is destroyed at that very moment, whose passion and so forth could there be?
And because of the cessation of the preceding [moment] by means of the subsequent foot.
Because at the time of the arising of the subsequent moment, the preceding moment has perished. || 196 ||
Because it is impossible for this [moment] to be the cause of the subsequent moment, the production of the universe would certainly not occur under this doctrine of momentariness. (197)
If non-existence itself were the cause, then everything would arise everywhere and at all times; or else, only that which exists previously could be its cause. (198)
A certain moment of the jar could not be the cause of those [moments] that arise subsequently;
otherwise, if it were so, there would either be a contradiction of the thesis or simultaneity.
And if that effect were to arise even when the cause is absent, [199]
Furthermore, there would also arise a contradiction with the thesis that the dominant cause, the cooperative cause, and so forth, are the causes for the arising of cognition. (200)
If you maintain that the production of another moment of the jar occurs within a single moment of the jar in order to avoid contradicting your own thesis, [then this is untenable]. (201)
The perception of cause and effect would occur simultaneously;
there would be no attainment of analytical or non-analytical cessation because of the lack of interruption.
And destruction is said to be twofold, according to the distinction between the gross and the subtle. || 202 ||
The former [moment] is fit for perception when a jar or similar object is struck by a staff;
the latter arises at every moment and is unfit for perception, being without continuity.

Those two [destruction and so forth] would not belong to an entity that always possesses its own nature, because there is no interruption [of that nature], as seen in the case of jars and other things when they undergo a change of state. (204)
However, because a destruction without any continuity is not observed, even in the case of a lamp going out, it is held that it merely attains a subtle state. (205)
And because there would be faults in both cases.

If you describe the attainment of insubstantiality by that which has been born, or the arising from the insubstantial, faults would follow; therefore, for you, neither of these two could possibly exist in any way whatsoever. (206)
For according to the doctrine of arising from the void, the effect would be of the nature of the void;
because whatever arises from something must indeed be of that very same nature. (207)

Just as the products of clay, gold, and so forth are seen to be composed of those very materials, so too, when that which has arisen falls into insignificance, the world would become identical with the Self. (208)
And that which is essentially void is neither accepted nor cognized;
therefore, because of these faults in both cases, this view is untenable. (209)
And because there is no distinction in the case of space.
The nature of being insubstantial is not possible in space; yet, regarding that [nature], we possess an uncontradicted cognition, just as we do in the case of earth and other such elements. (210)
Because it is constantly recollected that "the hawk falls here" due to its being the locus [of the action].
Nor is the momentariness of objects established by means of recognition.
The cognition "this is that very same [thing]," by apprehending the past and so forth,
therefore indicates a single entity qualified by two points of time.
If an entity were unstable, recognition would not be tenable;
the same refutation has been stated for both proponents of the existence of external objects. (213)
Not from the non-existent, because it has not been observed.

As for what was previously stated—that because the object does not persist at the moment of the arising of cognition, no object could ever be the object of a cognition—[that is now addressed]. // 214 //
Regarding this, another proponent of the Sautrāntika school, who maintains that objects are inferable, says:
"In this case, the mere existence of a thing as an object of cognition is not the cause [of its being known]. (215)
Since the status of an object as a domain of cognition consists in its being the cause thereof, for we observe various forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth within consciousness. (216)
Having first imparted its own form to the consciousness immediately thereafter, the object such as blue, having itself perished, is then inferred by persons. (217)
Since this diversity of cognition is produced solely by the object, it is incorrect [to claim otherwise];
for that form such as blue which is apprehended in cognition cannot possibly belong to the object. (218)
Even so, in some cases, there may be a semblance of a lost object;
for when the substratum has perished, the property is not seen, yet it is perceived elsewhere. (219)
For when the hibiscus flower has perished, how could redness remain in the crystal?
Therefore, the diversity of cognition would not be possible if the object were momentary. (220)
And thus, there is the accomplishment even for those who are indifferent.
If all things were momentary, then even for those who exert no effort, the accomplishment of all goals would surely occur simply by one who applies effort and so forth. (221)
Because at that very moment [the object] has perished, and because its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth are not admitted to be stable, unitary, and persisting. (222)
Success would be causeless even for those who make no effort;
since this fault is equal for both [positions], therefore perception is not real.
Thus concludes the section concerning the aggregate.
The locus of apprehension.
Non-existence [of external objects] is not [established], because of perception.
Among the four types of Buddhists, the views of two have already been refuted; here, the view of the third, the Yogācāra, is being refuted. (224)

That which is called the variety of cognition produced by the variety of objects is not [truly] possessed of an object, because it is merely the variety of the cognition itself, which possesses forms. (225)
For it is accepted that for those whose cognitions are formless, there is no manifestation whatsoever;
therefore, cognition that is manifesting must possess a form. (226)
The determination is that the aspect which is being cognized belongs to the cognition;
even its appearance as if external is rooted in error.

Furthermore, because of the rule of simultaneous perception, the object is likewise non-different from the cognition; moreover, this is [the case] even for those who maintain the existence of external objects. (228)
Even regarding cognition, its form must be admitted as being similar to the object; otherwise, how could cognition possess a unique character with respect to each respective object? (229)
Since all worldly transactions are established by that alone, the postulation of external objects other than consciousness is not at all logical. (230)
Thus, within this system of logic, the view of the Yogācāras is refuted;
it cannot be maintained that objects do not exist apart from consciousness. (231)
I know the jar, because of this unimpeded perception;
for here, the knower, the act of knowing, and the object all manifest equally as three distinct entities. (232)
The doctrine of one who asserts that only one cognition is true while the other two are false is surely laughable, as it is devoid of logical justification. (233)

The statement that "there is no difference [between subject and object] because they are necessarily perceived together" is contradictory, since concomitance (*sāhitya*) is a proof for the difference between objects. (234)

For it is precisely the capacity to bring about a linguistic convention corresponding to that object which constitutes the "form" (ākāra) of the cognition of it; a jar or the like would not be so [if it were the form]. (235)
That cognition which has a connection with a particular object possesses that object as its specific domain; such is the established rule. (236)
For it is proclaimed that the cognition of that [object] possesses the specific character (asādhāraṇatva) of the jar and so forth;
and because of its dissimilarity [to other cognitions], it is not like the cognition of one's own body and such.
Just as in the case of one's own cognition, so it is also with cognitions of external objects such as jars. || 237 ||
If it is argued that external objects do not exist because their emptiness of objective reality has been established, we say no;
for waking cognitions differ profoundly from dream-cognitions.
The doctrine that [cognitions] are devoid of objects is not tenable, for cognitions are weak;
indeed, they are produced by sleep or impaired senses and are subject to sublation. (239)
And the cognitions of the waking state are the opposite of this [dream state] and are not equal to it;
nevertheless, even in dream-cognition, the reality of the object is admitted from the standpoint of ultimate reality.
If cognitions were devoid of objects, then even the object to be proven would not be established,
because for you, even inference would be devoid of an object since it lacks a basis.
If that [cognition] were to possess an object, its status as knowledge would indeed be inconclusive;
for there is no existence [of an object] when it is not perceived.
Furthermore, the existence of a cognition devoid of an object is never possible anywhere. (242)
Because cognition that is without an agent and without an object is not perceived.
Therefore, the entire system of the Yogācāra school is also untenable. || 243 ||
Thus concludes the section on apprehension.
The Section on the Impossibility in Every Respect.
And because it is impossible in every way.
The positions of the three types of Buddhist partialists have been refuted;
now the Mādhyamika, who maintains the doctrine of universal emptiness, is being rejected. (244)
Origination is indeed difficult to define, whether from the perspective of existence or non-existence;
for instance, when a jar or the like is produced from clay or other materials that have been destroyed. (245)
And destruction arises as the crushing of that form; it is simply non-existence. Therefore, origination from existence is not accepted.
Nor is the latter position tenable, because of non-existence and because the arising of an existent is impossible;
thus, since arising is difficult to define, those [moments] that follow immediately after it [are likewise untenable]. // 247 //
Furthermore, since modifications do not exist at all, reality is said to be empty;
this view of the Mādhyamika is not tenable in any way whatsoever. (248)

Whether asserting that "everything exists" or "everything does not exist," or otherwise, the proponent of emptiness, having made such a thesis, would strive to establish his own desired conclusion. (249)

And because it is impossible in every respect, that which is desired [by the opponent] cannot exist; for in the case of an existing entity, there can be no such terms as "existent" or "non-existent," nor any corresponding cognitions thereof. (250)

For it has been stated that [the object] has its locus in the various states; therefore, its non-existence cannot be established from any source whatsoever, since its existence is intended in every respect. (251)
If it is maintained that everything is non-existent because it is empty, then existence would have to be declared by means of another form, because: || 252 ||

The very occurrence of a transformation into another form is what is expressed by the word "non-existence"; therefore, the crushing of the lump of clay consists in the production of the state of being a jar. (253)

The clay substance, when associated with the state of being a lump, is the producer; likewise, that very same [substance], when associated with the state of being a jar, is held to be the produced. || 254 ||
Therefore, the arising of an entity from non-existence is not accepted anywhere; thus, this view of the Mādhyamika is entirely inconsistent. 255.
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility in every respect.
The Section on the Impossibility [of Contradictory Attributes] in One [Entity].
Not [in one], because of the impossibility [of contradictory attributes].
Having thus set aside the Buddhist position, the doctrine of the Jaina is now cast aside here, as it presents itself through its similarity to the theory of atoms as the cause [of the world]. (256)
The Lord [considers] the world to consist of six substances through the divisions of souls and so forth;
there is no soul therein that possesses a dimension equal to that of the body. (257)
That entire reality is devoid of restrictive rules such as "it exists with the gods" and so forth;
it is everything, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, and likewise characterized by both permanence and impermanence. (258)
The Jaina doctrine—that [reality] consists of both distinct and non-distinct natures—is not tenable;
for attributes such as existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, like light and darkness. (259)
Since contradictory properties cannot exist simultaneously in a single object, this doctrine would not be tenable in the case of horsehood and buffalo-hood [inhering in one thing]. (260)
How is the simultaneous coexistence [of these qualities] possible in a single [individual], given that the soul presided over by Īśāna is said to be the cause? || 261 ||
"The defects remain in that same state"—this Jaina argument is illogical;
and in this way, the self would lack completeness.
When the body of the living being is thus accepted as being of equal measure [to the soul], || 262 ||

If this [consciousness], while residing within the body of an elephant, were to enter into a mosquito or similar small creature, it would be incomplete due to its occupation of only a limited space. (263)
Even in the case of entering a large body, there is no simultaneous pervasion of the whole;
nor is there non-contradiction even through succession, because of the resulting modifications and other defects.
Nor [is it established] by the assumption of states such as contraction and so forth. || 264 ||
The contradiction of this [position] can be avoided by its being comparable to a jar, provided it becomes the locus of defects such as mutability and impermanence. (265)
And because of the persistence of the final state, and because both are eternal, there is no distinction.
And that which is the dimension of the self at the time of liberation is indeed its natural state;
therefore, it is like the very nature of the self itself.
Since the measure existing at the time of liberation is eternal, it must be stated that this very same measure existed previously as well; such is the case with that reality which is the Self.
Previously, his body was like that of an ordinary human, which is highly inconsistent;
therefore, because these two states are mutually contradictory, this doctrine is untenable. (268)
Thus ends the section on the impossibility [of multiple natures] in a single entity.
The Section Concerning Paśupati.
On account of the inconsistency of [the soul being] the master.
Let there be no regard for the systems of Kapila and others that are outside the Veda;
but let there be great devotion toward the Pāśupata system proclaimed by the omniscient Rudra.
The claim that "respect must indeed be shown" is here refuted;
for while God is established by inference, He is not established by the Upaniṣads.
And the distinction between the efficient cause (nimitta) and the material cause (upādāna) is established by Paśupati:
the efficient cause is Viṣṇu, while the material cause is the unmanifest (avyākṛta). || 271 ||
Just as a potter and others create everything in the world, such as jars and the like, so too does the cause of liberation—namely, the wearing of the six seals—create [the world]. 272.
"Worship of the gods with a jar of liquor and likewise meditation on one's own *bhaga*—thus do the four types of Śaivas proclaim matters contrary to the Vedas. (273)
This doctrine of Paśupati is rejected because its [tenets] are mutually contradictory, because the Veda is likewise opposed to it, and because it is extremely inconsistent. (274)
Those who seek the supreme good and possess discernment should not at all respect the Vedas, which repeatedly declare that the world has both a causal agent and a material cause. (275)
Although it is heard here and there that the meditation on Nārāyaṇa, which consists of the speech of Brahmā, bestows liberation, [it is not so]. (276)
Words such as "Śiva" and others, according to the Nārāyaṇīya-anuvāka, have Nārāyaṇa alone as their ultimate referent; for it is heard there exactly so.
And this matter has already been very clearly established;
therefore, because it contradicts the Vedas, this doctrine is unacceptable. (278)
And because a substratum is untenable.
Since the Lord is postulated through inference based on mere signs, His presiding over [the world] must be understood as being like that of a potter, following what is observed [in the world]. (279)
It is not logical for Paśupati to preside over the Pradhāna anywhere;
for presiding is held to belong only to those who possess bodies, since he is bodiless. (280)
It could not possess a body, nor could it have parts;
for the faults regarding both its eternality and non-eternality have already been fully set forth. (281)
If it be argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, we say no, because of the existence of experience and so forth.
Just as the embodied soul's appropriation of instruments and so forth is possible,
so too is it possible for the Lord, though He is bodiless.

If it is argued that the body is the locus of primordial nature (prakṛti), we say no; for the body and so forth serve as the locus for the self only for the sake of experiencing the fruits of meritorious and other such karmas. (283)
In the same way, everything—including the enjoyment of the fruits [of karma]—would belong to the Lord as well.
Therefore, the possibility of the Lord presiding over the *pradhāna* is indeed not tenable.
Either it would have an end, or it would lack omniscience.
If Paśupati possesses unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa), then he would be subject to finitude like the individual soul (jīva), as well as being created and dissolved. || 285 ||
And consequently, there would be a lack of omniscience in every respect; therefore, this view should not be respected by those who desire the fruit of liberation. (286)
Thus concludes the section concerning Paśupati.
The Section on the Impossibility of Origination.
Because origination is impossible.
And because it shares commonalities with the Sāṅkhya and Yoga tantras, the Pāñcarātra Āgama—
proclaimed directly by the Blessed One— is also a means for awakening to the path of liberation.

In this context, the opposing position, which suspects the lack of validity [of our doctrine], is refuted by means of logical arguments, on account of the assertion that the birth of living beings is impossible. (288)
The Pāñcarātra Āgama is not stated here in this Tantra to be an authoritative means of knowledge;
for it asserts that the individual soul, named Saṅkarṣaṇa, is produced from Vāsudeva. (289)
From Saṅkarṣaṇa, the mind known as Pradyumna arises;
and from him, the ego-sense called Aniruddha is likewise born. (290)
For here, an origination of the individual soul (jīva) that contradicts scripture is perceived;
yet in scripture, by the words "it is not born," its beginninglessness is declared. (291)
And there is no instrument for the agent.
If it were held that the mind was born from Saṅkarṣaṇa, then the origin of both the agent— the individual soul—
and the instrument— the mind— would likewise be impossible.
"From this [Brahman] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs"—thus, according to the scriptural teaching on origination, the mind also arises from Brahman. (293)
Or, if consciousness and the other [aggregates] exist, there is no negation of that [self].
Thus, having raised the doubt regarding the lack of authority of this scripture by means of two sūtras, its authority is established by means of a pair of sūtras. (294)
In this context, by the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) and others, the Supreme Brahman is denoted;
for all three forms, beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa, are indeed Brahman. (295)
The authority of this scripture, which is devoted to making that meaning known, is by no means denied; for that supreme Brahman is indeed called Vāsudeva. (296)

In order to establish the relationship between the supported and the support, it is said that he who is compassionate toward those who have taken refuge manifests himself in four ways by his own will alone. (297)
The worship of the Four-Selfs is also the worship of Brahman;
therefore, Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are indeed the Supreme Brahman itself. (298)
Since this scripture possesses a form assumed at will and conveys such a meaning, it is indeed appropriate that its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not denied. (299)

In that regard, the three [deities] beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa are said to be, respectively, the presiding deities over the principles of the individual soul (jīva), the mind (manas), and the ego (ahaṅkāra). || 300 ||
Their description by means of words such as "living being" (jīva) is not contradictory, just as Brahman is understood through words such as "vital breath" (prāṇa) and "ether" (ākāśa). || 301 ||
And because of contradiction.

"For he is indeed determined to be without beginning and without end from the perspective of ultimate reality"—this is also stated in this very tantra, through the negation of the birth of the individual soul (jīva). || 302 ||
This Tantra is declared to be non-contradictory and the highest authority;
therefore, in the Mahābhārata, the author of the Sūtras, Bādarāyaṇa, [states as follows].
"By the statement, 'Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra,' the supreme authority of this speaker is established in its entirety. (304)
The best among the knowers of reality made its authority perfectly clear;
therefore, this scripture is considered distinct from all others, being peerless and unsurpassed. (305)

For the author of the Sūtras, who does not accept that the Pañcarātra lacks authority—just like the previously mentioned Āgamas—and for those who assert its lack of authority, [the following applies]. 306.
Since this position constitutes the opposing view, its refutation is appropriate in this section; therefore, the connection of this subject matter with the section remains intact. (307)
Through such eloquent sayings from the Mahābhārata as "This is better than a hundred thousand [others]," the intention of the author of the Sūtras is indeed very clearly understood. (308)
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility of origination.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter.
Salutations to the venerable Śrī Rāghavārya Mahādeśika.
Now begins the third quarter of the second chapter.
The Section Concerning Space (Viyan-adhikaraṇa)
Space is not [produced], because it is not mentioned [in the scripture].
Because the external systems such as Sāṅkhya rely on fallacious reasoning, and because they contain internal contradictions, their lack of coherence was stated previously. (309)
In order to demonstrate the absence of defects in every respect regarding his own position—that all things, both conscious and unconscious, are desired to have Brahman as their cause—[he says: 310.
Now, the manner in which that [space] is an effect is examined by means of the pair of feet (the two verses);
therein, first, the production of space is challenged and then established through logical arguments.
Space does not arise, because its arising is not heard of in scripture;
for space is partless, just like the self. || 312 ||
It cannot be said that there is no origination, because in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad the birth of fire and the other elements is heard [in the text]: "That [Being] created fire."
In this case, the scriptural statement regarding its origin is sublated because it contradicts the actual state of affairs;
however, [the object] does exist.
The origination of space certainly exists, because of the statement, "space was produced. (314)

For its scripture is indeed capable of declaring in every way that origination, even though it is not perceived by other means of knowledge, has occurred; for its object is things beyond the reach of the senses.
For its state as a partless substance would not prevent its arising;
since non-arising is not a cause [for its partlessness], it remains so for the self as well. (316)
Non-origination is not necessitated by partlessness; rather, it follows from scripture, because [partlessness] is impossible and because of the word [itself].
For in the passage "It created fire," the origination belongs to fire alone. (317)
Therefore, since the statement regarding the origin of space cannot be taken literally, the Taittirīya Śruti must be understood figuratively when it says, "Space was produced. (318)
And because the Veda declares the immortality of space in the passage beginning with "and air," it may be so,
just as the single word "Brahman" [is applied to multiple things].
Even though the word "produced" (saṃbhūta) is applied to sound in the ether, it is used in a figurative sense. || 319 ||

In the subsequent passage beginning with "of the wind" (vāyoḥ) and so forth, this word [“space”] would indeed possess its primary sense, just like the word “Brahman”; for it is a word [denoting a substance]. (320)

Therefore, it is recited in that very same place [the scripture] that [the term] refers to the Pradhāna by way of secondary usage (gauṇavṛtti), and that it refers to Brahman by way of primary usage (mukhyavṛtti) through the word "tapas. || 321 ||
There is no abandonment of the thesis because there is no deviation.
That by which "the unheard becomes heard" is established in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad;
and there is also the declaration regarding the knowledge of everything beginning with space.
Because the sky is not distinct from Brahman due to its being an effect of Brahman, there is no loss [of its nature]; therefore, that scriptural statement was not cited as being figurative.

Furthermore, the birth of the ether is understood from such words as "Being alone" (*sad eva*) and others, which declare the determination of the identity of the self and the other even at the time of dissolution. (324)
In the passage "That [became] fire," only the creation of fire is revealed;
however, its status as the first creation is not [stated], and therefore its birth remains established. (325)
But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the case of the world.
Because the Śruti declares, "All this has that as its Self," and because it states that everything from space onwards is an effect of Brahman, for all things whatsoever that are modifications— (326)
Their origin has already been stated for the most part, as in the statement regarding some of them: "These are the sons of Devadatta. (327)
Even the statement regarding the immortality of space indicates its long duration;
by this, the wind is also explained.
By this very same reasoning, the production of air as well has been declared.
The purpose of referring to Vāyu in the subsequent section is for the sake of further consideration;
here, the separate formulation of a rule for Vāyu is not intended as an extension [of a previous rule]. (329)
But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it is not logically tenable.
It is logically established that the production of the Supreme Brahman, the cause of all, is impossible in every respect, as well as that of everything else other than Him. (330)
Since it is impossible for all cognitions to be dependent upon a single cognition,
the non-arising of that which has already become an object of cognition could never occur.
Thus concludes the section concerning ether (viyad-adhikaraṇa).
The Section on Radiance.
From that [ether], fire [is produced]; for thus it says.

Since everything is an effect of Brahman, it was previously stated that the Supreme Being is the cause of the world; now it is explained that this causality is not direct, but occurs through an intermediary.
In this manner, light indeed arises from this wind alone;
for the Taittirīya Śruti declares, "From wind, fire."
The waters.
Therefore, water also arises from fire; such is the scriptural testimony, for the Śruti declares, "He created water from that," and "Water [arose] from fire," and so forth. (334)
Because it is a modification of earth, the word "effect" (kārya) is applied to the seed;
and likewise in the supplementary passage regarding the designation of the forms of the elements.
In the Śruti passage, "by means of water and heat," it is clearly understood that the earth is indeed denoted by the word "food" (anna). (338)
In a context where the subject matter is the same, there is another word stating "earth is distinct from water.
Therefore, it is firmly known that earth alone is what is denoted by the word "food" (anna). || 339 ||
Therefore, passages such as "From this, the vital breath (prāṇa) is born" are indeed consistent even if Brahman is the cause through a traditional succession.
But he [the individual soul] [arises] from that very meditation on Him, because of His characteristic mark.

The Supreme Self alone is the cause of the effects, such as the Mahat and the rest, having those respective things as its body, because of the indicative mark of His meditative contemplation upon them. (341)

For everywhere it is heard in scripture that the creation, which is the effect of that [will], is preceded by the volition "May I be many," and such an act of seeing (īkṣaṇa) is indeed of that nature.

This is possible only for this Supreme Being who has those respective bodies, for in such passages as "He who dwells in the earth" and "He who dwells in the waters," [the Lord] is described individually in each case. (343)
And its identity with each respective [individual] soul exists by virtue of being the body of that [soul];
for this is heard in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa concerning the Supreme Self. (344)
But because of the reversal [of the order], the sequence from this point onward is also logical.
From the sequence of succession beginning with "from space, air," and so forth, it follows that for all [elements], when reversed, the order is immediately preceded by Brahman. (345)
As stated in passages such as "From this, the vital breath (prāṇa) is born," the creation [of the world] from Brahman in its various respective forms is thus logically established. || 346 ||

If it be argued that consciousness and the mind [arise] in succession because of the gradual dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅga*), we say no, because there is no distinction [in the scriptural statements].
In the midst of the elements (bhūta) and the vital breaths (prāṇa), the stream of the senses and the mind arise in succession;
such is the meaning of what was previously well-stated.
If it is argued that this statement beginning with "ether" (etasya dīpti) refers only to a traditional succession because of the indicative mark "ether or air," we say: no, that is not so. (348)
Because [the world] is born from this, and because it is common to all things from the vital breaths down to the earth, the Supreme Person is superior even to those. (349)
For fire and the other elements are indeed the direct cause of all things;
thus, the words "fire" and so forth denote Brahman as possessing those respective bodies. (350)

Fearing that the designation "Brahman" might be merely figurative when expressed by groups of words established in common usage as denoting various specific objects in the world, he states the following reply.
But the designation [of the Self] as dependent on the moving and the non-moving is figurative, because it exists only when those [bodies] exist.
Words denoting the locus of the moving and the non-moving are indeed primary when applied to the Supreme Self,
because [the elements] such as fire and the rest are permeated by the state of Brahman through their identity with the Self.
Since everything has the body of Brahman as its essence and is a mode thereof, those various words denoting this or that ultimately resolve into Him alone. (353)
Because words expressing a mode terminate in the possessor of that mode, they are non-figurative (abhākta) with respect to cows and the like; for this reason, worldly people [accept this]. (354)
Those devoid of proficiency employ [the term] in only one part of the Vedānta;
therefore, Brahman alone, as qualified [by Māyā], is declared to be the cause of all. || 355 ||
Thus ends the section on light.
The Section on the Self (Ātmādhikaraṇa)
The Self is not [the body], because of its being heard [in scripture] and because of its eternity, as established by those [scriptural passages].

Previously, in the two logical treatises, it was stated that the insentient elements such as space and the rest are effects of Brahman by virtue of undergoing modification known as transformation of their own nature (svarūpa-pariṇāma). (356)

Having refuted the possibility of their origination—since it is precluded here as in the case of space and so forth—the fact that individual souls are effects of Brahman is stated by means of another method. (357)

Likewise, because of the proposition that all cognitions are [contained] within a single cognition, and also because of the determination of the oneness of the Supreme Self prior to creation; || 358 ||
If it is argued that there is an origination of the individual soul (jīva) because of scriptural passages such as "living beings [originate] from water," we say no; for the Self is not born. (359)
Its eternity is understood from such scriptural passages as "He is not born, nor does he die," as well as from texts such as "He is eternal, unborn, and constant. (360)
Because the effect and its cause are not different, and because the self is also an effect,
the proposition that the cognition of one thing entails the cognition of all things is established.
For being an effect consists merely in a single substance attaining another state;
and its other states consist of contraction and so forth. (362)

The birth of the individual soul (jīva) that is observed in relation to ether and the other elements is designated as a transformation of its own nature; however, such a transformation is indeed precluded in the case of the soul itself. (363)
The determination of the Lord's oneness prior to the creation of sentient and insentient beings is established precisely because of the absence of any differentiation of name and form. (364)
The scriptural texts that speak of the birth and death of the inner self (pratyagātman) are intended to inform us of its association with a body and so forth,
which cause the contraction of knowledge and other such limitations.
Thus concludes the section concerning the Self.
The Section on Knowledge (Jñādhikaraṇa)
For this very reason, [the Self] is a knower.
Previously, it was accepted that the individual soul (jīva) is an effect of Brahman by virtue of its attribute of knowledge;
here, however, the statement is made that such knowledge—which constitutes its very nature—does not belong to it.

According to such scriptural passages as "Consciousness is the sacrifice," the essential nature of the self is pure consciousness; or else, this self is insentient, with its intelligence being adventitious. (367)
Because consciousness is not perceived in this self during deep sleep and similar states, and because it possesses a consciousness dependent upon the senses even during waking perceptions. (338)
Nor does it perish after death, because consciousness is denied [to exist] in the liberated state;
furthermore, he is omnipresent because his effects are perceived everywhere. (669)
For this [Self] is not the seer when it is seen, according to such scriptural passages as "He sees the seer";
therefore, both its nature as a knower and its nature as consciousness are innate.
Thus it is understood that this Self is neither pure consciousness alone nor is it insentient;
it exists in all three states—bound, liberated, and both—and is always known as such.
If this all-pervading [self] were an eternal knower by its very nature, it would necessarily perceive everything at all times and in all places; to this, the following answer is given: || 372 ||
Of the departing, the going, and the returning.
On account of scriptural texts concerning departure and so forth, this self is indeed atomic and not all-pervading;
for in the Śruti it is stated that "this self departs. (373)
And the "going" is recited from the statement, "Whoever indeed [depart] from this," while the "returning" is recited as, "[they go] back to this world. (374)
These [powers], being of the nature of mastery, would be severely obstructed at the time of departure [from the body] and by one's own self in the two subsequent cases.
Even for that self which is stationary, [change] occurs in some way or another. || 375 ||

Departure [from the body] results from the separation from the physical form, but both going and returning do not [constitute liberation], because those latter two are accomplished by means of one's own self. (376)
Therefore, the atomicity of this group of selves is indeed certain.
If it is argued that "it is not atomic because it lacks that capacity," we say no, because of the context of the other [sūtra].
Having introduced the individual soul (jīva) with the words "He who is this," [the text continues] "this is the great unborn. (377)
If it is argued that the self is not atomic because of the statement regarding its greatness [in the passage beginning with "He who dwells in the earth"], we say no;
for in the Śruti passage beginning with "By whom this is known," it refers to one other than the individual soul (jīva).
Therefore, the greatness belonging to that [Self] resides in the wise man alone;
for this is established by both its own scriptural designation and by measurement.
This very word "atom" (aṇu) is used directly [in the sense of the self], as in the expression "this atom. || 379 ||
In passages such as "the hundredth part of the tip of a hair," the soul is described by extracting its atomic substance and then stating its dimension based on that very [substance]. (380)
The individual soul (jīva), existing in the states of being bound, liberated, or both, possesses the dimension of an atom (aṇu).
If it were atomic in size, its sensation would not pervade the entire body. (381)
In this regard, a resolution is presented according to another school’s perspective:
"There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood."
Just as [the sun], though situated in one part of the body, brings heat to all parts of the frame. || 382 ||

Just as a single drop of sandalwood paste quickly produces [coolness], so too does the self, though situated in only one part of the body, produce a sensation that arises throughout the entire body. (384)
At that very moment, this [consciousness] experiences it; therefore, there is no contradiction.
If it is argued that this is due to a difference in state (*avasthitivaiśeṣya*), we say no, because [this] is accepted in our hearts.
For indeed, due to the specific distinction of its abiding in particular locations within the body, [it is so designated]. || 384 ||
If it is argued that such a state exists in sandalwood but does not exist in the self, we say no; for there is the Vedic revelation: "For this [Self] is indeed within his heart. (385)
Because it is understood to reside within the specific region of the body known as the heart, its capacity to produce effects pervading the entire body occurs in certain locations. (386)
Now he states his own view regarding the living being existing in the present state:
"Or [the soul's movement occurs] due to its qualities, like light."
By means of his own quality of knowledge, the Self, residing in the heart, pervades the entire body.
Just as light proceeds from a gem that exists somewhere in a particular place, how can it be said that cognition possesses qualities distinct from its own essential nature? (388)
It is stated here that "it has indeed been said that the self is consciousness alone";
furthermore, it demonstrates this through the analogy of fragrance, showing their distinctness.
The negative concomitance (vyatireka) is indeed established by the cognition "I know. || 389 ||

Just as in the cognition "the earth possesses fragrance," the distinction between the fragrance and the earth is perceived, so too is the distinction of knowledge from the nature of the soul perceived. (390)
And scripture likewise shows this: "This one indeed knows," because there is a separate instruction.
For, by such scriptural passages as "He who knows," [it is established that] the Self is the knower. || 391 ||
For consciousness is indeed taught as being distinct [from the self]; how then can there be the statement "consciousness is the self"? To this, it is explained: || 392 ||
But that designation [of the Self] is due to its having those qualities as its essence, as in the case of the "wise one" (prājña).
Because consciousness is its essential quality, the Self is designated by the word "consciousness," just as the Supreme is so called because bliss is its essential quality. (393)
"This is Ākāśa, O Ānanda"—thus it is designated by the word "Ānanda";
and because it exists as long as the self exists, there is no fault, since it is perceived as such.
Because knowledge is necessarily connected to the very nature of the self, it is designated by the term "knowledge. (394)
The objection is not a fault, because it is a property of the eternal universal "cowness" (gotva);
for the expression "cow" is observed here in reference to [individuals] such as Khaṇḍa, as indicated by the word "and" (ca). (395)
Because the self is self-luminous, there is no fault in calling it "consciousness" (vijñāna); therefore, it is said that it is both knowledge and the possessor of the quality of knowledge. (396)

"How can it be said that being a property necessarily connected to the very nature of cognition is [the case], given that it is not perceived during deep sleep and so forth?"—this doubt is here refuted. (397)
But because this [unmanifested soul], though existing, is capable of manifestation, just like masculinity and so forth.
Since that reality which is knowledge does not manifest during deep sleep and similar states,
yet manifests in the waking state and so forth, it persists as long as the self exists.

Just as the masculinity of a body, though present in childhood, does not become occasional because it is manifested in youth despite having been unmanifested; so too [is the case with the self]. (399)
The scriptural statement "he does not exist after death" certainly does not declare an absence of knowledge in the liberated state;
rather, it negates only the knowledge of previously experienced births and so forth. (400)
Regarding the claim that the Self is pure consciousness and all-pervading, the following fault is demonstrated:
otherwise, there would result either the consequence of perpetual perception or non-perception, or else the restriction of one or the other.
And because the self is omnipresent and consists solely of consciousness at all times. (401)
Either perception and non-perception would occur simultaneously, or there would be perpetual perception, or else its opposite. (402)
This all-pervading one, whose nature is consciousness, would be the cause of both worldly existence and liberation, or rather, of the perception of the self and the perception of other things. (403)

Or if that [cause] is the cause of only the other, yet it is the cause of both, then both would exist for it everywhere and at all times. Or else, let both [the cause and its effect] exist [simultaneously]. (404)
At that time, non-apprehension would indeed be nothing other than apprehension;
for if there were only non-apprehension, there would never be any apprehension at all. (405)
Since, according to my view, [the self] always resides within the body, it is established that the perception of the self occurs only there and not elsewhere. (406)

The position that [the self] possesses adventitious cognition is likewise subject to the aforementioned fault, because selves are all-pervading and because [cognition] would be common to all, as would the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth. (407)

"The self is of the nature of knowledge, atomic in size, and likewise possesses the attribute of eternal knowledge"—this is the meaning established in this treatise by means of authoritative evidence and reasoning. (408)
Thus concludes the section on knowledge (jñādhikaraṇa).
The Section on the Agent (Kartradhikaraṇa).
The creator [of the world], because the scripture has a purposeful meaning.
The soul's status as a knower and its atomic nature were established previously;
here, in this context, its agency as well is being established. (409)
Agency belongs to the *pradhāna* alone; it cannot belong to the Self (*ātman*), according to such Kaṭha Upaniṣad passages as, "If the slayer thinks he slays... (KaṭhU 2.19).
Its agency in actions such as killing is denied;
one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer. (411)
"The Lord’s words, such as 'there is no agent other than the qualities,' indicate that his true nature is non-agency; the notion of agency in the self is a delusion. (412)
Therefore, it clearly states that the individual soul (jīva) is indeed the enjoyer;
for agency belongs only to primordial nature (prakṛti), while enjoyment alone belongs to the self (ātman). (413)
Thus, the [opponent’s] incorrect view is that the self alone is the agent, because the scripture has a purpose;
for it is precisely because of its teaching that it is a scripture, and that teaching consists in instigation. (414)
The scripture functions as a motivator by means of generating awakening;
therefore, the insentient *pradhāna* cannot be awakened. (415)
The purposefulness of the scriptures belongs to this enjoyer who is endowed with consciousness;
for agency alone, as the fruit, can belong to the performer. (416)
That which was stated regarding its lack of agency in the act called "killing" is justified by its immutability and its eternity, due to the absence of anything in it that could be killed. || 417 ||
In the course of worldly existence, its agency in active processes arises from its association with the guṇas;
therefore, the statement that the guṇas are the agents is also logically consistent.
The reason for this is stated right here: "It is attachment to the qualities that is its cause.
Furthermore, its agency is declared right here: "The locus, as well as the agent... and so forth. (419)
Therefore, it is established that the individual self alone is both the agent and the enjoyer,
because of its being the material cause and because of the teaching regarding the ripening [of karma].
Having grasped these vital breaths within his own body, he moves about.
Thus, his agency regarding the appropriation of the vital breaths and so forth, as well as in the act of moving about, has been taught;
therefore, he alone must indeed be the agent. (421)
And because there is a designation in the action; for if it were not so, there would be a reversal of the instruction.
"Consciousness extends the sacrifice and it also extends ritual actions";
thus, because of its designation as the agent in all activities [it is established]. (422)

If it is argued: "Surely this agent is not called the Self by the word 'consciousness' (vijñāna), but rather it is simply the intellect (buddhi) described as having the form of the internal organ," that is not so.
If that were so, there would indeed be a reversal of the instruction here;
for "by means of consciousness" (vijñānena) would have been read as an instrumental case. || 424 ||
Therefore, in the Śruti, the term "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers specifically to the individual self (jīvātman);
for, as in the case of perception, there is no such restrictive rule [as that it must belong to the supreme self].
Furthermore, there would be no restriction regarding perception, given the prior omnipresence of the self. (425)
Just as it was stated there, so too here, even though this self is non-agential and Prakṛti is the agent, there would be no restriction regarding its being the enjoyer. (426)
Since primordial nature (prakṛti) is common to all puruṣas, all actions would result in experience for every person, or else they would not result in experience for anyone at all. (427)

For even if there is a distinction between internal organs, since selves are all-pervading, their commonality is unavoidable; therefore, a systematic arrangement [of experiences] is not established. || 428 ||
Therefore, agency belongs to this [Self] alone, and not to primordial matter (prakṛti) in any way, because of the reversal of their respective capacities.
If Prakṛti possesses agency, then for anything other than that, it is in every respect [non-existent].

Because the capacity for being an enjoyer is impossible for that [Self], the state of being an enjoyer must therefore belong to Prakṛti alone; thus, the power of being an enjoyer would not belong to the Self, but rather to Prakṛti. (430)
Therefore, the conscious [self] is neither the agent nor the enjoyer, because it does not abide in itself and because of the absence of meditative absorption (samādhi).
If that Prakṛti were the agent in the means of liberation, namely meditative absorption (samādhi), [then liberation would not be possible]. || 431 ||
She would be the agent, and concentration [would be the object], thinking "I am other than Prakṛti" and "I am the ego"; for it is not possible to meditate that "I am other than Prakṛti. (432)
And just as it is with the carpenter and the axe.
Even when one is endowed with the faculties of speech and so forth, when one desires something, then one acts; and when one does not desire it, then one does not act. || 433 ||

Just as a carpenter, though equipped with tools such as an adze, acts or refrains from acting according to his own will, so too the insentient *prakṛti* acts as a creator [only when presided over by the conscious principle]. (434)
For, in the absence of causes such as desire and so forth, agency would indeed exist at all times;
therefore, it is well established that agency and enjoyership belong to the individual soul (jīva) alone. (435)
Thus concludes the section concerning the agent.
The section concerning dependence on others.
But it [is known] from the word "cuts" (√tan) preceded by the prefix "para-."
The agency of the individual soul (jīva) which was previously established by means of logical arguments is now established here as being dependent upon the Supreme Self (parātman). 436.
The agency of the self is indeed dependent only upon itself and not on another;
for if it were dependent on another, the injunctions and so forth would become purposeless. (437)
If it is argued that "only he who is incapable of acting by his own intellect is impelled [by another];
therefore, the agency of the individual soul (jīva) consists in its independence," we say that this is not so. (438)

For the agency of this individual soul (jīva) is indeed dependent upon the Supreme Self, according to such scriptural passages as, "He has entered within as the ruler," and "He who dwells in the self. (439)
And because of such statements from the Gītā as "I am the author of all," the agency of the individual soul is thus held to be dependent upon the Supreme Self. (440)
But [the Lord] depends on the effort performed [by the individual soul], because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and for other such reasons.

In all actions, that which is first performed by the individual soul (jīva) according to its own will, and that which is subsequently dependent upon the Supreme Self, occurs through the granting of permission [by the latter]. || 441 ||
And this meaning is established by the non-futility of injunctions, as well as by [the Buddha's] restraint and favor;
therefore, it is known through the Supreme Self.
Even though the individual soul (jīvātman) has been set in motion, it remains fit for injunctions and prohibitions;
therefore, it is established that the agency of the soul is dependent upon another. (443)
Indifference, consent, and instigation are the forms of the Lord;
among these, the first occurs in the initial activity of the inner self (pratyagātman).
There is indifference, and when activity begins from the second moment onward, there is the state of being a consenter;
for in the absence of that [indifference], even the activity of the self would be impossible. (445)
Whether in favor of or against the Lord,
that man who is extremely resolute in this matter is the one who acts as the impeller.
Thus concludes the section concerning dependence on another.
The Section on the Parts (Aṃśādhikaraṇa)
The soul is a part [of the Lord], because of the designation of difference, and also because otherwise; moreover, some record that He is called a fisherman, a cowherd, and so forth.

Previously, it was stated that the agency of the individual soul (jīva) is dependent on another; therefore, the relationship between the individual soul and Brahman is like that between a king and his servant. (447)
Because an absolute difference is understood [from perception], the doctrine that relies on the non-primary sense of scriptural passages asserting their non-difference is here refuted. (448)
The individual soul (jīva) is absolutely distinct from the Supreme Self, according to the Śruti which states, "the Knower and the Unknower.
The scriptural texts asserting non-difference are not primary, because they convey a contradictory meaning. (449)

Either Brahman itself is deluded as the individual soul (jīva), because of the teaching that Brahman is the Self, as seen in the scriptural passages identifying them, such as "This Self is Brahman" and "That thou art. (450)
The scriptural texts concerning difference, however, merely restate the difference established by perception;
or else, the individual soul (jīva) is that which is Brahman conjoined with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), as indicated by the aforementioned scriptural texts on distinction. (451)
It would be impossible for this limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) to be imagined through delusion, because the established distinction between bondage and liberation would be entirely untenable. (452)
But the scriptural mention of difference is merely figurative; the individual soul (jīva) is not accepted as a part of the Lord.
For being a part consists in being a portion of a single entity, and that cannot apply to this [soul]. (453)
If that [jīva] were a single part of Brahman, then the entire mass of its defects would belong to the Supreme.
Furthermore, the jīva is not a fragment of Brahman, because fragmentation and so forth are impossible for it. (454)

If it is argued thus, [we reply]: the individual soul (jīva) is not a part (aṃśa) of Brahman, because of the teaching of difference and because of the designation of non-difference; for some schools of scripture maintain that the supreme [Brahman] is one.
By the scriptural statement "the fishermen are Brahman," even the state of being a fisherman and so forth is taught;
by this, it is designated as pervading all individual souls. (456)
That which is a single part of a distinguished entity and is an inseparable qualifier (apṛthaksiddha-viśeṣaṇa) is precisely what is denoted here by the term "substance" (dravya). || 457 ||
Brahman is always distinguished from both the conscious and the unconscious;
that Brahman is the body of the individual soul (jīva), as heard in the scripture beginning with "whose self... (yasyātma...). 458.
For the body is a particular attribute consisting of substances that are non-separately established [from the self];
therefore, the previously mentioned status of being a part (aṃśatva) of the Supreme applies to the individual soul (jīva). (459)

Therefore, the fact that words denoting the body have as their ultimate referent the embodied soul is established by the principle of *ākṛti* (form); this applies to all words that denote living beings. (460)

Because the reality extends as far as Brahman, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) heard in the initial [scriptural passages] would indeed be primary, without recourse to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). || 461 ||

However, the scriptural texts concerning difference everywhere declare the mutual distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) by way of their essential nature and intrinsic being; therefore, this [scriptural testimony] possesses primacy.

Therefore, for the proponents of the Siddhānta, the primacy of all the Śruti is unimpaired; thus, the claim that the individual soul (jīva) must be absolutely distinct from the Supreme is refuted. (463)
The state of delusion can never belong to the eternally faultless omniscient Brahman; therefore, this position as well is refuted. (464)
Because it would entail the consequence that [the self] is the substratum for another's pleasure, pain, and so forth, this third position as well has been decisively rejected. (465)
Therefore, the position that the individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman is the correct one,
on account of the wording of the mantra.
From the mantras of the Puṃsūkta, beginning with "pādo'sya viśvā bhūtāni," [he should worship]. || 466 ||
In this context, the individual soul (jīva) is indeed a portion of Brahman; the word "foot" (pāda) denotes a part.
This is also recorded in Smṛti.
A portion of My very self, eternal and having become a living soul, exists in the world of the living.
Thus, indeed, more than a hundred times in the Gītā, the nature of the individual soul (jīva) is recorded;
however, "But as with light and so forth, the Supreme is not thus."
The individual soul (jīva) is said to be a portion of the Supreme Self, like light and other such qualities. || 468 ||

Just as light is a constituent part of a gem and so forth, and serves as its qualifier, so too is the state of being embodied a qualifier of the supreme self when it is distinguished by that [embodiment]. (469)
The individual soul (*jīva*) would be a specific part (*aṃśa*) whose nature is a particular qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*);
likewise, genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth, would be merely parts of the qualified entity. (470)

The portions consisting of substance, which always possess the single form of being qualifiers, belong to both the individual soul and the Lord, who are designated as the qualified and the qualifier respectively. (471)

Because their own-natures and essential natures are absolutely distinct from one another, a living being (jīva) which possesses a certain own-nature and a certain essential nature cannot be another. || 472 ||
The omniscient one, whose resolve is true, who is faultless, the Supreme Person;
and they remember [him].
Parāśara and others are portions of the Self, just as [the sun] is of its own radiance.

And they remember [the power of fire] in such cases as "the light of the fire situated in one place," and [they argue] against the opponent with the words "whatever is created by which," and so forth. (474)
For they clearly state the subtle nature of this individual soul (jīva):
"Permission and prohibition [apply] to it because of its connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth."
And although all living beings, beginning with the twice-born, are equal in being portions of Brahman, || 475 ||

Just as for certain individuals, there is the permission of Vedic recitation and the like, and the prohibition thereof, based on the connection with a body that is either pure or impure, such as that of a Brahmin or others. (476)

The fire of a learned Brahmin (śrotriya) is brought from his house [to the cremation ground]; he, having gone to the cemetery, is carried around, and furthermore, just like the food of a learned Brahmin.
In this context, it is said that what is to be grasped from one accused of a crime and so forth should likewise be abandoned;
because there is no continuity, there is no confusion.
And because living beings are distinct in each body and are of atomic dimension. || 478 ||
Furthermore, due to the mutual distinction between individual souls, there would be no confusion of experiences;
for in both these views, it is Brahman alone that is bound by ignorance and its limiting adjuncts. (479)
The establishment of enjoyment would not be possible; therefore, that pair is incorrect, as they are merely appearances.
They establish the concealment of the reality of ignorance by the omniscient Brahman. || 480 ||

Appearances are the causes; and there may be sublation because of the scripture’s faultlessness, even in the doctrine that the distinction [of objects] is due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi) imagined through ignorance, as in the previous case.
