Even in the doctrine that the individual soul (jīva) is Brahman conjoined with real limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it is stated here that the regulation [of experience] arises from unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), which is the cause for the distinction between those adjuncts. || 482 ||
Because there would be no restriction regarding what is unseen.

Because the limiting adjuncts, the causes, the unperceived [karmas], the substratum, and the other [the self] are one, there is likewise no establishment of the restriction of those unperceived [karmas]. || 483 ||

Furthermore, because it is impossible for the unseen limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) to cut away [the soul] from another through their own connection, there could be no established order of experience. (484)
And it is the same regarding intentional meanings and so forth.

Even regarding volitions and the like, which have the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as their cause, that [specific] determination of the Lord would not be possible for the very reason previously stated. (485)
If it is argued that [the distinction] is due to a difference in location, we say no, because [all such locations] are included within [the whole].
The regions of Brahman associated with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) are distinguished from those regions of Brahman not so associated; therefore, there is a fixed order of experience.
If this is argued, it is not so; for when all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) move, the space itself is included within them, as is the case with a location that was previously unconditioned. (487)
Therefore, the fluctuation of enjoyments is difficult to restrain for everyone;
and because it constitutes the entire domain of Brahman, all suffering would accrue to him alone. (488)

Therefore, it is well established that this individual soul (jīva) is itself a constituent part (aṃśa), by way of being a qualifier, within the Supreme Brahman which is qualified by both the conscious and the unconscious. || 489 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the parts (Aṃśādhikaraṇa).
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter.
The Fourth Quarter of the Second Chapter.
The Section on the Origination of the Vital Breaths (Prāṇa)
Likewise, the vital breaths.
The fact that ether and the rest are effects of Brahman was stated previously; here, it is stated that the same applies to the sense organs and other instruments of the individual soul.
Just as the living being (jīva) is not produced, so too is the collection of sense-faculties;
for even prior to creation, the sense-faculties exist by virtue of their established measure.
"The seers, indeed, are they; who are they? The vital breaths (prāṇas), indeed," so says the Śruti.
Even though it speaks of their origin, it declares their persistence even during the dissolution.
The view that the scriptural passage concerning the birth of living beings is to be interpreted figuratively is not correct;
for prior to creation, the oneness of the supreme self has been firmly established. (493)
Just as from the scriptural statement of origin, "From this [Self] the vital breath (prāṇa) is born," [the breath is understood to be non-eternal],
so too the sense organs arise, because there is no statement regarding their eternity.
The Supreme Self, described in the passage beginning with "The vital breaths indeed," must belong to this very [Self];
for omniscience, understood through the word "Seer" (ṛṣi), cannot belong to insentient things.
Regarding the statement "the vital breaths are the seers," how could there be a mention of plurality?
This very doubt—that plurality is impossible here—is thus dispelled. (496)
Because a secondary sense is impossible, and because it is heard [in scripture] prior to that.
In this context, the use of the word "many" would be figurative, because at that time no manifold objects exist;
furthermore, there is the scriptural teaching that the Supreme Self alone existed previously.
Because speech is preceded by that [mind].
Because everything—including all names denoting the supreme Self as well as space and the rest—is preceded by creation, the Supreme Person is higher than the vital breaths. (498)

Because prior to creation there was an absence of ether and the other elements—which possess name and form—and because at that time no activity of the sense organs, such as speech and so forth, was possible for anyone. (499)
At that time, the sense organs do not exist; therefore, the designation "prāṇa" applies here [to the breath].
This is not a designation for them, but rather for the Supreme Self alone; and the Vedic usage here is well-established as such.
Thus concludes the section concerning the origin of the vital breaths.
The Section on the Seven Destinies.
And because the seven [realms] are specifically distinguished as states of existence (gati).
The fact that all the sense organs are effects has been established previously; here, their number is determined through reasoning within this inquiry. (501)

By the scriptural statement "there are seven vital breaths," the movement [of the senses] along with the individual self (jīvātman) is declared for only seven; however, by the statement "when five," [the number is reduced]. (502)
And because these alone are joined [with the object], there is a specific statement regarding them:
"The five beginning with hearing, along with the intellect and the mind—these indeed are the seven. (503)
The sense organs, not speech and so forth, [are meant] because of the absence of movement by the self; the designation "prāṇa" applied to these things of minor utility is merely figurative. (504)
But since hands and the like remain [in their respective positions], it is not thus.

While the living being (jīva) remains within the body, even the five [limbs] beginning with the hands are indeed its instruments; therefore, it should be understood that there are not only seven [instruments]. || 505 ||

"These ten are the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the ten are the sense organs (indriyas)," according to both Śruti and Smṛti, because there is no distinction in their being instruments of the individual soul (jīva). (506)
The five beginning with the ear, the five beginning with the hand, and the mind individually—these constitute the eleven sense-faculties; for here, indeed, there is a statement of a lower number.

Because of the intention to express only that specific function in each respective case, there is a distinct mention during the analysis of yoga of the ear and other senses by means of the mind and so forth. (508)
Because of the predominance of the nature of the cognitive faculties (jñānendriya), there are eleven sense organs;
therefore, the restrictive statement that there are "only seven" would not hold, as it would contradict the authoritative source (tanmāna).
Thus concludes the section concerning the arrival together.
The Section on the Atomicity of the Vital Breath (Prāṇa)
And they are atomic.
The number of the sense organs has been previously determined according to their authoritative sources;
in this present section, their dimensions are being defined.
The claim that "all [prāṇas] are infinite" implies their omnipresence because the scripture teaches their infinity is inconsistent. (511)
All vital breaths (prāṇas) do not depart [from the body] together, because of the teaching regarding their movement;
and since they are established as being of limited size and are imperceptible, they are atomic (aṇu).
In that regard, the scriptural teaching of infinity refers to the infinity of its effects;
and it is "preeminent" because it is the cause for the maintenance of the body, being endowed with the quality of preeminence. (513)

If it is argued that the vital breath (prāṇa) is not born because of the scriptural statement regarding its existence in its own effects prior to creation, and that the scriptural mention of its birth must be interpreted otherwise, as in the case of the individual soul (jīva); || 514 ||
It is stated that the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) also arises just like the sense organs, because of the scriptural text concerning its origin: "From this [Self] the vital breath is born. (515)
For, just as in the case of the individual soul (jīva), there is no scriptural hearing of a prohibition against its origination;
and furthermore, because that would contradict the determination of the oneness of the Supreme prior to creation. (516)
Furthermore, this scriptural passage, "He breathed forth without wind," does not indeed declare the existence of the function of breathing during the dissolution. (517)
That [scripture] declares the existence of the one Supreme Brahman, because it speaks of the absence of air in that very same place by saying "it is not windy" (avātam). || 518 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the minuteness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The Section on the Activity of Air (Vāyukriyādhikaraṇa)
Nor are [the vital breaths] the functions of air, because they are taught separately.
It has been stated that the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is also produced like the sense organs; its true nature is now investigated and described here. (519)

If it is argued that the supreme vital breath is merely air, based on the Vedic scripture stating "that which is prāṇa is air," and that there is no well-known status as "vital breath" (prāṇatva) in the non-dual reality of the elements— then [the following is said].
Whether one asserts that "prāṇa" refers to air or to functions such as inhalation,
neither of these two positions would be consistent with valid means of knowledge.
Neither air nor its activity can be the vital breath (prāṇa);
rather, it is simply air in the state of possessing the capacity to sustain the body and so forth. (522)
From this [Being] are born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind, and all the sense organs;
and because space and wind are mentioned separately from the vital breath, [it follows that the Being is distinct]. (523)
Prāṇa cannot be mere air, nor can it be its activity for that very reason;
furthermore, no separate mention of activity is seen in the case of fire and the other elements. (524)

If it is argued that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is a modification of air (*vāyu*), and therefore, like fire (*tejas*) or other elements, this [breath] too must be a distinct element, then it is said in response to this doubt: || 525 ||
But it is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them and other such reasons.
Like the eye, the ear, and so forth, the vital breath (prāṇa) is considered an instrument of the individual soul (jīva);
and its status as such an instrument is [established] along with those other sense organs.
From its teaching in the *Prāṇasaṃvāda* and other such texts, this is understood;
for it is only when there is a commonality of nature that its recitation is appropriately joined with them. (527)
This meaning is understood even from the specific mention among the instruments;
therefore, like fire and so forth, this prāṇa cannot be a different element. (528)
And there is no fault because of non-performance; for thus [the scripture] shows.

Furthermore, the fault that is alleged against this [scripture]—namely, that it is devoid of action consisting of benefit to the living being—is not applicable, because the scripture [is indeed so]. (529)
The phrases "when [the soul] has departed" and "even more wretched" clearly demonstrate the activity known as the maintenance of the body, the senses, and the vital breaths. (530)

Because it sustains the body and so forth by being beneficial to the living soul (jīva), this vital breath (prāṇa) possesses the status of an instrument (karaṇa), just like the sense organs; thus, its nature as an organ remains unimpaired.
The fivefold activity is designated as being like that of the mind.

Just as desire and so forth are [states] of the mind, and because desire is volition (saṅkalpa), even though there is a difference between the function and its effect, they are not admitted to be different principles. || 532 ||
Thus, by the expression "prāṇa" and "apāna," it is established that apāna and the others are merely different functions (vṛttibheda) of prāṇa, and not a separate reality.
Thus ends the section concerning the function of air.
The Section on the Greatest and the Smallest (Śreṣṭhāṇutvādhikaraṇa)
And it is atomic.
It was stated previously that the wind, when it has entered into a different state, is designated by the term "prāṇa"; here, its measurement is now being defined.

Because of the scriptural hearing of "the vital breath does not depart" and so forth, this primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), like the sense organs, is atomic; [this is so] until there is the realization of its infinity. (535)
The Vedic scripture beginning with "He is equal to these three worlds" indeed declares his sovereignty over the maintenance and excellence of all living beings. (536)
Thus concludes the section concerning the excellence of atomicity.
The Section Concerning the Presiding over Light and Other Elements.
But light is the primary substratum, because of the scriptural statement regarding it as being with breath, just like the vital air.
Thus, the production and other characteristics of the vital breaths and the sense organs have been described.
It is maintained that fire and the like do not depend upon those [organs] for their own substratum. (537)

The claim that the activation of the collection of sense organs by the individual soul and by fire and other elements is under their own control due to independence is refuted by valid means of knowledge.

The activation of the sense organs and so forth by fire and other elements occurs together with the individual soul (jīvātman) through the will of the Lord, according to the statements of the Śruti. (539)
The scriptural passage beginning with "He who, dwelling in fire, controls it, is the Self," and so forth, establishes this;
and because that [Self] is eternal.
Because the state of being presided over by another self is fixed for all [beings]. || 540 ||
It is stated that their status as presiding deities arises solely from His volition;
by the words "created by Him" and so forth, it is shown that the Lord is always the controller.

For the entry of consciousness into the conscious and unconscious is indeed heard in scripture and is also recorded in the Smṛti, such as in the passage beginning with "Having pervaded... Therefore, the meaning stated [by us] is entirely consistent. || 542 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the presiding over light and the other elements.
The Section on the Senses (Indriyādhikaraṇa)
These are the organs, because they are designated as such, with the exception of the best one.

The claim that everything— including the eyes and so forth— is an "organ" (indriya) because they serve as instruments for the living being (jīva), with the eye being the most excellent, is here refuted.
If it is argued that all of them must be considered sense organs because they are instruments and because they are designated by the term "prāṇa" without distinction, we say: no. (544)

Those vital breaths (prāṇas) that exceed the [five] principal ones are clearly manifest within the sense-faculties (indriyas), because of the statement regarding the sense-faculties beginning with "the ten and one" and so forth. || 545 ||
Because of the scriptural statement of difference and because of the distinction [between them].
"From this [Being] are born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind, and all the sense organs"—because of such statements, this vital breath is mentioned separately from the sense organs. (546)

It is clearly understood that the status of being a sense-faculty (indriyatva) belongs only to those others; however, the status of the mind as a sense-faculty is established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), since it has been mentioned separately. 547.
Furthermore, because it differs in nature from the eyes and other [senses] which are superior, this [Self] does not possess that [nature];
for while its activity exists during deep sleep, no such activity is observed in the sense organs.
However, for the eyes and other [senses], their function consists of cognition and so forth;
whereas the maintenance of the body and the senses belongs to this [Self]. Therefore, it does not possess the nature of a sense organ. (549)
Thus concludes the section on the faculties (indriya).
The section concerning the fashioning of names and forms.
But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who performs the tripartition, because of the scriptural teaching.
Since it was previously established that the collective creation is produced by Brahman alone,
it is certain that the great elements, the sense organs, and so forth, are effects of Brahman.

"The creation of the individual forms of gods and others was performed by the Four-faced One alone"—by removing such doubt regarding embodied beings, whether divine, mortal, or otherwise, [the Lord]... 551.
This section is undertaken to ascertain that [the Self] is the cause of that [world];
it concerns the manifestation of names and forms, which is the individual creation of the manifold universe.

The activity belongs to the material cause itself, which is the form of the collective living being (samaṣṭijīva), as is shown by the scriptural passage on distinction beginning with "by this living self" (anena jīvenātmanā). || 553 ||

"How can it be that the Supreme Being says, 'I shall explain this'?"—this objection is indeed resolved, for since the individual soul (jīvātman) is a portion of the Supreme, such a statement is entirely logical. (554)
If it is argued that therefore this evolution is merely the primordial cause (dhātu), that is not so;
for this is taught as the evolution of that which was already made tripartite. || 555 ||
The individual creation consisting of the manifestation of name-and-form belongs to the Supreme Self;
however, this process of triplication cannot be performed by the Creator.
The birth of the Four-faced One indeed occurs immediately after the creation of the cosmic egg;
the manifestation of that creation arises solely from the tripartite elements of fire, water, and food.
In that [egg], Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds, was born;
having come together and joined with one another, they produced the egg.
Thus it is recorded in the Smṛtis; therefore, this is declared to be the detailed creation (vyāṣṭi-sṛṣṭi) proceeding from the very Supreme Self in the form of the four-faced Brahmā. || 559 ||
The scriptural instruction, "I shall manifest names and forms," is well-consistent with this;
so too is the statement of distinction, such as "by means of this living self," and so forth.
For it is perfectly consistent to understand the meaning as "by the self whose body is the individual soul" (jīvātmadehakenātmanā);
the word *jīva* [in this context] refers to that which has the individual soul as its body, just like the words *tejas* and so forth. 561.
Therefore, the Śruti declares, "By means of the living self (jīva-ātman)";
and here, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the two indicated terms is stated in its primary sense.
Furthermore, there is a single authorship for both the entry and the differentiation;
therefore, the differentiation of name and form is an activity of the Supreme Self. (563)

In this context, the manner in which the threefold transformation occurs among the objects created by Brahmā is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "Food, when eaten, becomes threefold," and so forth; therefore, he [is called] Vidhi.
The threefold making performed by the Piercer (Brahmā) is thus rendered logical; for [the scripture] says, "He manifested names and forms," and "He made each one threefold. (565)
The statement that there is also a sequence of priority here is refuted;
[the elements] such as flesh and so forth belong to the earth, while those of the other two [realms] are according to their respective names.
By the words "food" and so forth, the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) is not being described here. || 566 ||
The threefold transformation of food that has been eaten and so forth is described here;
that which is the grossest part [becomes feces], and so on, in successive order.
Feces, flesh, and the mind are transformations of the substance of food;
urine and blood—these are the transformations of water. (568)
"Bone, marrow, and speech"—these are the modifications, as are heat and vigor;
for it is said here that there is a threefold processing (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of fire, water, and food. (569)
In that case, since flesh arises from earthy excrement and the mind from [earthly] thought in succession, it would follow—
due to its subtlety and extreme minuteness— that it must attain the nature of fire.
For it is accepted that earth, water, and fire, when not yet tripartite (trivṛtkṛta), possess by their very nature, respectively, the qualities of grossness, subtlety, and extreme subtlety. (571)
Because of the introductory statement, "The waters were drunk, and likewise the fire was eaten," and so forth,
there is thus the attainment of the watery and fiery states respectively in those two successive stages.
For indeed, the remainder of the sentence is stated exactly according to the words:
"Breath consists of water" and "Speech consists of fire. (573)
If the previously mentioned method of triplication is explained here, it is due to the relative grossness and subtlety of the body, urine, and breath respectively. (574)
Furthermore, it would follow that the earth and fire elements [respectively] consist of bone and marrow;
likewise, the earth-nature and the water-nature would also apply to bone and marrow respectively. (575)

Therefore, it is only of that which has already been made tripartite prior to food and the rest that a threefold transformation is spoken of here; consequently, the process of tripartition itself is not mentioned in this context.
The tripartition (trivṛtkṛti) occurs prior to the manifestation of names and forms; it is more powerful because of the sequence of meaning, and thus the order of the textual reading is set aside.

The passage beginning with "O Agni, that which is red" is a demonstration of the threefold nature [of the elements], because Śvetaketu was situated within the egg [of the universe] along with the fire and other elements contained therein. (578)
Because it is impossible to demonstrate that [Brahman] in external objects, its manifestation is therefore effected through the effects of the triply-combined [elements]. (579)
But on account of its preponderance, there is a designation of that; indeed, there is a designation of that.
In this context, it is appropriate that the words "food," "water," and "fire"— which denote pure elements—
refer instead to the earth and the other elements as they have been made tripartite (trivṛtkṛta).

Indeed, because each [topic] is extensive, [the word "food" (anna) and so forth] occurs once in each [section], or else in all three; the repetition of the words indicates the completion of the chapter. (581)
Thus ends the section concerning the fashioning of names and forms.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter.
Thus ends the second chapter.
May there be prosperity.
Salutations to the venerable Śrī Rāghavārya Mahādeśika.
Salutation to our lineage of gurus.
*ka-d-ṛ-v-ad-dha-dya-ṇ* *ṛ-ḍ-ḍa-ṇ-n-r-ṭh-ṭh-an-r-ṭh-ṭh-a*.
Chapter Four, Third Pāda.
The Section Concerning the Path Beginning with Light (Arcir-ādy-adhikaraṇa)
[The soul departs] by way of the path beginning with light, because that [path] is well-known [from scripture].
The commencement of the journey for the knower of Brahman who has departed from the gross body—by means of a specific channel through the grace of the Heart—has been explained previously. (189)
Now the path of that wise one as he proceeds is being determined;
in all the Vedas, the single path with light as its entrance is proclaimed. (190)
"Does the knower go to Brahman by that [path] alone, or by this one, or by others, or by paths mentioned elsewhere? Therefore, since there is doubt here regarding the lack of a fixed rule," || 191 ||
Because the paths are not of a single form and are likewise independent of one another, the statement that there is no fixed rule in this matter is simply not logical. (192)
The path beginning with light is described as being one and the same everywhere;
therefore, he indeed proceeds by that single path alone. 193.
Because it is recognized everywhere, that single path in the Śrutis is taught in all the Vedas with variations of deficiency and excess. (194)
Just as there is a combination of the qualities of knowledge [in the case of the Upaniṣads], so it is here as well:
there is a combination elsewhere of those [qualities] which are heard in connection with a single effect [elsewhere]. (195)
Therefore, since the path is one and the same as heard in all the Upaniṣads, it is well established that all the learned must proceed by that very same path. (196)
Thus concludes the section concerning the path beginning with light (the *arci-rādy-adhikaraṇa*).
The Section on Air (Vāyvadhikaraṇa)
Vāyu [is reached] after the year, by way of both the non-specific and the specific.
In the section concerning the path beginning with light, after the year, the sun is heard of in one place, while in another, the world of the gods and the world of the Maruts are mentioned. (197)

Regarding these two heard in the middle [of the mantra], there is a doubt as to whether they have different meanings or are one and the same, O Marut; [the answer is] that they have different meanings because of the difference in the words. (198)

Moreover, because the two [terms] have different meanings due to the word "ūrdhva" and the ablative case ending, they would, according to the method of the scripture, fall between the year and the sun. (199)
And because there is no distinction [in his state], that wise man may proceed according to his own will;
yet such a person shall not go to Vāyu after more than a year.
Because it is stated that [the soul] moves specifically by means of the wind alone, without distinction, the term "devaloka" here refers to the world (loka) of the gods (deva). 201.
He speaks of the wind in general, saying, "He goes to that wind"; yet here, the word "wind" also expresses it in its specific sense. (202)
Therefore, by those two words, it is indeed Vāyu that is denoted.
Consequently, after a year, he should go to that very Vāyu. || 203 ||
In the Veda, it is said that "Vāyu is the dwelling-place of the gods";
since he is the one who blows here, there is thus a consistency with the stated meaning. (204)
Thus ends the section concerning the air.
The Section on Varuṇa.
[The word] *taṭitaḥ* [is used] because of its connection with Varuṇa.
In the Chāndogya and other Upaniṣads, the sequence of the path beginning with the Radiance (arcis) is taught;
therein, the placement of Vāyu above the Year is established.

Regarding the consideration of whether these [deities] beginning with Varuṇa should be placed above Vāyu according to the textual order, or at the very end because lightning is mentioned [therein]: 206.
According to the Kauṣītaki [Brāhmaṇa], the abode of Pracetas is above Vāyu;
therefore, because it contradicts the sequence of Vāyu and Arka, [the abode] of Marutvat is not [there].
If it is argued that Prajāpati also enters into that very [place], we say no;
for there is a mutual relationship between lightning and Varuṇa based on their abiding within the clouds. (208)
The abode of this Varuṇa is established above the lightning;
thereafter, the abode of Indra and Dhātṛ is established above Varuṇa.
Because they are recited [in that order] and because they abide at the end for those who have arrived;
thus is this sequence established for the series of the subtle body (ātivāhika).

The rays, the day and so forth, the fortnights, the northern solstice, the year, the wind, and those originating from the sun, the moon, lightning, Varuṇa, Indra, and the lotus-born [Brahmā]. || 211 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Varuṇa.
The Section Concerning the Conveying Body (Ātivāhikādhikaraṇa)
The subtle body (ātivāhika) [is the subject], because of the mark of that.
Are these, such as the "flame" (arciḥ) and so forth, signs of the path, or are they the grounds of enjoyment for the wise, or are they the conducting deities (ātivāhika)? (212)
These [words] serve as indicators for thought regarding villages and the like; indeed, such is seen to be the worldly instruction concerning the path for words expressing time. (213)
Because it is impossible for these [worlds] to possess the nature of signs, they must be planes of experience (bhogabhūmi);
for it is taught in scripture that "these alone are the days and so forth," which establishes their status as worlds (loka).
Some followers of particular Vedic branches recite the word "world" (loka) as referring to the path beginning with light (arcis);
however, these [beings] are not appointed by the Supreme Self as the bearers of the path.

On the path, for the knower, there is a non-human [conductor] because of the mark consisting in being a conductor who causes others to go; this is known from the concluding statement: "He leads them. (216)
Because the lightning is observed to be the bearer of the [sacrificial] oblation, it belongs to those who precede it;
and for the others who are mentioned without distinction, that same [lightning] is [the deity]. (217)
Therefore, it is determined that there is a relationship of being the carrier of the path;
for, due to the absence of enjoyment, it is precisely the state of being the carrier of the path while on the way. (218)
The word "world" (loka) is appropriately used here; these terms, such as "light" (arcis) and the rest, refer to the presiding deities who, being identical with those [stages], proclaim them. (219)
Since scripture declares that only the person consisting of lightning (Vaidyuta) leads one here to Brahman, how can Varuṇa and the others be considered "conveyors" (Ātivāhika)? 220.
Then, by that [weapon], it was destroyed by the lightning-like [missile].
And their upward journey from the lightning occurs by means of the Vaidyuta [deity], for scripture declares that he alone leads them, as he is the one who causes them to attain Brahman. (221)
For that very non-human [guide], the attendants beginning with Pāśyā are the auxiliaries;
therefore, all those beginning with Arcis are the conductors for the wise.
Thus concludes the section concerning the subtle body (the *ātivāhika*).
The Section on the Effect (Kāryādhikaraṇa)
Bādari [holds that the soul] has a body, because its movement is thus possible.
Previously, those who lead [the soul] on the path beginning with light were described;
here, however, those who travel [that path] are defined, setting aside other opinions. (223)
Does the group beginning with light lead those who meditate upon the effect (the created world) to the four-faced Brahmā, or does it lead only those who meditate upon Brahman, or both? 224.

Regarding the doubt as to whether those who meditate on the individual soul (jīva) as being identical with Brahman are also led to the effected realm (kārya), Bādari says that it is only those who meditate [on Brahman] who are led there.
Since the attainment of the goal is possible only for one who meditates upon Hiraṇyagarbha, that Brahman is complete everywhere for one who meditates upon it in order to attain it. (226)
Movement to another location is not at all logical, because [the Self] is always already attained [there].
In this context, the effect of supreme knowledge is indeed only the destruction of ignorance.
For movement is considered necessary for the sake of reaching a location that is spatially delimited;
therefore, the group headed by the Rays leads the worshiper of the effected Brahman.
And because it has been specified.
"From the statement 'the mental person [goes] to the worlds of Brahmā' and from the use of the word 'worlds,' [it follows that] the non-human [messenger] leads the one who meditates upon Dhātṛ. (229)
It is made known that he leads [the soul]; having thus departed by way of the path of light (arcirmārga), he directs his intention toward the assembly hall and the residence of Prajāpati.
Therefore, the path beginning with light leads that person to the vicinity of Brahman;
since this is thus established, how could the Lotus-born [Brahmā] lead them to Brahman itself? (231)
It is stated here that the expression is not by means of the neuter word "Brahman";
rather, that designation is used because of proximity.
The designation of the Creator as "Brahman" may arise from his proximity to Brahman. || 232 ||

Indeed, because he is the first-born, there exists proximity to him [Brahmā], even for the Creator who has reached the realm up to the world of Brahmā, according to the scriptural statement beginning with "up to the world of Brahmā. (233)
To the objection that "return is not to be abandoned," the following answer is given:
because it is stated [in scripture] that upon the dissolution of the effect, [the soul] goes from there to the Supreme together with its presiding deity.
And even upon the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha, non-return [to saṃsāra] is logical. || 234 ||
When the world, which is the effect, perishes, that Creator who presides over it—the Brahmā—speaks of the attainment of Brahman even for this wise one, saying, "This is Brahman. (235)
And because of Smṛti.
When the time for reabsorption has arrived, all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state at the end of the highest [Brahmā], together with Brahmā himself.
From this traditional teaching (smṛti), this meaning is understood:
therefore, Bādari declares that [the path] beginning with light leads only those who meditate upon the effected Brahman (kārya-brahman).
In these three sūtras, Jaimini states his own final conclusion:
"Jaimini [holds that the word 'self'] refers to the Supreme [Self], because it is the primary meaning."
This path beginning with light leads only those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman.
Because the word "Brahman" is used in its primary sense there, it is He who leads them;
for the Supreme Brahman, being eternal, cannot undergo the act of going.

Even though the Knower is omnipresent, he indeed goes to a specific abode, because the supreme scripture teaches that this is preceded by the destruction of all ignorance and results in the attainment of Brahman. || 240 ||
Due to the word "world" (*loka*) and the frequent occurrence of such expressions, there is no cognition of [the world] as being self-existent (*svayaṃbhū*);
rather, by the logic of the "chief of the Niṣādas" (*niṣādasthapati*), a *karmadhāraya* compound is appropriate. (241)
When the meaning "Brahman alone is the world" has been determined as a single sense, the use of multiple expressions is justified, just as in the cases of "Aditi" and "the nooses. || 242 ||
There exist, according to authoritative proof, infinite worlds that are non-material (aprākṛta) and fashioned by the will of the perfect Brahman. (243)
And because it is seen [in scripture].
The scriptural passage beginning with "From this body" clearly demonstrates that for one who has departed by way of the path starting with light, there is the attainment of the supreme Brahman. (244)
And there is no intention directed toward the effect.

The statement "He goes to the assembly hall and the abode of Prajāpati" is an expression of intention regarding the effect (kārya), namely Hiraṇyagarbha; this is clear from the scriptural passage beginning with "having shaken off [evil]" (dhūtvā). || 245 ||
Because he declares the world to be uncreated, which is something to be fully realized, and because of his intention that "I am fame," identifying himself with the self of all. (246)
Therefore, the group beginning with light leads the worshiper of Brahman alone to that very goal; this is the opinion of the sage named Jaimini. (247)
On this point, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states his own established conclusion:
"He leads those who do not rely on symbols," so says Bādarāyaṇa,
because there would be faults in either case, and because of the nature of their resolve (*tatkratu*).
The host headed by Arciṣmān leads others away from those who rely on the [Vedic] mantras as their support. || 248 ||
Thus the venerable and noble Bādarāyaṇa considers it:
either through the vision of Brahman, or they worship everything in its respective form. (249)
Those who meditate upon this entire collection of sentient and insentient beings as symbols, those who contemplate the Supreme Brahman, and those who worship the Self—[all these are included]. (250)
These two types of persons are by nature liberated from that which consists of Brahman;
those known as "those who take non-symboles as their support" abide in both ways. || 251 ||

The one whose face is light does not lead those who rely on the symbols anywhere; otherwise, there would be an inconsistency with scriptural passages such as "the supreme light" in the context of the effect. (252)

If there were a restrictive rule that [the soul] must be "only supreme," then the scriptural statement "those who know it thus" would be contradicted; since there is a fault in both positions, [the scripture] therefore leads to two kinds [of souls]. (253)

In this regard, the following point is established: even by the principle of "according to one's resolve" (tatkratu-nyāya), whatever form is meditated upon in worship, that very same form is indeed what is attained. || 254 ||

Those who are devoted to the knowledge of the five fires worship their own pure nature as the Self, having realized that the Self is of the essence of Brahman through the realization "I am the Self. (255)
Since their journey via the path of light and so forth is heard of in the Śruti,
it is stated that for one who has gone by that path, there is the attainment of Brahman and non-return.

But for those who take the symbols as their support, because there is an absence of the two kinds of meditation, and because they practice a meditation mixed with the non-sentient, it is not so according to the principle of "as is one's resolve" (tatkratu-nyāya). || 257 ||
For this very reason, the journey via the path beginning with light and the attainment of Brahman occur;
and by the logic already stated, their return is likewise unavoidable. (258)

For it is precisely because the individual soul (jīva) is the subject qualified [by the attributes] in the meditation on the five fires (pañcāgnividyā), that the attainment of liberation (kaivalya) is held to occur for those devoted to it while they are still on the path. || 259 ||

And at the appropriate time, from that place, the upward path through the "mouths of light" leads to the attainment of Brahman and non-return; this is established by means of valid authority. || 260 ||
And he demonstrates the distinction.
The scripture clearly shows that for those who meditate on the symbols (pratīka), there is no dependence on the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) until they reach the state called "name. (261)
And there is only a very slight distinction in the fruit; therefore, the consistency of the stated meaning holds.
The statement "they all [attain liberation] together with Brahmā" refers to those of meritorious deeds. (262)
Beyond that is Hiraṇyagarbha, reached through the practice of yoga;
therein lies the indication of the attainment of Brahman for those who have mastered the sciences.
"The host headed by Arciṣmān leads both types of those previously mentioned who meditate on what is not a symbol"—thus everything is consistent. (264)
Thus concludes the section on the effect (kāryādhikaraṇa).
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter.
The Fourth Quarter of the Fourth Chapter.
The Section on Manifestation upon Attainment (Saṃpadyāvirbhāvādhikaraṇa).
The manifestation [of the self] upon attaining [Brahman] occurs by its own nature, because of the word "by itself" (svena).

In the preceding section, it was stated that for the wise one who has set out by way of the path beginning with light, there is the attainment of Brahman by means of the divine being known as "not-human. (265)
By this fourth quarter-verse, the state of one who has attained liberation is described;
for such is the statement beginning with "evamevaiṣa" which is heard in the Sāman.
Does this statement refer to the manifestation of the individual soul's own nature, or to the assumption of a realized form through the attainment of Brahman? (267)

This being the case, [it is argued] that because the essential nature [of the self] is seen to be devoid of bliss during states such as deep sleep, and because that [bliss] is eternally manifest even then; || 268 ||
By this, the connection with a previously non-existent form characterized by exclusive bliss is expressed;
therefore, the statement "he is manifested" becomes appropriate. (269)

If it is argued that "for this [self] experiences bliss alone" implies an infinity of happiness as heard in scripture, we say no; for what is being described here is the attainment of the Supreme Light. (270)
Because of the qualification "by itself" in the phrase "the manifestation of its own nature," that qualification would indeed be redundant if there were a connection with an adventitious form. (271)
Even in the absence of that [external object], because its own nature is established here, it is said that speech is eternally attained in its own essential form. (272)
It is stated here that [the claim] "he is manifested" is futile;
for he is liberated, as it has been asserted.
Freed from karma and the body produced by it, he possesses his natural form. || 273 ||
By the scriptural statement "it is manifested," it is established here that [the Self] is eternal; for although its own nature is already attained, it is [concealed] by ignorance. (274)
The liberation of that which was concealed is called "manifestation" (abhiniṣpatti),
because it alone is the subject promised as the goal to be realized in the Śruti.

For it has been stated repeatedly that the nature of the individual soul (jīva), which has abandoned the body born of karma and transcended the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], is the subject to be explained here.
Indeed, in the passage beginning with "But this very [Self]," a formal proposition is seen here:
how could the manifestation of one's own essential nature alone constitute the goal of human life? (277)
The Self [is the subject] because of the context.
"That this Self is adorned with the eight qualities by its very nature" is known from the context itself, as previously stated. (278)
Since the context is "that which is the Self," it is certain that this refers to the individual soul (jīva);
therefore, these eight qualities belong to that soul by its very nature.
That which was previously concealed manifests through the attainment of Brahman; it is not newly produced. Thus spoke the venerable seer Śaunaka. (280)
For this is clearly stated by the passage beginning with "Just as the moonlight is not created" (yathā na kriyate jyotsnā);
therefore, it is logical that manifestation, termed "expansion," occurs upon the dissolution of bondage. (291)
Thus concludes the section concerning the manifestation upon reaching [the state of Brahman].
The Section on Being Seen as Non-Differentiated.
Because it is seen as non-distinct.
In this [chapter], the manner in which the experience of the perfect Lord occurs for the individual soul (jīva) when its true nature has manifested in the highest abode is contemplated. (282)
Is the liberated one experienced as separate from Brahman, or rather as non-different from it by being a mode (prakāra) of it? Such is the doubt. (283)
"He attains [that]"—thus it is stated in the Upaniṣads beginning with "When he sees," and in the Smṛti as well, this knowledge [is attained] by the liberated one through the Supreme Self. (284)
The statement that "one experiences [the self] as distinct from the body due to the designation of similarity, equality, and commonality with the Lord of Literature" is not correct.
He experiences his own self as non-different from Brahman, because he perceives his own self, freed from limiting adjuncts, exactly as it truly is. || 286 ||
Through such statements as "That thou art," "This Self," "All this has that as its essence," and "He who [is] in the Self," [the world] is always of the nature of the Supreme Self. (287)
That it is the mode of the inner self (pratyagātman) by virtue of being its body has been established many times previously as its very nature (svarūpa). || 288 ||
Therefore, one always experiences the Lord as "I am Brahman";
this statement regarding equality and shared attributes refers to the liberated inner self (pratyagātman). (289)
It declares that the liberated soul's own nature is equal to Brahman, and likewise, scripture speaks of its union with Brahman as the manifestor.
There is no contradiction whatsoever in saying that he speaks of the experience of those qualities;
therefore, being liberated, he experiences his own self as non-different from Brahman. (291)
Thus concludes the section concerning the perception [of Brahman] as non-differentiated.
The Section on Brahman.
Jaimini [holds that the soul is] of the size of the body, on account of the introductory statements and so forth.

The manifestation of one's true nature has been described; now that true nature is investigated: Is the essential nature of the individual soul (jīvātman) endowed with the eight qualities, or is it otherwise? (292)

When there is doubt as to whether [the Self] is mere consciousness or both [consciousness and form], it is [described] as being connected with Brahman and endowed with qualities such as freedom from sin. (293)
Jaimini states that [the qualities] manifest through introductory statements and the like;
for those qualities which are heard in the Dahara-vidyā passage as being connected with Brahman [are indeed such]. (294)
These [attributes] are presented here in this statement of Prajāpati concerning the individual soul (jīva);
by the words "at the beginning" and "there," the mention of eating and so forth is expressed. (295)
Therefore, it is his view that the individual soul (jīva) does not have knowledge as its essential nature;
for [the soul] consists of that [knowledge], because it is of the nature of pure consciousness (cit), according to Auḍulomi.
Consciousness alone is his form; by that very [consciousness] he manifests.
And Auḍulomi also maintains that [the self] consists of only that much, based on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad passage beginning with "Just as a lump of salt... (3.2.13). || 297 ||
From the restrictive statement "a mere mass of consciousness," it is understood that its essential nature consists of consciousness alone. (298)
The words such as "freedom from evil" (hatapāpmatva) are intended to signify the absence of modification;
here, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states his own established doctrine.
Even so, because of such a presentation and because [the soul] exists previously, Bādarāyaṇa maintains that there is no contradiction.

Even though this [Self] is of the nature of consciousness, by the force of the statement regarding the eight qualities, the existence of those eight qualities is necessarily required; thus, there is a mutual [relationship] between the two.

There can be no sublation of the two [propositions]: "being of the nature of consciousness" and "being endowed with the eight qualities," for it is not logical for things established by equal means of valid cognition to sublate one another. (301)
In the scriptural passage "a mere mass of consciousness," there is an emphasis;
the entire Self is eternally distinct from the insentient and is self-luminous. (302)
"Even though its location is very small, its light does not depend on anything else"—this meaning is expressed here by the very sentence of the illustration; thus it is understood.
For when a piece of salt is known by the tongue as having a single taste, its color, hardness, and so forth, which are known by the eye and other senses, are not contradicted. (304)

And just as, even when there is a difference in taste, fruits and the like may possess a uniform flavor throughout due to their particular state, so too in that solid mass of rock-salt (saindhava), there is a richness of a single flavor everywhere.
Likewise, the self also has the nature of pure consciousness everywhere.
Therefore, it is established that manifestation occurs in both forms. || 306 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning Brahmā.
The Section on Volitional Resolve (Saṅkalpādhikaraṇa)
Because it is stated that [the creation] occurs from mere volition alone.
The manifestation of the eight qualities was previously described regarding the liberated soul; here, however, the final one—the quality of having true resolve—is considered. (307)
The passage beginning with "he seeks there" and so forth is recited with reference to liberation;
in that context, is the attainment of kinsmen and the like said to be accompanied by further effort? (308)

Or [is it] by mere volition alone, as in the case of another? When such a doubt arises—given that even kings, who possess the renown of being able to will things into existence, achieve their desired objects [only through effort]— [the answer follows].
If it is argued that, because effort is observed in the world, the same must apply even to one who is liberated, we say:
not so; for such a person’s attainment of that state is accomplished by mere volition alone. (310)

In this context, from the statement beginning with "merely by his resolve" (*saṅkalpād evāsya*), and because of the restrictive particle *eva* used here, it is indeed established that there is no dependence on anything else. (311)
Indeed, no scriptural passage is seen here that asserts dependence upon effort, by which a restriction of the particle "eva" could be stated here as well, as was done previously. (312)
And for this very reason, he has no other superior.
Since he whose wish is unfailing is liberated, he is therefore the sovereign over others;
and his state of being the sovereign over none else consists in his independence from karma.

Furthermore, it is taught that for this liberated one, "he becomes his own lord" (svarāṭ), meaning he possesses the state of being his own lord, which consists in freedom from the power of karma. || 314 ||
Thus concludes the section on the resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
The Section on Non-existence (Abhāvādhikaraṇa)
Bādari says that [the soul] becomes non-existent, for thus [the scripture] declares.
It has been stated that for one who is liberated, the creation of ancestors and so forth arises from mere volition (saṅkalpa);
here, a specific detail regarding that volition is being described.
Regarding the liberated one, does the body, the senses, and so forth exist, or do they not?
When this doubt arises as to whether they exist according to his will or do not exist at all— || 316 ||
The teacher Bādari maintains that for the liberated one there is an absence of the body and so forth;
for there is the Śruti beginning with, "For indeed, while he is possessed of a body... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1).
Having stated that suffering is unavoidable when joined with a body, [the scripture] declares the bodiless state of the liberated one by saying, "from this body. (318)
Jaimini [maintains that the soul] possesses conscious being, because of the teaching of its alternative states.

The teacher Jaimini maintains that there is the actual existence of the body and the senses; due to the contemplation of its various conceptualizations, this [self] becomes onefold or threefold. (319)
Indeed, various modes such as "fivefold" or "sevenfold" are heard in scripture;
however, multiplicity of nature is not possible for that which has the indivisible self as its essence. (320)
Therefore, it is certain that the multiplicity of elements resides within that body;
as for the statement regarding bodilessness, its purpose is directed toward the absence of [a material] body.
Therefore, Bādarāyaṇa holds that it is of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice.
Bādarāyaṇa maintains that he is considered liberated by mere resolve, being both embodied and yet bodiless, like the sacrifice known as the Dvādaśāha.
Just as it becomes twofold according to the injunctions for sacrifice and initiation— namely, the *sattra* and the *ahīna* through the distinction of resolve (*saṅkalpa*)— so too is it here.
When the collection of causes such as the body exists, then that [creation] is produced by the Self alone;
it is stated in the subsequent sūtra that there is no such restrictive rule. 324.
In the absence of a body, [the existence of the soul] is established as in the case of the twilight.
Since the experience of enjoyment is possible through that body and so forth created by the Supreme Self itself, He does not create them Himself.

Even though his volition is true, it is just as in a dream, by means of those instruments of enjoyment created by the Supreme Self, as described in such passages as "Then [he creates] chariots... and so forth.

Just as one who is bound enjoys [the fruits of action], so too does the liberated one enjoy, by his own will, through those various worlds such as the realm of the ancestors created by the Lord for His own sport; he himself experiences the essence of that divine play.
In the state of existence, it is like the waking state.
When the objects such as the body created by his own volition exist, the liberated one himself enjoys the flavor of divine play, just like the enjoyment of a man in the waking state. (328)

Just as the Lord himself, having created Daśaratha and others, enjoys [the fruits of their actions], so too he sometimes creates the fathers and other ancestors of the liberated ones out of his own playful spontaneity (līlayā). 329.
Indeed, those who are already liberated sometimes, by their own will as masters, create worlds such as their own fathers, all of which are included within His divine play (līlā). || 330 ||
Now, the conceit of selfhood of the atomic individual soul (jīva) enters into multiple bodies like a lamp; for scripture shows it thus.
Just as a lamp, while remaining in one place, [illuminates] by virtue of its own radiance; || 331 ||
Just as there may be possession by many spirits for one whose self is situated in a single place,
so too there is possession of all bodies by the consciousness that has become one's own radiance.
And just as, even within a single body, the self-identification with the Self is observed in all limbs through the pervasion of consciousness by the Self residing in the region of the heart. (333)
In the same way, this scripture beginning with "on the tip of a hair" (vālāgra) demonstrates [the subtle nature of the self];
and the scripture stating "by the conscious Self" (prājñena ātmanā) demonstrates the voidness of both external and internal cognition. // 334 //
Regarding the question, "How can there be omniscience for one who is liberated?", it is stated here:
"It is manifested in relation to either deep sleep or union [with Brahman], for it has been revealed [in scripture]."
That statement refers to either deep sleep or death, but not [to liberation]. || 335 ||
Indeed, this subject of the liberated self has been revealed by the Śruti itself;
for the Śruti says: "I am indeed not these elements," and so forth. (336)

For one who asserts that this [Self] is like deep sleep or death due to its lack of awakening, [the scripture] states "He sees everything" and so forth, declaring omniscience in the state of liberation. (337)
Therefore, the statement "by one who is wise" cannot refer to one who is already liberated;
consequently, the liberated one must possess a body, though at times he may also be bodiless.
Thus ends the section concerning non-existence.
The Section Concerning the Exclusion of the Worldly Activity [of the Lord] (Jagadvyāpāravarjādhikaraṇa).
[The Lord is] exempt from the activity of governing the world, because of the context and because of His non-proximity [to it].
It was previously stated here that for one who is liberated, the creation of the body and so forth within the experience of the supreme Brahman occurs through mere volition alone. || 339 ||
Even though he desires the truth, it is said that he does not possess the status of creator of the world;
nor does he possess universal sovereignty here—what then could be called liberated lordship? (340)
Alternatively, if there is doubt as to whether this is indeed the experience of the Supreme Self,
[the answer is found] in the Śruti, because of the statement regarding the supreme equality of the liberated one with the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, because of the mention of "the state of having true resolve," there is also lordship over the universe;
if this were not the case, the meaning of the Śruti would not be tenable. (342)

Let it not be so; for this [state] is one from which sovereignty has been released and which is devoid of worldly activity, since the supreme [state] is described as being characterized by the very nature of the creation of the world and so forth. (343)
Furthermore, because the individual soul (jīva) is not the subject under discussion, in all instances where the creation and so forth are described—
such as "from which beings are born," "Being alone," or "Brahman indeed was this"— [the Supreme Self is intended].
In many Śrutis, it is clearly stated that "Nārāyaṇa alone" is indeed Brahman, whose very nature is the governance of the universe. (345)
In every such context, there is no proximity of the liberated one;
therefore, it is established that the sovereignty of the liberated consists in being devoid of the activity of creating the world. (346)
If it be argued that [the soul's ascent] is due to direct scriptural instruction, we say no, because the statement refers to one who occupies the circle of authority.

If it is argued that his engagement in the activity of the world is taught by such scriptural passages as "He became the Lord of all sounds" (*sa svarāḍ abhavat*), we reply: no, for this does not apply to those who hold offices such as that of Dhātṛ and others. (347)
For it is not heard here in this teaching that there is the enjoyment of worldly pleasures for those who abide in the worlds;
rather, [it concerns] all the enjoyments of the Supreme Self for those who abide in the worlds of office. (348)
The meaning is that he enjoys those things which have become his manifestations (vibhūti);
for indeed, if he were to enjoy the experiences existing within the modifications (vikāra) like one who is bound, that would be the case. (349)
In that case, it would follow that the object of experience is both small and finite; this is addressed here:
"And it does not abide in its transformations, for thus it declares its state."
That Brahman has all modifications destroyed and possesses all sovereign powers.
The liberated one experiences the single-mindedly auspicious state of these supreme selves;
for the worlds, being included within his sovereign power, constitute the objects of enjoyment for the liberated.
For the scripture beginning with "When indeed he [sees] himself in that" declares his abiding as the enjoyer within the changeless, supreme Brahman. (352)
And thus, perception and inference have been demonstrated.
The governance of the creation, maintenance, and so forth of the entire world belongs to the Supreme alone;
for the liberated one, however, there is only the direct experience of the Supreme Self. (353)
The Śruti and Smṛti both demonstrate this: first, the Śruti passage beginning with "From fear of Him the wind blows" and "Of this very Imperishable," and then the Smṛti. (354)
"I pervade this entire universe"—thus they have stated at the beginning and likewise here that the Supreme alone is the cause of bliss for the liberated one. (355)
For it is clear to you that "this very one indeed causes bliss," and "me as well";
therefore, there is supreme equality as well as the power of true resolve. (356)
It is established that the liberated soul is indeed excluded from the activity of the world;
and this is because of the scriptural indication of equality only in respect to experience.
"He enjoys all desires while liberated," so it is stated in the Yajurvedic Śruti.

Because of the statement regarding his equality with that [Brahmā] in respect to the mere experience of enjoyment known as the realization of Brahman, and because of the indicative mark (liṅga), it is understood that the liberated one possesses sovereignty, excluding only those effects [of the world] belonging to that [creator]. (358)
If liberation from sovereignty were dependent on another, then the Supreme Person, being independent, could by His own will cause even one who is liberated to return [to bondage] once again. (359)
The resolution of this doubt—"perhaps"—is stated here:
"Non-return, on account of the scriptural word; non-return, on account of the scriptural word."
The non-return of the liberated one is understood from the scripture itself. || 360 ||

Just as it is understood through the means of valid cognition known as verbal testimony that the Supreme Self exists, endowed with all attributes and being the cause of the birth and so forth of the world. (361)
Likewise, being well-pleased by their worship, he himself, having dispelled the ignorance of those who worship him, [bestows] bliss consisting of his own direct experience.
It is understood by that very [text] that "having caused [the soul] to reach [Brahman], it does not cause it to return";
and likewise, the passage beginning with "he, indeed, conducting himself thus," and so forth, conveys the same. (363)
And for him who experiences the Brahman from which all excellence has departed, the words of the Blessed One—"Having attained Me, there is no rebirth," and so forth—[are fulfilled]. (364)
For one whose bonds of karma have been severed, there can be no return by his own will;
moreover, the Supreme Lord possesses the power of true resolve and is exceedingly dear to the Self.
Having found one who is liberated and possessed of knowledge, he shall never return;
for in the Śrī Gītā, He Himself has indeed said, "He is dear to Me. (366)
Therefore, it is established that there is no return for him in any manner whatsoever.
The repetition of the sūtra indicates the completion of the treatise. (367)
Thus, having respectfully written down these matters taught by my teacher, may the wise forgive any defects in word or meaning, as well as my audacity. (368)
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
And the treatise is completed.
Furthermore, this glorious and sinless one, whose body is the entire universe,
has expounded his own doctrine through both the Sūtras and the words of the Mahābhārata— namely, that devotion (bhakti) and renunciation (nyāsa) are the means, and the attainment of Him is the fruit.
May Viṣṇu Vyāsa dwell eternally within my mind. || 369 ||
Formerly, Hari, assuming the form of a woman and offering nectar as a means for the gods to enjoy it for a long time, dispelled the dissatisfaction that had arisen in their minds; then,
becoming a preceptor and attaining the highest stage of life (uttamāśrama), [he taught] that which arises from the ocean of the Vedas.
I worship that Lord of Ascetics who bestowed the nectar of the Bhāṣya upon the earthly gods (brahmins) for the sake of liberation. || 370 ||
Beholding the Vedic knowledge— expounded through the stages of ritual placement (nyāsa), honored by the best of the Raghus and Yadus, yet afflicted by the Daitya Kali— the Lord of Gurus,
who dwells on the mountain of the elephant [Girivraja], assumed the form of that supreme pair [Rāma and Kṛṣṇa] and, with his wondrous arrows in the form of scriptures, [defeated him].
Having conquered him on earth, he protected that land; I take refuge in that Śrutavantasūri. || 371 ||
The compassionate one, by granting me— the ignorant one who was like a mere stone— contact with the dust of his lotus feet,
has rendered me free from the ocean of manifold misfortunes and worthy of the highest bliss.
I worship that supreme Lord of the Raghus, the noble descendant of Raghu. || 372 ||
In the Kali age, when the [number of] seasons, arrows, and sky-arrows have passed, this work composed by Śrīvāsakṛti was created; may it endure as long as the moon and stars exist. 373.
Thus ends the *Śrī-Śārīraka-Kārikāvalī*.
Salutations to the venerable Rāghavārya Mahādeśika.
Salutations to the venerable Śrī Vedānta Rāmānuja Mahādeśika.
Salutations to the great teacher Śrī Raṅgarāmānuja.
Salutation to our lineage of gurus.
Salutations to the Supreme Brahman, the Sovereign Lord of Gods, accompanied by the illustrious Mahādevī as his consort.
May there be prosperity.
The Section Concerning Those Whose Effects Have Not Yet Begun.
But the former [karmas] indeed have their effects not yet begun, for that is their limit.

It is stated therein that prior to the arising of knowledge, there is the destruction of previously performed meritorious and non-meritorious karma; for no specific distinction is heard regarding this in the case of the [two] attainments.
In this context, the claim that "there is the destruction of all karmas" is refuted:
does it mean the total destruction of both prior merit and sin? (69)

Regarding the doubt as to whether [only] those two types of karma that have not yet begun to yield their fruit [are destroyed], since no specific distinction is heard in the scripture stating that "all [karmas] are exhausted," [the view is that all are destroyed]. (70)
If it is argued that there is a total destruction of those two karmas, we say no;
for it is only the karmas that have failed to set forth toward the yielding of their fruit that perish. (71)
But that karma which has already begun does not cease for him until the end, because it is heard in the Śruti that there is a delay lasting until the liberation from the body. (72)
And because the maintenance of the body is impossible once all karma has been destroyed, therefore the destruction of merit and demerit whose fruits have not yet begun occurs. (73)
Thus concludes the section concerning those [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun. Next is the section concerning the Agnihotra and other such rites.
But the Agnihotra and other such rites are for that very purpose [of liberation], because it is so seen in scripture.
It was stated previously that there is no connection between prior knowledge and subsequent merits;
therefore, when there is an absence of desire for the fruits of meritorious deeds, [there is no connection] with obligatory duties (nityakarman).

In this context, the doubt that [the duties] are not to be performed is warded off by the fact that the Agnihotra and other duties of the stages of life (āśrama) are equal in their merit. It is not tenable to say that those [worldly actions] are "not to be done" simply because they do not adhere to what ought to be done.
This ritual action, such as the Agnihotra and others, consists of both obligatory and occasional duties.
This [observance] must be performed daily solely for the sake of the effect known as the arising of knowledge (vidyotpatti), because it is seen in the Veda that its purpose is that very effect. (77)
For if one abandons that [practice], the arising of knowledge will not be accomplished for one whose self is thus defiled;
indeed, that knowledge must be repeated day after day as long as one lives. (78)
And this meaning is indeed expressed by the words "conducting himself thus";
therefore, for the sake of the arising of knowledge, that duty of the stage of life (āśrama-karman) must certainly be performed.
If those rites such as the Agnihotra have knowledge as their fruit, then even previously accumulated merit is exhausted through that enjoyment. (80)

What could possibly be the subject of the statement, "The good deeds of a friend," if it refers to what remains after being experienced or to that which has already begun to bear fruit? This is what is being addressed here. (81)
For some, moreover, there is another [form] for both.
For even the performance of good deeds and other such acts belonging to the stages of life, such as the Agnihotra,
prior to the attainment of knowledge, [contribute] to both of the two subsequent meritorious actions.
The fruit of powerful karma being obstructed, that meritorious deed performed with desire may become infinite; such is the meaning of the scriptural statement regarding that subject.
According to some reciters of the Vedic branches, his sons [inherit] the legacy;
likewise, the statement regarding the destruction of attachment through knowledge refers specifically to that same subject.
Since there is the possibility that even a performed action may have its fruit obstructed,
he reminds us here of what was stated previously in the sūtra beginning with "yad eva" (BrSū 3.4.26).
For it is said, "By knowledge alone," and indeed,
the fruit of the meditation on the Udgītha thus described is the prevention of obstacles to the swift production of the fruit of the sacrifice. (86)
For one whose merit has been obstructed by [worldly] attachment, the attainment of the stages [of yoga] is impossible;
therefore, those duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma) must be performed with reverence by the wise man. 87.
Thus concludes the section concerning the Agnihotra and other rites.
The Section on the Destruction of Other [Defilements].
But having exhausted the others through experience, he then attains [liberation].

Previously, the destruction of merit and demerit that have not yet begun to produce their effects was described; here, the specific manner of the destruction of those that have already begun to produce their effects is demonstrated. (88)
When [the karma] has begun to yield its fruit, do merit and demerit perish?
Or is there no fixed rule regarding this at the conclusion of the body born of knowledge or the body born of the womb? (89)

When the doubt arises here as to whether [the attainment occurs] at the end of that body or at the end of another body, [it is resolved] by the scriptural text "For him, so long... regarding the worshiper who has attained Brahman. (90)
If it is argued that there is no such thing because scripture teaches only a delay lasting until the fall of that body, and that its destruction occurs at the end of that body, we say: no. (91)
If [the karma] were to perish through experience alone while engaged in the granting of its fruit, then Brahman would be attained; for the destruction of those two is impossible. (92)

Without the enjoyment of the fruit, there is the experience of the fruits of those two [karmas] whose results have already begun from within a single body; this is because of the rule that [the experience occurs] by means of whichever physical frame [is currently occupied]. (93)
The enjoyment of the fruit would come to an end, and at its conclusion, there would be the destruction of these two;
for his liberation from karma is intended by that much alone. (94)
Therefore, there is no fixed rule regarding the destruction of those two [karmas] whose fruits have already begun;
likewise, that which was previously performed but has not yet begun to bear fruit remains unexhausted.
That [karma] is infinite, accumulated since beginningless time, and it is of two kinds;
that which was performed immediately before ceases through the power of knowledge (vidyā). || 96 ||
But a faulty act committed through negligence does not adhere to you;
rather, his merit is lost, and his sin is shared with both friend and foe. (97)
"I shall not grant the fruit of merit or evil deeds to this person"—such is the intention of another; by that, the destruction of those two [the merit and the evil] is declared. (98)
Moreover, for this wise one, there is the transfer of merit to his friend and the transfer of the fruit of sin to his enemy;
[he gives] the fruit of merit to his servant and the fruit of sin to that very enemy. (99)
Thus, the conceptualization of self and other resides within the body of the yogi;
here, in this quarter, the fruit arising from the majesty of knowledge is considered. (100)
Thus ends the section concerning the destruction of other [defilements].
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter.
The Second Quarter of the Fourth Chapter.
The Section on Speech.
Speech [is merged] in the mind, because it is so seen and because of scripture.
In the preceding section, the fruit of knowledge for the wise person who has performed meditation was declared to consist in the destruction of both merit and demerit. (101)

In this chapter, the entry into the channels (nāḍī) of the dying man who possesses knowledge—which constitutes the beginning of the path to the world of liberation—is described as the fruit of that knowledge. 102.
First, the manner of departure from the body is explained;
for it is recorded in scripture here that "speech merges into the mind. (103)
When it is argued that the nature of speech is accomplished within the mind,
or alternatively, that it is merely a function of speech— such being the doubt here [arising]— 104.
The dissolution of the organ of speech into the mind is not being propounded here;
for this organ, moreover, does not have the mind as its cause. (105)
To say that the activity of speech dissolves into the mind is incorrect;
rather, it is taught that the organ of speech is indeed joined with the mind. (106)
For even when this faculty of speech is stilled, the activity of the mind is observed;
moreover, sound is perceived only when the nature of speech is fully present. (107)
Since there is no dissolution in the absence of a cause, the term "attainment" (saṃpatti) here indeed refers to the state of union; it does not signify dissolution, as that is impossible. || 108 ||
For this very reason, all [the following rules] apply accordingly.
Since at that time there is merely a conjunction with the mind and not a dissolution of speech, for this very reason all the other sense organs also follow after speech. (109)
Therefore, the scriptural passage beginning with "they merge in the heart" (hṛdi saṃpadyante) is appropriate; for indeed, the dissolution of all the sense organs does not occur in the heart.
Thus concludes the section concerning speech.
The section on the mind.
That mind is the vital breath, according to the subsequent [scriptural] passage.
The mind, joined with all the senses, becomes united with the vital breath (prāṇa), according to the statement in the Sāman [Upaniṣad]: "And from the mind comes the vital breath. (111)
"O gentle one, the mind consists of food," according to such scriptural statements, because [the mind] has as its material cause food, which itself has the earth as its primal source. || 112 ||

Because the scripture states that "the vital breath consists of water," the mind has water as its material cause through the medium of earth; thus, it resides within the waters that serve as the constituent material (upādāna) of the vital breath.
In this regard, there may be the doubt that "dissolution would occur"; the resolution of that very doubt is as follows:
it is taught that the vital breath (prāṇa) is nourished by the mind being nourished by food. || 114 ||
And here, "nourishment" (āpyāyana) consists in the production of functional capacity;
it is not stated here that the mind and the vital breath are modifications of food and water. (115)
For mind and breath are indeed modifications of the ego and space;
therefore, the conjunction of mind with breath is sanctioned by scripture. (116)
Thus ends the section concerning the mind.
The Section on Supervisors.

The vital breath (prāṇa) is joined either with fire (tejas) or with the individual soul (jīva); regarding this, there is doubt. If it is argued that it is joined with fire alone because of the scriptural statement "the breath [is joined] with fire," that is not so.

The departure of the vital breath (prāṇa) is logically possible only with respect to the individual self (jīvātman), who is the presiding lord of the organs; for here, scripture declares that at the time of departure, the breath follows after that self.

In the same way, there is the acceptance [of the teaching] that "the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after [the self]," as well as the previously mentioned departure and the foundation [of the self], namely, the question of "in whom does it depart? (119).
"Having joined with the individual soul (jīva), that [soul] joined with prāṇa is then joined with fire (tejas)";
thus the Śruti declares, "prāṇa is joined in fire," and so forth. (120)
Just as it is correct to say that "the Yamunā goes to the ocean" even when she has already joined with the Gaṅgā on her way to the sea, so too is it the case here.
Thus ends the section concerning direct perception.
The Section on the Elements (Bhūtādhikaraṇa)
Regarding the departure of the vital breath (prāṇa) endowed with the individual soul (jīva) from the elements, its merging into fire has been taught;
yet, when there is doubt as to whether it merges into fire alone or into the elements that have already merged [into fire], [the following is stated].
The statement that [the self] is in fire alone because of the scriptural mention of "mere light" is not correct;
rather, it is appropriate that [the self] is in the elements, because of scriptural passages such as "consisting of earth. (123)
For it is said that the individual soul, as it migrates, consists of all beings; this is so even when it attains dissolution sequentially into each element, such as fire and the rest. (124)
It is now stated here how the cited scripture may be rendered consistent with reason. || 125 ||
For [the Lord] does not manifest [Himself] in only one [place].
Because each individual element is incapable of performing its function within the fire alone.
Neither is it joined [to the body], for the Śruti and Smṛti clearly demonstrate its incapacity for action;
the Śruti declares that these [elements] are each threefold, indeed threefold.
From this, the traditional teaching (smṛti) arises that [the elements] come together in mutual conjunction;
therefore, the threefold fire (trivṛtkṛtaṃ tejaḥ) is joined precisely within the gross elements (bhūta). || 127 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the elements.
The Section Concerning the Commencement with the Soma-Pressing (Āsuti).
And there is equality [of attainment] from the commencement of the path until the reaching of immortality, without having burned away [the subtle body].
Regarding the doubt as to whether this departure is the same for both the knower and the other, or belongs only to the ignorant one—it is indeed for the knower here. (128)

If it is argued that because immortality is heard in the passage, "When all are completely released," there is no departure [of the self] for anyone other than the ignorant one, we say: no, that is not so.
Because it occurs through an approach [to the heart], this departure is the same even for the man of knowledge;
for his exit is by way of the channels, though some say there are a hundred. (130)
From such Vedic statements as "When all are completely liberated," it is understood that [liberation] is attained even without having burnt away the connection with the body and the senses. (131)
Indeed, that which is called immortality consists of the destruction of attachment;
