in this context, the statement regarding the attainment of Brahman refers specifically to the time of meditation. (132)
Even in that state, there is the designation of "saṃsāra" because of its continued existence.
And that immortality is established as having the very nature previously described, because until the state of attaining Brahman is reached, it is designated as saṃsāra. (133)
Having traveled by way of the path of light (arcirmārga) to that extraordinary realm,
as long as Brahman has not been attained, so long does the cycle of existence known as embodiment persist.
The duration of that [state] is taught by such expressions as "for so long" and so forth. || 135 ||
And it is subtle by measure, because it is perceived as such.
For the subtle body of this wise one follows after [the soul].
Therefore, bondage is not burnt here; likewise, it is grasped by means of pride, by the path of the gods, by the words of conversation, and by the moon. 136.
Because [the self] is perceived as possessing a subtle body through such statements as "depending on that," it therefore persists;
thus, bondage has certainly not been burnt away here.
Not by crushing.
Therefore, all desires are liberated for him of whom this is the authoritative Vedic revelation;
for it declares immortality through the destruction of his bondage.
And from this very same reasoning, heat [is also established].
Because of the logical proof for the existence of the subtle body somewhere, heat is perceived in some part of the gross body of the wise person before death. (139)
Nor does this [heat] belong to the gross body, because it is not perceived elsewhere;
therefore, that perception of heat is based on its departure (utkrānti).

If it be argued that there is no departure from the body even for the wise, because of the denial [of such a path] following the sequence of going and coming, we say: no, for in some [scriptural texts] it is clearly stated [to be from the body].
Furthermore, the statement that the departure [of the soul] is the same for the wise person is not tenable.

In the Śruti, because of the prohibition of departure with the words "his vital breaths [do not depart]," it is not the case that the non-separation of the vital breaths from the individual soul (jīva) is being stated here. || 142 ||
In this context, it is not the departure of the vital breaths from the body that is being negated; rather, for one who does not desire, the prāṇas do not depart from the self of the meditator. (143)
For they do not depart, since they remain together for the purpose of traveling the path beginning with light;
moreover, in the Śruti, it is stated that the soul alone is the point of departure (the apādāna) from the body. 144.

According to the clear statement of the Mādhyandinas, "But he does not depart from there," the vital breaths (prāṇas) of the meditator who attains Brahman do not become separated [from the body]. 145.
And it is recorded in tradition.
The departure through the central channel (mūrdhanya-nāḍī) is recorded even for the wise, clearly stated in such passages as:
"Of them, one stands above, having pierced [the head]," and so forth. (146)
Thus ends the section concerning the commencement of rebirth.
The section on the excellence of others.
Others say that these are indeed so; for thus it has been said:

Do the subtle elements, joined with the multitude of sense organs, the vital breaths, and the individual soul, proceed toward their respective functions according to their karma and according to their knowledge? (147)
When it is argued that they are joined with the Supreme Self, this doubt arises:
because the experience of pleasure and so forth is not observed in the interval [between death and rebirth] within the Supreme Self. (148)
If it is argued that they depart without being joined [to subtle elements] according to their karma, that is not so;
for such subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) become united with the Supreme Self. 149.

For the Śruti declares, "The splendor of the Supreme," and according to that Śruti, the effect [of consciousness] is to be conceived as resting through union with Brahman during deep sleep and other such states. (150)
Just as it is there, so it should be here as well: the Lord is the place of rest.
Therefore, it is established that the subtle elements of the beings merge into the heart. (151)
Thus ends the section concerning the excellence of others.
The Section on Non-Differentiation (Avibhāgādhikaraṇa).
There is no division, because of the scriptural statement.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether this attainment within the Heart (hārda) consists of dissolution into the material cause (upādāna), or rather takes the form of non-differentiation from the Supreme Self (paramātman): 152.

If it is argued that because [the Self] is the cause and because of the statement regarding attainment, there is indeed an "attainment of the cause" in the Supreme Self—this is not so, because of the passage beginning with "speech and mind. (153)

Because the term "attainment" (saṃpatti) must be supplied everywhere through grammatical connection (anuṣaṅga), and because it is impossible for there to be a discrepancy in expression when something has not been explicitly stated. || 154 ||
In this case as well, non-separation alone is the logical meaning; therefore, at that time, the attainment of the heart's fulfillment is said to be solely for the rest of one who is exhausted. (155)
Thus concludes the section on non-differentiation.
The Section on the Abode of That [Brahman].

Then, there is the blazing of the highest flame; with its door illuminated, [the soul] proceeds by the power of knowledge (vidyā) and through the application of recollection of the path which is the remainder of that [knowledge], being favored by the one dwelling in the heart, by means of the channel that exceeds the hundred.
Thus, the departure [of the soul] has been described as equal for both the wise and the ignorant;
however, the distinction here regarding that [departure] belonging to the wise is said to depend upon knowledge. (156)
Just as the word "one hundred and one" was heard in the Vedic statement, so too the departure of the knower occurs through that very channel which is superior to the hundred channels. || 157 ||

Regarding the doubt as to whether this restriction—that for one who is ignorant [of the true nature of things], [the cognition] must be of something else—is appropriate here or not, that restriction is not tenable. (158)
Because the channels are extremely subtle, they are very difficult to distinguish; moreover, because they are so numerous, it is impossible for a person to grasp them all. (159)

If it is argued that the statement "a hundred and one" merely restates a spontaneous departure [of the soul], it is not so; for [that departure occurs] due to the worship performed while residing in the heart. (160)
And through the power of knowledge and by contemplating the movement of its limbs, he is instantly favored with heartfelt affection by the pleased [deity]. (161)
Then his heart becomes its primary locus, as if illuminated;
thus, with the gateway revealed by the Supreme Self through the heart, [he perceives]. 162.
The wise one himself departs through a channel exceeding a hundred [in number];
it is clear in the Taittirīya and other texts that Nārāyaṇa is within the heart.
Thus concludes the section concerning that abode.
The Section on Following the Capacity for Assimilation (Naśmyanusārādhikaraṇa)
Following the rays.
Now, by the statement "by these very [rays]," it is declared that the knower proceeds to the upper region only by following the rays of the sun. (164)
Is this restriction applicable, or not? Regarding this doubt, [the answer is] "no," because for a learned person who dies at night, it is impossible to reach the rays [of the sun]. (165)
A restrictive rule regarding that matter is not appropriate, for the statement refers to what is applicable to one side [of the argument].
It is not the case that the knower of Brahman goes upward at that time solely by following the rays. (166)

Since the restriction "only by these" implies that [the other causes] are merely occasional, the restriction would be redundant; for even at night, the sun's path could still be traced by its heat-marks.
For even at night during the summer, the existence of rays is indeed perceived due to the attainment of heat;
whereas in winter, because of the abundance of snow, the heat is not properly apprehended. || 168 ||

For the constant connection between the channels (nāḍīs) and the rays (kiraṇas) is indeed heard [in scripture]; therefore, by following those very rays, the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. 169.
Thus ends the section concerning the following of the rays.
The Section on Nighttime.

If it is argued that [the journey] does not take place at night, we say no; for the connection [between the soul and the path] persists as long as the body exists, and scripture shows that the attainment of Brahman occurs even for the knower who dies at night.
Regarding the inquiry as to whether this is so or not, the Smṛti states, "By day or by night," and so forth. (170)
If it is argued that because death at night is censured and because it is a cause for falling to lower states,
one who dies at night cannot attain Brahman— that is not so.
Since the connection with karma persists as long as the body exists, the attainment of Brahman is indeed established for those actions preceded by knowledge. (172)

Because [the sins] are destroyed by the commencement of knowledge, because there is no connection with future sins, and because karma whose effects have already begun persists until the end of the final body. (173)
There is no doubt that through the absence of the cause of bondage, one attains Brahman;
"only so long is there delay until one is liberated," so says the Śruti. (174)
For the statement beginning with "and by day" demonstrates this very point;
thus, everything here is perfectly consistent when understood as referring exclusively to those who are ignorant. (175)
Thus concludes the section concerning the night.
The section concerning the southern solstice.
And for this reason, [the same applies] even during the southern course of the sun.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether or not there is attainment of the Lord for the wise one who departs during the southern solstice, the Śruti states: "Now, he who [departs] by the southern [path]..."

Because it is stated that others attain union with the Moon upon his death, and because it is observed that one who has attained that [state] returns again according to the teaching "this very same path. (177)

If it is argued that because we observe Bhīṣma and others waiting for the month of Udaṅ (the northern solstice), one who has departed during the *apara-ayana* (southern solstice) does not attain Brahman— that is not so.
For this reason, it is stated that even one who has died at night attains the Lord;
for that very reason, due to the absence of the cause of bondage, he [attains Him] during the northern course of the sun.
Even for one who has died, the attainment of the Supreme Brahman occurs at that very moment;
the statement regarding his union with the Moon is intended merely as a point of rest.
The statement regarding returning would pertain to the domain of the ignorant;
furthermore, the attainment of the glory of Brahman is declared in the remainder of this very passage. (181)
The waiting for the month of Māgha by Bhīṣma and others was indeed for the purpose of awakening the excellence of that specific time for those who attain death at will through the power of yoga.

And for the sake of setting forth the Dharma, there is therefore a connection with the meaning already stated; for it is recorded in the Smṛti: "At what time [one attains] non-return, and at what time return... (183).
A specific time is indeed prescribed for those who are about to die;
therefore, it is explained here how the aforementioned purpose is rendered consistent.
These two are recorded in the Smṛti as pertaining to yogins, and they are indeed based on the Smṛti.
Both that path which leads to the gods and that path which leads to the ancestors must be remembered daily as constituent parts of yoga. (185)
Indeed, for those intent on yoga, these two [rites] are prescribed; death is not remembered here [as a factor].
For one about to die, however, a specific time is prescribed, as it is feared below [that death might occur prematurely]. (186)
"O Pārtha, one who knows these two paths [does not return]"—this is the conclusion here.
Because of the predominance of those who identify with Time (Kāla), it is said "wherein Time [prevails]. (187)
And therefore, even at night, the wise man who has departed through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) on the right side,
having grasped the rays of the sun, goes upward and reaches Brahman.
Thus concludes the section concerning the southern course [of the sun].
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter.
